grammar.t: My vs mine: possessive adjective vs possessive pronoun
grammar.x: My vs mine: possessive adjective vs possessive pronoun · A possessive adjective (my, our, your, his, her, its, their) always needs a noun right after it: my book, their offer . · A possessive pronoun (mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs) replaces the whole “adjective + noun”, so no noun comes after it: This book is mine (= my book). · When the subject is “You and X”, the possessive is your ; when it is “You and I” or “He and I”, it is our . The first person decides. · Form · I · We · You · He / She / It · They · Adjective (noun follows) · my · our · your · his / her / its · their · Pronoun (stands alone) · mine · ours · yours · his / hers · theirs · Look right after the word. A noun there → my / your / our / their. Nothing there → mine / yours / ours / theirs. Possessives never take an apostrophe: its, yours, theirs (never your's, their's). It's = it is / it has. · I have decided that I won’t work at *yours* company anymore. · your · A noun (company) follows, so the adjective form is needed. · *Their* is the best offer you can get. · Theirs · No noun follows; theirs = their offer. · I can’t buy this car because *it’s* cost is out of my budget. · its · It’s means “it is”. The possessive is its. · You and Rohan should not waste *his* time wandering here and there. · your · You + third person → your. · You and I have done *my* best to make her happy. · our · You and I → our. · He and I will leave no stone unturned to complete *ours* assignment. · our · A noun (assignment) follows → our. · e · This laptop is not mine; · it must be your’s · because your name is on it. · No error · The possessive pronoun is “yours”, without an apostrophe. · qg4tj20 · rule · f · The decision was ___, not ours, so they must face the consequences. · theirs · their · their’s · them · No noun follows, so the possessive pronoun “theirs” is needed. · qbu36fj · rule · e · The company changed · it’s logo last year · after the merger. · No error · “It’s” means “it is”. The possessive adjective is “its logo”. · q3h6d1r · rule

grammar.t: Reflexive pronoun after certain verbs
grammar.x: Reflexive pronoun after certain verbs · Some verbs, in these meanings, must have an object. When the doer does the action to himself, a reflexive pronoun (myself, ourselves, yourself, himself, herself, itself, themselves) fills that object slot. · Verbs to remember: absent, present, adapt, adjust, acquit, exert, apply, hurt, prostrate, submit, resign, reconcile, introduce, avail, amuse, enjoy, satisfy, avenge, pride. · The reflexive must agree with the subject: “The minister and his members absented themselves .” · Learn them with their prepositions: absent oneself from , avail oneself of , pride oneself on , adapt oneself to , resign oneself to , apply oneself to , reconcile oneself to . · He *introduced to* the Chairman as the General Secretary of the party. · introduced himself to · “Introduce” needs an object: whom did he introduce? Himself. · He *prostrated* before his master who taught him in school. · prostrated himself · Prostrate is transitive here, so it needs “himself”. · The minister and his cabinet members absented *himself* from the meeting. · themselves · Plural subject → themselves. · That was our first business-class journey, so we tried to *avail of* all the facilities. · avail ourselves of · From the lecture homework: avail + reflexive + of. · f · We tried to avail ___ all the facilities of the hotel. · ourselves of · of · us of · ourself of · “Avail” takes a reflexive object and the preposition “of”. · q67s46n · rule · e · Several students absented · from the class · to watch the match. · No error · Absent needs a reflexive object: “absented themselves from”. · q11mgdoe · rule · f · She prides ___ her punctuality. · herself on · on · herself in · her on · The pattern is “pride oneself on something”. · qjo886i · rule

grammar.t: Each / Either / Neither + of + plural noun + singular verb
grammar.x: Each / Either / Neither + of + plural noun + singular verb · In “Each of the boys”, the real subject is each : one boy at a time. “Of the boys” only names the group he is picked from. · So the noun after “of” is plural, but the verb is singular and the pronoun that refers back is singular too (his / her). · Either and neither mean “one of two” and follow the same pattern. · Each / Either / Neither + of + plural noun → singular verb + his/her. The “of” is your signal to go singular. · Each of the boys *have* completed *their* assignment. · has … his · Each → singular verb and singular pronoun. · Each of these 5 students *have* worked very hard on this project. · has · Each of → singular verb. · They told me that neither of them *were* present when the accident happened. · was · Neither of → singular verb. · e · Each of the players · have been given · a new kit. · No error · Each of → singular: “has been given”. · q1yj2b4a · rule · f · Neither of the two answers ___ correct. · is · are · were · have been · Neither of + plural noun takes a singular verb. · q1ohkfau · rule · e · Either of these two roads · lead to · the railway station. · No error · Either of → singular verb: “leads”. · qrgmn2o · rule

grammar.t: Out-of-class comparison: “that of” / “those of”
grammar.x: Out-of-class comparison: “that of” / “those of” · A comparison must be between the same kind of things. “The air of Delhi is more polluted than Mumbai” compares air with a city . That is wrong. · Repeat the compared noun with that of (singular) or those of (plural), or use an apostrophe: “than that of Mumbai”, “than Rahul’s”. · Ask: “What is being compared?” Air ↔ air, speed ↔ speed, salaries ↔ salaries. Singular noun → that of. Plural noun → those of. A person’s name → Rahul’s. · The air of Delhi is more polluted than *Mumbai*. · that of Mumbai · Delhi’s air is compared with Mumbai’s air, so “that of Mumbai” (that = air). · The maximum speed of my car is way more than *yours*. · that of yours · Speed is compared with speed: that of yours = the speed of your car. · Rohit’s sense of humour is better than *Rahul*. · Rahul’s · Sense of humour ↔ sense of humour. No need to repeat the noun; the apostrophe does it. · f · The climate of Shimla is cooler than ___. · that of Patna · Patna · those of Patna · of Patna · Climate is compared with climate, and “climate” is singular, so “that of Patna”. · qvl2ubk · rule · e · The salaries of government teachers · are better than · private school teachers. · No error · Salaries are compared with salaries: “than those of private school teachers”. · qwzsw6q · rule · e · My handwriting is · much neater than · that of my brother. · No error · Handwriting is compared with handwriting using “that of”. The sentence is correct. · qx7u7df · rule

grammar.t: Who, whom, which, that, what
grammar.x: Who, whom, which, that, what · Who (subject) and whom (object) are for people. Which is for things, and also for a whole clause. That is used for emphasis: after superlatives, only, all, same, the few, none, nothing, and when the antecedent is a person and a thing together. What means “the thing which” and has no antecedent before it. · Who or whom? Rewrite the relative clause with he/him. “The girl ___ you had slapped” → you had slapped her → whom. “Sahil, ___ just started” → he started → who. · he → who, him → whom. After the same / only / the few / superlative / all → that. No noun before it and it means “the thing which” → what. · The girl *who* you had slapped in the class complained to the principal. · whom · You slapped her → object → whom. · Sahil, *whom* just started last week, is already doing good at his new job. · who · He started → subject → who. · The car *which / who* is standing in front of my house is my father’s. · which · A car is a thing. · You have never questioned any decision of your master, *that* is a proof of your loyalty. · which · The relative refers to the whole previous clause, so “which”. · The few people *who* came to my party are my only friends. · that · After “the few” → that. · He told me that he saw the same boy *who* killed your dog. · that · After “the same” → that. · I cannot predict *that* might happen if you don’t submit your fees on time. · what · No antecedent; “the thing which” → what. · You shouldn’t judge a person when you don’t know *that* he has gone through. · what · “The things which he has gone through” → what. · In the lecture sentence about Sahil, “doing good” should also be “doing well” (well is the adverb; see Rule 17). · f · This is the same pen ___ I lost yesterday. · that · which · who · what · After “the same”, the relative pronoun is “that”. · qivwvmt · rule · f · I don’t know ___ he wants from me. · what · that · which · whom · There is no antecedent and it means “the thing which”, so “what”. · q1qseo6w · rule · e · The man whom · came to our house yesterday · is my uncle. · No error · He came → subject → “who”. · q1cigbrr · rule

grammar.t: The relative pronoun takes its verb from its antecedent
grammar.x: The relative pronoun takes its verb from its antecedent · Who / which / that have no number of their own. They copy the number of the noun they refer to (the antecedent). · “He is one of those who can sacrifice their lives.” Who refers to those (plural), so the verb and pronoun are plural. · “This is one of the best novels that have been written.” That refers to novels, which is plural. · Exception: “the only one of the girls that has scored…” Here that refers to “the only one”, so it is singular. · Find the noun just before who/that and match the verb to it. “One of those who” → plural. “The only one of … who” → singular. · He is one of those who can sacrifice *his* life for the country. · their lives · Who → those (plural). · This novel is one of the best novels that *has* been written in the last 10 years. · have · That → novels (plural). · Roshni is the only one of the girls that *have* scored more than 98%. · has · That → the only one (singular). · e · She is one of those women · who never loses · patience in a crisis. · No error · Who refers to “those women” (plural), so “never lose”. · qgxoljr · rule · f · He is the only one of the students who ___ cleared the exam. · has · have · were · are · Who refers to “the only one”, so the verb is singular. · qnc863u · rule · e · This is one of the most interesting books · that has been published · this year. · No error · That refers to “books” (plural): “that have been published”. · q11hzfs2 · rule

grammar.t: When the subject is “one”
grammar.x: When the subject is “one” · When the subject is the indefinite pronoun one , keep using “one” forms all through the sentence: one’s, oneself. Do not switch to he, his or himself. · One → one’s → oneself. Never one → his. · One should respect *his* parents. · one’s · The subject is “one”. · One should never criticise others if *he* is not sure of *his* facts. · one … one’s · Keep “one” throughout: “if one is not sure of one’s facts”. · One should adapt *himself* to changing conditions. · oneself · Reflexive of one → oneself. · The printed answer for the second sentence changes only “his”. Change both: “if one is not sure of one’s facts”. · f · One should always keep ___ promises. · one’s · his · their · ones · With the subject “one”, the possessive is “one’s”. · q1nf0jh7 · rule · e · One must do · his duty · honestly and sincerely. · No error · Subject “one” → “one’s duty”. · qfp76ig · rule · f · One should not overestimate ___. · oneself · himself · themselves · itself · The reflexive form of “one” is “oneself”. · q11i8wm4 · rule

grammar.t: All / some / most / half / % / fraction + of + noun → verb follows the noun
grammar.x: All / some / most / half / % / fraction + of + noun → verb follows the noun · Words of quantity (all, some, most, a lot, lots, plenty, half, 20 percent, one-third, two-fifths) do not fix the number themselves. The verb follows the noun after of . · Countable plural noun → plural verb: “Some of the students were absent.” Uncountable or singular noun → singular verb: “Half of the class has …”, “Most of the milk has …” · Skip the quantity word, read the noun after “of”, and match the verb to it. · Some of the students *was* absent yesterday. · were · Students is plural. · Half of the class *have* not completed the assignment. · has · Class is a singular collective noun. · All of the chairs *was* in perfect condition. · were · Chairs is plural. · f · Most of the milk ___ gone sour. · has · have · are · were · Milk is uncountable, so the verb is singular. · q1hk5jmi · rule · e · Forty percent of the students · has failed · in English this year. · No error · Students is plural: “have failed”. · q12f3lfd · rule · f · Two-thirds of the city ___ flooded last night. · was · were · have been · are · City is singular, so “was”. · q7gi4up · rule

grammar.t: Pronouns in a comparison: subject with subject, object with object
grammar.x: Pronouns in a comparison: subject with subject, object with object · After than / as … as, a verb is usually understood: “You are stronger than he (is).” So the pronoun must be in the case it would have in that hidden clause. · “I like you more than him ” means “than I like him”. “I like you more than he ” means “than he likes you”. The case changes the meaning. · Finish the sentence in your head. Than he (is) / than I (am) / as smart as he (is). · You are stronger than *him*, so you can easily defeat him. · he · Than he is. · Their tallest player was shorter than *me*. · I · Than I was. · You are as smart as *him*. · he · As he is. · f · She sings better than ___. · I · me · myself · mine · Than I (sing). · q1ptehmf · rule · f · I trust you more than ___ (meaning: than I trust him). · him · he · his · himself · The hidden clause is “than I trust him”, so the object form. · q2gnudi · rule · e · My younger brother · is now as tall · as me. · No error · As I (am): “as tall as I”. · qle5c45 · rule

grammar.t: Object case after prepositions
grammar.x: Object case after prepositions · Between, with, besides, including, excluding, but (= except), like, unlike, together with, along with, as well as, and not, in addition to, rather than, accompanied by, no less than, nothing but are prepositions or prepositional phrases. · A pronoun after a preposition is its object, so it takes the object form: me, him, her, us, them. · Between you and me . Everyone but him . Like her . If you can put “to” or “for” there, it is object case. · Between you and *I*, he is not dressed properly for the occasion. · me · Between is a preposition. · Everyone but *he* was happy to receive a gift on Christmas. · him · But = except, a preposition. · f · Everyone went to the fair except ___. · him · he · his · himself · Except is a preposition, so the object form. · q6i3h8c · rule · e · Between you and I, · this plan · will not work. · No error · Between is a preposition: “between you and me”. · q1xmszdj · rule · e · Unlike his brother, · he · never complains. · No error · The sentence is correct. · qhn18e2 · rule

grammar.t: Ordinal before cardinal: “the first five”, not “the five first”
grammar.x: Ordinal before cardinal: “the first five”, not “the five first” · An ordinal (first, second, last, next) picks the position; a cardinal (one, two, five) counts. The ordinal comes first: the first five questions, the last two men. · “The five first questions” would mean five different questions that are each “first”. That is impossible, since only one thing can be first. · Position before count: first five, last ten, next three. · He has solved the *five first* questions of the exercise. · first five · Ordinal before cardinal. · The policeman checked only the *ten first* trucks in the line. · first ten · Ordinal before cardinal. · Fifteen men went into the lion’s den, but only the *two last* survived. · last two · Ordinal before cardinal. · f · The ___ chapters of the book are the most difficult. · last three · three last · last third · three lasts · Ordinal (last) comes before cardinal (three). · qc5dttg · rule · e · Only the two first · rows of the hall · were reserved for guests. · No error · Ordinal before cardinal: “the first two rows”. · qtsrpmd · rule

grammar.t: Each / either / neither / every + singular noun + singular verb
grammar.x: Each / either / neither / every + singular noun + singular verb · Without “of”, these words are adjectives and take a singular noun: each boy, every cousin, either side. · The subject then is singular, so the verb and the later pronoun are singular too. · Each / every + singular noun + singular verb. “Every cousin of mine is coming.” · Each boy of this class *were* called by the principal. · was · Each boy → singular. · According to the rules, each speaker *were* allowed five minutes. · was · Each speaker → singular. · I am going only because every cousin of mine *are* coming. · is · Every cousin → singular. · I know that each player of our team *have* tried his best. · has · From the lecture homework. · f · Every student and every teacher ___ present at the assembly. · was · were · are · have been · Every … and every … still takes a singular verb. · q1hhoi91 · rule · e · Either side · of the road · are lined with trees. · No error · Either side → singular: “is lined”. · q163i7j2 · rule · f · Each window in the building ___ been cleaned. · has · have · were · are · Each + singular noun → singular verb. · q24n42f · rule

grammar.t: Some vs any
grammar.x: Some vs any · Some is used in positive sentences. Any is used in negative sentences and questions. · Exception: in a request or an offer, “some” is used even in a question: “Would you like some tea?” · Yes-sentence → some. No / never / question → any. Polite offer → some. · I don’t have *some / any* experience of this field. · any · Negative sentence. · She told me she needed *any* time to think about my proposal. · some · Positive sentence. · You are all invited, but please don’t bring *some* presents. · any · Negative sentence. · f · There isn’t ___ milk left in the fridge. · any · some · a few · many · Negative sentence → any. · qxt8qxe · rule · e · She has not · made some mistakes · in this essay. · No error · Negative sentence → “any mistakes”. · q1yjtgee · rule · f · Would you like ___ more rice? · some · any · a few · many · An offer takes “some” even in a question; rice is uncountable. · q4n1va · rule

grammar.t: Adjectives that cannot be compared
grammar.x: Adjectives that cannot be compared · Some adjectives are already absolute: something cannot be “more perfect” or “very unique”. Do not use very, more, most or -er/-est with them. · The list: impossible, universal, eternal, chief, ideal, supreme, perfect, unique, excellent, full, empty, entire, dead, free, circular, rectangular, complete, extreme, round, square. · If the word already means 100%, it cannot go to 110%. Replace “the most unique” with “a unique”. · I can assure you that this school is *most excellent*. · excellent · Excellent cannot be compared. · I see it as *the most ideal* place to get married. · an ideal · Ideal cannot be compared. · I guess some humans are born with *the most unique* talents. · unique · Unique cannot be compared. · The architect said those tiles would look *most excellent* in our house. · excellent · From the lecture homework. · e · The jar was · completely empty · when I checked it. · No error · “Completely” is not a degree of comparison; it only emphasises. The sentence is correct. · q16lnjou · rule · f · This is ___ solution to the problem. · an ideal · the most ideal · a more ideal · the idealest · Ideal is an absolute adjective. · q1fk0bc8 · rule · e · His answer was · more perfect · than mine. · No error · Perfect cannot be compared. Rewrite: “His answer was perfect; mine was not.” · qn4ir3c · rule

grammar.t: Comparing one member with its own group: “than any other”
grammar.x: Comparing one member with its own group: “than any other” · If a person is compared with a group he belongs to, take him out of it: “Rohan is taller than all the other boys of his class.” Otherwise he is being compared with himself. · The same logic applies to “than any other ” and “no other … as … as”. · Same group → add other . Different group → no “other”: “Mumbai is bigger than any city in Kerala.” · Rohan is taller than *all the boys* of his class. · all the other boys · Rohan is one of those boys. · Rahul is more hardworking than *all the employees* of our company. · all the other employees · Rahul is an employee too. · I think *no animal* is as cunning as a fox. · no other animal · A fox is itself an animal. · f · Mount Everest is higher than ___ peak in the world. · any other · any · all · every · Everest is itself a peak in the world. · q3xk1iq · rule · e · Delhi is larger · than any other city · in Nepal. · No error · Delhi is not in Nepal, so no “other”: “than any city in Nepal”. · q1ifxp · rule · f · Sachin was better than ___ batsman of his era. · any other · any · all · each · Sachin belongs to that group, so “any other”. · qdtukaz · rule

grammar.t: No “more” with -er, no “most” with -est
grammar.x: No “more” with -er, no “most” with -est · A comparative (stronger) or superlative (nicest) is already complete. Adding more or most makes a double comparison. · To strengthen a comparative, use much, far, a lot . To strengthen a superlative, use by far, much . · More + -er = wrong. Most + -est = wrong. Much stronger / by far the nicest. · He is *more stronger* than Ajay. · much stronger · Double comparative. · The younger one is *more prettier* than the older one. · much prettier · Double comparative. · He is *the most nicest* person I have ever met. · by far the nicest · Double superlative. · He should answer as he is *the most wisest* among us. · the wisest · From the lecture homework. · f · This road is ___ than the highway. · much narrower · more narrower · most narrow · very narrower · Strengthen a comparative with “much”. · qahm1eh · rule · e · She is by far · the most cleverest girl · in the class. · No error · Double superlative: “the cleverest”. · q1gfntxy · rule

grammar.t: Pairs that are often confused
grammar.x: Pairs that are often confused · Later (time) vs latter (the second of two). Farther (distance) vs further (more, additional). · Good is an adjective, well is an adverb (but “I am well” = healthy, an adjective). Bad is an adjective, ill can be an adverb: “ill-treated”. · Far in questions and negatives; a long way in positive sentences. Last (final) vs latest (newest). Next (order) vs nearest (distance). · Latter = दो में से बाद वाला. Farther = दूरी. Further = और आगे / अतिरिक्त. · Of these two cuisines, I would love to have the *later* one. · latter · Second of two. · Let’s postpone this meeting to a *latter* date. · later · Time. · I wanted to discuss that topic *farther*. · further · More discussion, not distance. · My college is located *further* than hers. · farther · Distance. · This new restaurant serves *well* Indian food. · good · Describes a noun (food). · I prepared a lot, but the meeting didn’t go *good*. · well · Describes a verb (go). · He was grossly *bad* treated by you. · ill · Adverb before a participle. · He is not an *ill* person. · bad · Adjective before a noun. · How *far / a long way* is the library from your house? · far · Question. · He is good at shooting the ball into the net from *far*. · a long way · Positive sentence. · f · Have you read the ___ issue of the magazine? It came out yesterday. · latest · last · latter · later · Newest → latest. · q1djc9fz · rule · f · For ___ details, contact the office. · further · farther · farthest · furthest · Additional information → further. · qyam6dw · rule · e · She speaks English · very good · for a beginner. · No error · The word describes the verb “speaks”, so the adverb “well”. · q6xcmp7 · rule

grammar.t: -ing adjective vs -ed adjective (present vs past participle)
grammar.x: -ing adjective vs -ed adjective (present vs past participle) · The -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling: a confusing question, an interesting novel, a horrifying man (डरावना). · The -ed / V3 form describes the one who feels it, or something that has undergone the action: a confused student, a horrified man (डरा हुआ), a lost book. · -ing = gives the feeling. -ed = gets the feeling (or has undergone the action). · He solved that *confused* question very easily. · confusing · The question causes confusion. · He gifted his girlfriend a very *interested* novel. · interesting · The novel causes interest. · I could not find my *losing* book. · lost · The book has been lost. · f · The film was so ___ that half the audience fell asleep. · boring · bored · bore · bores · The film causes boredom. · qrxala8 · rule · e · The tired workers · sat down · after an exhausted day. · No error · The day causes the tiredness: “an exhausting day”. · q1dh2cp · rule · f · The ___ passengers were rescued by the navy. · stranded · stranding · strand · strands · The passengers have undergone the action. · q1c7yfbq · rule

grammar.t: Little, a little, the little; few, a few, the few
grammar.x: Little, a little, the little; few, a few, the few · Little / few = hardly any (negative sense). A little / a few = some (positive sense). The little / the few = all of the small amount that exists. · Little and its forms go with uncountable nouns (money, sugar, sleep). Few and its forms go with countable plurals (days, students). · “Very little”, never “very a little”. “The few” / “the little” always has a “that / which / who” idea: all that there was. · Could you give me *___* sugar? · a little · Positive request for some. · I offered him *a little* money that I had with me. · the little · All the small amount I had. · I got very *a little* sleep last night. · very little · Negative sense; very + little. · The doctor advised him to rest for *the few* days. · a few · Positive sense, some days. · The school cancelled the debate as *a few* students participated. · few · Negative sense, hardly any. · *A few* pastries that I had kept for you were finished by him. · The few · From the lecture homework: all the pastries I had kept. · f · There is ___ hope of his recovery; the doctors have given up. · little · a little · the little · few · Negative sense with an uncountable noun. · q1cvi58m · rule · f · ___ friends he had deserted him in his bad days. · The few · A few · Few · Little · All of the small number he had → the few. · q1sknk08 · rule · e · I have · a few money left, · so I can buy a snack. · No error · Money is uncountable: “a little money”. · qewl2na · rule

grammar.t: Choose the right degree from the meaning
grammar.x: Choose the right degree from the meaning · Comparing two → comparative (better, stronger, wiser). Comparing three or more → superlative (best, smallest). · When two adjectives are joined by “and” in a comparison, both must be in the same degree: “stronger and wiser than”. · Count what is compared: two → -er, more than two → -est. Check every adjective joined by “and”. · Rahul is stronger and *wise* than Mahesh. · wiser · Both adjectives must be comparative. · We bought dresses from the same store, but mine is *best* than hers. · better · Two things → comparative. · I got the *smaller* one of all the options available. · smallest · More than two → superlative. · f · Of the two sisters, Meera is the ___. · taller · tallest · most tall · more taller · Two people → comparative. · q1o59tsi · rule · e · This is the · more beautiful place · I have ever visited. · No error · Compared with every place → superlative: “the most beautiful place”. · qmeyri6 · rule · f · She is cleverer and ___ than her brother. · more hardworking · hardworking · most hardworking · hardworkinger · Both adjectives joined by “and” must be comparative. · qjna57t · rule

grammar.t: Fall / fell, rise / raise, lie / lay
grammar.x: Fall / fell, rise / raise, lie / lay · Each pair has one verb that happens by itself (intransitive, no object) and one that you do to something (transitive, takes an object). · Verb · V2 · V3 · Meaning · fall · fell · fallen · गिरना (no object) · fell · felled · felled · गिराना, e.g. fell a tree · rise · rose · risen · उठना / बढ़ना (no object) · raise · raised · raised · उठाना / बढ़ाना / पालना · lie · lay · lain · लेटना / पड़े होना (no object) · lay · laid · laid · लिटाना / रखना · Is there an object right after the verb? Yes → fell, raise, lay. No → fall, rise, lie. grammar.t: V3 used as a verb vs special adjective forms
grammar.x: V3 used as a verb vs special adjective forms · Some verbs have a separate adjective form. When you need the verb (with has / had / was), use the normal V3. Use the special form only as an adjective before a noun. · Verb (V3) · Adjective form · melted · molten (molten gold) · proved · proven (a proven fact) · sunk · sunken (a sunken ship) · shrunk · shrunken (a shrunken shirt) · struck · stricken (a grief-stricken family) · shaved · shaven (a clean-shaven face) · drunk · drunken (a drunken driver) · loaded · laden (a laden truck) · After has / have / had / was, use the verb form: has melted, could not be proved. Before a noun, use the adjective: molten lava, sunken ship. · He has already *molten* some gold for your necklace. · melted · A verb is needed after “has”. · The charges against him could not be *proven* in court. · proved · Passive verb after “be”. · f · The ship ___ near the coast in 1912. · sank · sunken · sinked · sunked · A past-tense verb is needed; sunken is only an adjective. · q1bbohbw · rule · e · The volcano poured out · streams of melted lava · for days. · No error · Before a noun, the adjective form is “molten lava”. · qocxdku · rule · f · A ___ driver caused the accident last night. · drunken · drunk · drinking · drank · Before a noun, the adjective form “drunken” is used. · q1oi1lhq · rule

grammar.t: Stative verbs have no -ing form
grammar.x: Stative verbs have no -ing form · Stative verbs describe a state (thinking, owning, feeling, senses, liking), not an action. So they are not used in continuous tenses. · The list: think, believe, consider, have, own, possess, look, seem, appear, consist, contain, comprise, feel, smell, taste, sound, know, resemble, like, love, want, agree, hate, forgive, forget, remember, depend, exist. · When the same verb means an action, -ing is fine: “I am having lunch” (eating), “She is tasting the soup” (testing it). · State → simple tense (I remember, he resembles, I have known). Action meaning → -ing allowed. · I *am vaguely remembering* that I met him at a concert. · vaguely remember · State of memory. · He *is strongly resembling* his brother. · strongly resembles · State of likeness. · I *have been knowing* Mr Verma for the last 5 years. · have known · From the lecture homework. · f · This box ___ old letters and photographs. · contains · is containing · are containing · has been containing · Contain is stative. · qqlfs1z · rule · e · I am not understanding · what you are trying · to say. · No error · Understand is stative: “I do not understand”. · q18h8t2l · rule · e · The chef is tasting · the soup to check · the salt. · No error · Here “tasting” is an action (testing), so -ing is correct. · q8b9suc · rule

grammar.t: No “as” after make, choose, elect, appoint, call, consider…
grammar.x: No “as” after make, choose, elect, appoint, call, consider… · With make, choose, elect, select, anoint, appoint, name, call, think and consider, the complement follows the object directly: “They elected him captain .” · Consider him a friend. Appoint her principal. Adding “as” is the error. (Regard, treat, describe and see do take “as”.) · I consider him *as* one of my closest friends. · (remove as) · Consider + object + complement. · The team decided to make him *as* captain. · (remove as) · Make + object + complement. · f · The committee appointed her ___ of the project. · the head · as the head · to the head · for the head · Appoint + object + complement, without “as”. · q13ywhju · rule · e · We all regard him · as the best teacher · in the school. · No error · Regard takes “as”. grammar.t: Active or passive? Doer or receiver
grammar.x: Active or passive? Doer or receiver · If the subject does the action → active. If the subject receives it → passive: be + V3. · Check tense too: “was treating” (past continuous active) → “was being treated” (past continuous passive). · Ask: can the subject do this? A car cannot steal; it is stolen. Children can tease; they are teasing. · My car *stole / was stolen* by somebody. · was stolen · The car receives the action. · Somebody *stole / was stolen* my car. · stole · Somebody is the doer. · The wounded woman *was treating* by the doctor. · was being treated · The woman receives the treatment. · Some children *were being teased* the animals. · were teasing · The children are the doers. · f · The new bridge ___ next year. · will be opened · will open · will be opening · opens by · The bridge receives the action. · q8z68wa · rule · e · English is spoken · in many countries · all over the world. · No error · English receives the action. Correct passive. · qapnu39 · rule · e · The thief caught · by the police · near the station. · No error · The thief receives the action: “was caught”. · q1tr4m4n · rule

grammar.t: Used to / be used to / be used + infinitive
grammar.x: Used to / be used to / be used + infinitive · Used to + V1 = a past habit that has ended: “I used to play cricket.” · Be / get / become used to + V-ing = accustomed to (आदत होना): “I am used to working at night.” Here “to” is a preposition. · Be used + to-infinitive = passive of “use” (इस्तेमाल किया जाना): “The car was used to carry drugs.” · Habit that ended → used to play. Accustomed → am used to playing. Was utilised → was used to carry. · When I was a child, I used to *playing* cricket with my father. · play · Past habit → used to + V1. · I worked at a call centre for 7 years, so I am used to *work* night shifts. · working · Accustomed → used to + V-ing. · The stolen car was used to *carrying* illegal drugs. · carry · Passive of use → to + V1. · In America he became used to *drive* on the right. · driving · From the lecture homework. · f · My grandfather ___ walk five kilometres every morning. · used to · was used to · is used to · use to · A past habit → used to + V1. · q12qq5t7 · rule · e · She is used to · wake up early · because of her job. · No error · Accustomed → used to + V-ing: “waking up”. · q1a4e0je · rule · f · This knife is used to ___ vegetables. · cut · cutting · cuts · being cut · Passive of use → to + V1. · qtz0bdl · rule

grammar.t: Need and dare
grammar.x: Need and dare · As modals (mostly in negatives and questions) they take a bare V1 and no “to”: “You need not worry ”, “How dare you say that?” · As main verbs they behave like ordinary verbs with “to”: “You do not need to pay ”, “He needs to rest.” · need not + V1 / dare not + V1 / How dare you + V1. With do / does / did, use “need to”. · You need not *to worry* about this mole. · worry · Modal need → bare V1. · How dare you *to say* these words to my father? · say · Modal dare → bare V1. · You *do not need pay* anything. · do not need to pay / need not pay · Main verb need takes “to”. · f · You ___ come to office tomorrow; it is a holiday. · need not · need not to · do not need · not need · Modal need → need not + V1. · q1iowf0a · rule · e · He dared not · to speak · in front of the manager. · No error · Modal dare → bare infinitive: “dared not speak”. · q16ii7hb · rule · f · She ___ to finish the report by Monday. · needs · need · needn’t · need not · A positive sentence with “to” uses need as a main verb: needs to. · qc3agrq · rule

grammar.t: Can, may, could, might
grammar.x: Can, may, could, might · Can : ability, informal request, negative possibility (It can’t be true). May : polite permission or request, and possibility. · Could : polite request, remote possibility, past of can. Might : weaker possibility, and past of may in reported speech. · Ability → can. Asking permission politely → may I. Asking someone to do something politely → could you. Reported past → might. · Let Shruti handle clients as she *may* speak several languages. · can · Ability. · I forgot my phone; *will* I use yours to call home? · may · Asking permission. · *May* you come with me to the clinic? · Could · Requesting someone to act. · He told me that he *may* join Aman’s batch. · might · Past reporting verb → might. · f · ___ I come in, sir? · May · Can · Might to · Will · A polite request for permission. · q1j3ax0x · rule · e · She said that · she may be late · for the meeting. · No error · Past reporting verb → “she might be late”. · q1nupjrk · rule · f · He is only three, but he ___ read simple words. · can · may · might · must · Ability → can. · q1vao18e · rule

grammar.t: Would, should, ought to, must
grammar.x: Would, should, ought to, must · Would : polite request, past habit, past of will. Should : general advice. grammar.t: Uncountable nouns: no a / an / one / many / -s
grammar.x: Uncountable nouns: no a / an / one / many / -s · These nouns are treated as a mass or an idea, so they cannot be counted. Do not use a, an, one, two, these, those, many or a plural -s/-es with them. The verb stays singular. · Material-type: bread, soap, shampoo, sand, iron, paper, hair, brick, food, grass, garbage, filth. · Abstract-type: scenery, machinery, jewellery, cutlery, crockery, stationery, luggage, baggage, money, evidence, equipment, furniture, advice, work, music, information, knowledge, wealth. Others: business, research, abuse, percentage, alphabet. · To count them, add a unit: a piece of advice, an item of furniture, a cake of soap, a loaf of bread, a lot of luggage. · Our NGO helps people who collect *garbages* for a living. · garbage · Uncountable. · Her house survived because it was made of the best quality *bricks*. · brick · The lecture lists brick as a material noun. · The scientists had all the *equipments* they needed. · equipment · Uncountable. · Tourists visit Kashmir to see the beautiful *sceneries*. · scenery · Uncountable. · Go to a nearby store and bring *a soap*. · a cake of soap · From the lecture homework. · In everyday English “bricks” is also common. In SSC questions, follow the lecture list and treat brick as a material (uncountable). · f · She gave me a very useful ___. · piece of advice · advice · advices · advise · Advice is uncountable; count it with “a piece of”. · qr5elma · rule · e · All the furnitures · in this room · are made of teak. · No error · Furniture is uncountable: “All the furniture … is made”. · q1ws92v3 · rule · f · How much ___ do you have for this trip? · luggage · luggages · the luggages · a luggage · Luggage is uncountable. · q5zzds0 · rule

grammar.t: Nouns that look plural but are singular
grammar.x: Nouns that look plural but are singular · These end in -s but name one subject, game, disease or thing, so they take a singular verb. · Subjects: physics, mathematics, economics, politics. Games: billiards, darts, athletics, dominoes. Diseases: rickets, measles, mumps, diabetes, rabies, shingles. Others: innings, news, summons. · Name of a subject, game or disease + singular verb. “The news is good.” “A summons was issued.” · Mathematics *are* one of the subjects I have found very difficult. · is · Subject name → singular. · Darts *are* a form of throwing game. · is · Game name → singular. · The news of her promotion *were* the reason for her smile. · was · News → singular. · Rickets *cause* problems in the calcification of bones. · causes · Disease name → singular. · Even after receiving many *summons*, he didn’t appear in court. · summonses · From the lecture homework: summons is singular, its plural is summonses. · f · Measles ___ a highly infectious disease. · is · are · were · have been · Disease name → singular. · q1qaygmh · rule · e · Economics are · my favourite subject · in college. · No error · Subject name → singular: “Economics is”. · q1isz6ni · rule

grammar.t: Nouns that are always plural
grammar.x: Nouns that are always plural · These nouns are always plural and take a plural verb. · Pairs: scissors, tongs, pliers, pincers, bellows, trousers, pants, pyjamas, shorts, spectacles, glasses, binoculars, scales, fetters, shackles. · Also: compliments, thanks, congratulations, regards; valuables, eatables, belongings, goods, surroundings, movables; ashes, remains, ruins, proceedings, clothes, outskirts, arrears, dues, alms, riches, earnings, savings, proceeds, odds. · To make them singular, use “a pair of”: “A pair of scissors is on the table.” Then the verb follows “pair”. · The binoculars *was* not in focus. · were · Always plural. · Tongs *is* used by my grandmother to make chapatis. · are · Always plural. · All his goods *was* packed in boxes. · were · Always plural. · The outskirts of the city *has* some good hospitals. · have · Always plural. · f · My spectacles ___ broken. · are · is · was · has been · Always plural. · qq6cg1c · rule · f · A pair of scissors ___ lying on the table. · is · are · were · have been · The verb follows “a pair”, which is singular. · q18sif7q · rule · e · His savings · was spent · on his daughter’s wedding. · No error · Savings is always plural: “were spent”. · qtnvawg · rule

grammar.t: Nouns that look singular but are plural
grammar.x: Nouns that look singular but are plural · Cattle, vermin, police, gentry, peasantry, people, poultry, cavalry, clergy, infantry and children have no -s, but they always mean many, so they take a plural verb. · No “a” and no “-s” with these: never “a cattle” or “polices”. The police are / cattle are / people are . · Cattle *was* considered wealth in ancient times. · were · Always plural. · Poultry *is* domesticated birds kept for eggs and meat. · are · Always plural. · The police *was* informed by the locals. · were · Always plural. · Most people *doesn’t* exercise daily. · don’t · People → plural. · f · The cattle ___ grazing in the field. · are · is · was · has been · Always plural. · qt3uzfy · rule · e · The police has · arrested · the main suspect. · No error · Police → plural: “The police have”. · q6lk28p · rule

grammar.t: Same form in singular and plural
grammar.x: Same form in singular and plural · Deer, sheep, fish, species, series, aircraft, offspring, issue (children), whereabouts, headquarters, wages and means do not add -s for the plural. The verb follows the meaning. · Wages as income → plural verb. Wages as result or reward (“the wages of sin is death”) → singular. · Means as money or resources → plural verb. Means as a method or medium → singular or plural by the meaning (one means / various means). · Never add -s: aircrafts, sheeps, deers, headquarter are all wrong. Read the determiner: “two series are”, “this series is”. · I saw the remains of some *aircrafts*. · aircraft · Same form. · Two series of lectures *is* scheduled for next week. · are · Two series → plural. · The wages of the workers *was* increased. · were · Income → plural. · The wages of burning midnight oil *are* always worth it. · is · Result → singular. · His means *is* not enough to support a large family. · are · Money → plural. · Various means *was* used to contact their family. · were · Various → plural. · Our company has set up its new *headquarter* in South Delhi. · headquarters · From the lecture homework. · f · Three ___ were grazing near the river. · sheep · sheeps · sheepes · sheep’s · Same singular and plural form. · q1fjmham · rule · e · This series of books · are very popular · among children. · No error · This series → singular: “is very popular”. · q1ercqqz · rule

grammar.t: Plural of compound nouns
grammar.x: Plural of compound nouns · In a compound noun, make the main noun plural, the part that the rest describes: brothers-in-law, commanders-in-chief, passers-by, lookers-on, step-daughters. · Words ending in -ful are one word, so add -s at the end: mouthfuls, spoonfuls, bagfuls. · With man / woman showing gender before a profession, make both plural: men teachers, women doctors. · Which one is the real person? The brother (in law) → brothers-in-law. The passer (by) → passers-by. · Both of his *brother in laws* live in Agra. · brothers-in-law · Main noun: brother. · All the *man teachers* were called by the principal. · men teachers · Gender word + profession → both plural. · Some *passer bys* stopped to help him. · passers-by · Main noun: passer. · She gulped down two *mouthsful* of coffee. · mouthfuls · One word; -s at the end. · f · Both his ___ are lawyers. · sons-in-law · son-in-laws · sons-in-laws · son-in-law · Main noun: son. · q1ct9pki · rule · e · Three spoonsful · of sugar · are too much for tea. · No error · -ful is one word: “three spoonfuls”. · qpgzm09 · rule

grammar.t: Use the collective noun
grammar.x: Use the collective noun · English has a specific word for many groups. grammar.t: Apostrophe: joint possession, pronouns, and -s endings
grammar.x: Apostrophe: joint possession, pronouns, and -s endings · Two owners of the same thing joined by “and” → apostrophe only on the last one: “David and Mindy’s car” (one car). Separate things → both: “Ram’s and Shyam’s bags”. · Some pronouns take ’s: everybody’s, somebody’s, nobody’s, everyone’s, someone’s, one’s, anyone’s. · A plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe: parents’, students’. For words ending in an s / sh sound before “sake”, use only the apostrophe: for goodness’ sake, for conscience’ sake. (“For God’s sake” is the fixed form.) · One thing shared → last name only. grammar.t: ’s with non-living things (allowed cases)
grammar.x: ’s with non-living things (allowed cases) · Normally, non-living things use “of”: the leg of the table. But ’s is allowed in these cases: · Personification: the Sun’s fury, Death’s icy hands, Nature’s law, Fortune’s favourite, the country’s honour. Dignified objects: the court’s order, duty’s call. Celestial bodies: the Earth’s atmosphere, the Moon’s surface. · Time, weight, value and distance: a day’s journey, a ton’s weight, two metres’ gap, a pound’s worth. Idioms: at a stone’s throw, at one’s wit’s end, for heaven’s sake. · Sentences using these forms are usually “No error” in SSC. · No one will be saved from the *sun’s fury* this time. · (no error) · Personification. · Mohit has received a *court’s order* barring him from the hotel. · (no error) · Dignified object. · Experts have noticed changes in *Earth’s atmosphere*. · (no error) · Celestial body. · We sat at a *2 metres’ gap* from each other. · (no error) · Distance. · This resort is at a *stone’s throw* from the beach. · (no error) · Idiom. · e · The table’s leg · was broken · during the shifting. · No error · An ordinary object uses “of”: “The leg of the table”. · q1jano0o · rule · e · It is only · an hour’s drive · from here to the lake. · No error · Time → ’s is allowed. grammar.t: Linking verb + adjective, action verb + adverb
grammar.x: Linking verb + adjective, action verb + adverb · A linking verb does not show an action; it connects the subject to a quality of the subject. The word after it describes the subject , so it is an adjective. · Linking verbs: be forms, become, get, grow, feel, smell, taste, sound, keep, remain, prove, look, seem, appear, turn. · An action verb is described by an adverb: behaved rudely , ran quickly . · Test: replace the verb with “is”. If the sentence still makes sense (He got mad → He is mad), use the adjective. · She behaved very *rude* with Ajay’s parents. · rudely · Behave is an action. · He got really *madly* when he saw them. · mad · Get is linking here. · She kept *calmly* during the interrogation. · calm · Keep is linking here. · I don’t feel *safely* here. · safe · Feel is linking. · When he heard the news, he became really *sadly*. · sad · From the lecture homework. · f · The flowers smell ___. · sweet · sweetly · sweetness · more sweetly · Smell is a linking verb here → adjective. · q2hq6wy · rule · e · The soldier fought · brave · till the end. · No error · Fight is an action → adverb: “fought bravely”. · q1xko5yu · rule · f · The milk has turned ___. · sour · sourly · sourness · to sour · Turn is linking here → adjective. · qnaql32 · rule

grammar.t: Same form for adjective and adverb: fast, hard, late, straight
grammar.x: Same form for adjective and adverb: fast, hard, late, straight · Fast, hard, late, straight, early, daily, weekly, monthly and yearly work as both adjective and adverb with the same form. · Adding -ly often creates a different word: hardly = barely (ना के बराबर), lately = recently. “Straightly” and “fastly” do not exist. · Everyday (one word) is an adjective: everyday life. Every day (two words) is an adverb of frequency: I study every day. · Worked hard (mehnat se) vs hardly worked (barely). Came late vs lately (recently). · We have to make some *choices hard* in life. · hard choices · The adjective goes before the noun. · Reeta came home *lately* because of the traffic. · late · Late = not on time. · She had to take an *every day appointment* with a therapist. · appointment every day · Adverb of frequency. · Yash told him *straightly* to stop bothering him. · straight · “Straightly” is not a word. · f · He works ___ to support his family. · hard · hardly · hardy · hardness · Works with effort → hard. · qcmu1yj · rule · e · She runs so fastly · that nobody · can catch her. · No error · “Fastly” is not a word: “runs so fast”. · q1ogsqva · rule · f · I have not seen him ___. · lately · late · later · latest · Recently → lately. · q15lnhk9 · rule

grammar.t: Adjectives ending in -ly
grammar.x: Adjectives ending in -ly · When -ly is added to an adjective, you get an adverb (nice → nicely). When -ly is added to a noun , you get an adjective (man → manly). · So these are adjectives, not adverbs: godly, kingly, queenly, fatherly, motherly, brotherly, friendly, manly, womanly, miserly, niggardly, lively, lovely, deadly, cowardly, costly, likely. · To use them as adverbs, write “in a … manner” or “like a …”. · She treats me in a motherly manner. He behaved like a coward. He spoke in a friendly way. · She always treats me *motherly*. · like a mother / in a motherly manner · Motherly is an adjective. · He has a very deep and *manly* voice. · (no error) · Adjective before a noun. · Those who act *cowardly* in danger are not fit for the army. · in a cowardly manner · Cowardly is an adjective. · He always acts *miserly*. · like a miser · Miserly is an adjective. · He doesn’t treat me *friendly*. · in a friendly manner · From the lecture homework. · f · He spoke to the new employee ___. · in a friendly manner · friendly · friendlily · friend · Friendly is an adjective. · q1qopg0v · rule · e · The children · behaved very · lovely at the party. · No error · Lovely is an adjective. Use “behaved very nicely” (or “in a lovely manner”). · q3ocfkp · rule

grammar.t: Where adverbs of frequency go
grammar.x: Where adverbs of frequency go · Indefinite frequency (often, seldom, always, rarely, never, usually, hardly ever): before the main verb, after the first helping verb, and after “be”. · Definite frequency (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, every day): at the end of the clause. · Regularly, frequently and occasionally can go in either place. · I rarely have. She has always been. He is never late. He goes to the gym daily. · I *have rarely* time for painting. · rarely have · Before the main verb “have”. · He *daily goes* to the gym. · goes to the gym daily · Definite frequency → end. · f · She ___ to office by bus. · usually goes · goes usually · usually is going · is usually going · Indefinite frequency before the main verb, simple present for habit. · q7ea7sm · rule · e · He never is · late for · his classes. · No error · After “be”, the adverb comes after the verb: “He is never late”. · qyi3ykh · rule · e · We meet · our grandparents · monthly. · No error · Definite frequency at the end. Correct. · qtla12i · rule

grammar.t: Too much / much too; still / yet
grammar.x: Too much / much too; still / yet · Too much goes before a noun: too much money. Much too goes before an adjective or adverb: much too angry. · Still shows an action continuing; it is placed before the main verb (after “be”): “He is still recovering.” · Yet is used in negatives and questions, usually with the present perfect, at the end of the clause: “She hasn’t finished the book yet.” · Much too + adjective. Too much + noun. Still = अभी भी (continuing). Not … yet = अभी तक नहीं. · His teachers were *too much angry* with him. · much too angry · Before an adjective. · You have spent *much too money* on your suit. · too much money · Before a noun. · He cannot come because he is *yet recovering*. · still recovering · Continuing action. · She *hasn’t still finished* reading the book. · hasn’t finished reading the book yet · Negative present perfect → yet at the end. · f · This coat is ___ expensive for me. · much too · too much · very much · much · Before an adjective → much too. · q6pdht9 · rule · e · There is much too · sugar · in this tea. · No error · Before a noun: “too much sugar”. · qwnfubb · rule · f · Has the parcel arrived ___? · yet · still · already yet · till · A question in the present perfect → yet at the end. · q1cqrums · rule

grammar.t: Inversion after a negative adverb or an adverb of place
grammar.x: Inversion after a negative adverb or an adverb of place · When a sentence begins with a negative or limiting adverb (never, seldom, rarely, hardly, scarcely, barely, no sooner, not only, little, nowhere, only then), the helping verb comes before the subject: Adverb + helping verb + subject + main verb. · When a sentence begins with an adverb of place, the main verb comes before the subject, and the verb agrees with that subject: “Away went the thief.” “Near the house were three bodies.” · “So / neither + helping verb + subject”: “Rajesh joined me, and so did Kunal .” · Never have I… Barely had she… Hardly had he… Here comes the bus. Down fell the tree. · *Barely she had* got back in bed when the alarm went off. · Barely had she · Inversion. · *Never I have* encountered such rudeness. · Never have I · Inversion. · Two metres from their house *was* lying three dead bodies. · were · The subject (three bodies) is plural. · Rajesh joined me and *so Kunal did*. · so did Kunal · So + helping verb + subject. · Two miles beyond those buildings *were* located a small temple. · was · From the lecture homework: subject is “a small temple”. · f · Seldom ___ such a beautiful sunset. · have I seen · I have seen · I seen · did I saw · Negative adverb first → inversion. · qz23vjx · rule · e · Not only he sings · but he also dances · very well. · No error · Negative opening → inversion: “Not only does he sing”. · q1qwl6i4 · rule · f · I don’t like coffee, and ___. · neither does my wife · neither my wife does · my wife neither does · so does my wife · Negative agreement: neither + helping verb + subject. · q1v4116t · rule

grammar.t: A / an vs the
grammar.x: A / an vs the · A / an introduces something for the first time, or one of many. The points to something specific: already known, defined by a clause, or the only one. · “I saw the fireman who saved my life ” — the clause makes it specific. “My uncle gifted me an expensive watch” — any one watch, first mention. · Can the listener tell exactly which one? Yes → the. No → a / an. · I was happy to see *a* fireman who saved my life. · the · Specific: defined by the clause. · I can’t believe that he lives in *the* small flat in that society. · a · One of many flats, first mention. · My uncle gifted me *the* expensive watch on my birthday. · an · First mention. · *A* man whom we met on the way is my brother-in-law. · The · Specific: defined by the clause. · He wanted to buy *the* big house for his parents. · a · From the lecture homework. · He stole *a* charger of my phone. · the · From the lecture homework: my phone has one specific charger. · f · ___ book you lent me was very useful. · The · A · An · No article · Specific: defined by “you lent me”. · q19wha2c · rule · e · I bought a pen yesterday, · but a pen · does not write well. · No error · Second mention of the same pen: “but the pen”. · qko5tun · rule · f · I saw ___ elephant in the zoo yesterday. · an · a · the · no article · First mention, vowel sound → an. · q159qrm9 · rule

grammar.t: A vs an: go by the sound
grammar.x: A vs an: go by the sound · Use an before a vowel sound , and a before a consonant sound. The spelling does not matter. · Vowel letter, consonant sound (“yu” or “wa”): unit, unique, utopia, universal, uniform, useful, union, university, European, eulogy, one, once. → a . · Consonant letter, vowel sound: hour, heir, heiress, honest, honour, honorary. Abbreviations starting with F, H, L, M, N, R, S, X (said “ef, aitch, el, em, en, ar, es, ex”): an FIR, an SMS, an MNC, an LLB, an MLA. → an . · Say the word aloud. “A-unique” sounds right because unique starts with “yu”. “An-FIR” because F is said “ef”. · My brother has *an unique* sense of humour. · a unique · “Yu” sound. · I will not hesitate in lodging *a FIR* against you. · an FIR · “Ef” sound. · The spammer sent him *a SMS*. · an SMS · “Es” sound. · They awarded him *a honorary* degree. · an honorary · Silent h. · f · He is ___ MLA from Patna. · an · a · the · no article · M is said “em”, a vowel sound. · q1f4lkst · rule · f · She studies at ___ university in Delhi. · a · an · the · no article · University starts with a “yu” sound. · q5olbtj · rule · e · He waited for · a hour · at the station. · No error · Silent h: “an hour”. · q18ve7eq · rule

grammar.t: A proper noun used as a common noun takes an article
grammar.x: A proper noun used as a common noun takes an article · When a famous name is used to mean “a person like him” or “a thing like it”, it becomes a common noun and takes an article: a Sachin (a great batsman), the Robin Hood of his area, the Shakespeare of India (Kalidas). · “Like …” meaning → add a / the. The same name used for the real person → no article. · He is known as *Robin Hood* of his area. · the Robin Hood · Used as a common noun. · Accept that you are not *Sachin*. · a Sachin · A great batsman like Sachin. · f · Kalidas is often called ___ Shakespeare of India. · the · a · an · no article · A proper noun used as a common noun, made specific by “of India”. · qar6i7y · rule · e · He thinks he is · a Einstein · because he topped the class. · No error · E here sounds like “ai”, a vowel sound: “an Einstein”. · q1vpqkzs · rule

grammar.t: No article with places used for their purpose, and with certain names
grammar.x: No article with places used for their purpose, and with certain names · School, college, university, hospital, church, temple, jail, prison, market, bed, court: no article when you go there for its main purpose. “Go to school ” (to study), “go to bed ” (to sleep). With another purpose, use the: “She went to the school to meet the principal.” · No article with names of games, days, months, colours, seasons, festivals, subjects, languages, cities, most countries, continents, single lakes, diseases and meals: play cricket, on Monday, in June, Diwali, Hindi, Asia. · Exceptions: countries with a plural or “union” name take the (the USA, the UK, the Netherlands). Oceans, rivers, mountain ranges and groups of islands take the. · Purpose → no article. Visiting for another reason → the. · You should send your children to *the school*. · school · To study: its purpose. · Yamini came home and went to *the bed*. · bed · To sleep. · We always wait for *the Christmas*. · Christmas · Festival name. · As soon as I can, I will shift to *the Australia*. · Australia · Country name. · f · My father goes to ___ every Sunday to pray. · church · the church · a church · an church · For its main purpose → no article. · q1lmd0k1 · rule · e · The mother went to · the hospital · to see her sick son. · No error · She is visiting, not being treated, so “the hospital” is correct. · q1px6nzc · rule · f · Do you know how to play ___? · chess · the chess · a chess · an chess · Game name → no article. · q1kyusbt · rule

grammar.t: Nouns joined by with / along with / as well as → verb follows the first
grammar.x: Nouns joined by with / along with / as well as → verb follows the first · With, along with, together with, as well as, besides, including, excluding, except, like, unlike, but, in addition to, accompanied by, followed by, and not, but not, rather than are not true joiners like “and”. They add extra information. · So the subject is only the first noun, and the verb agrees with it. · Put the phrase in brackets: “The prime minister (accompanied by his bodyguards) comes …” Read the sentence without the bracket. · The prime minister accompanied by his bodyguards *come* to the Red Fort every year. · comes · Subject: the prime minister. · All the languages besides Hindi *is* spoken by the new student. · are · Subject: all the languages. · Rahul unlike his friends *have* never missed my class. · has · From chapter 1 homework: subject is Rahul. · f · The captain, along with his players, ___ reached the stadium. · has · have · are · were · Subject: the captain. · q3zxl5c · rule · e · The teacher as well as · the students · were present. · No error · Subject: the teacher → “was present”. · qitot9d · rule · f · The students, and not their teacher, ___ responsible for the noise. · are · is · was · has been · Subject: the students (plural). · qn61r19 · rule

grammar.t: Each / either / neither / every: all singular
grammar.x: Each / either / neither / every: all singular · Each / either / neither + of + plural noun → singular verb. Each / either / neither + singular noun → singular verb. · “Each boy and each girl” / “every man and every woman” → still singular, because each one is taken separately. · Each, every, either, neither → always think “one at a time” → singular. · Each of my cats *were* fed by my neighbour. · was · Each of → singular. · Each chapter of the new book *are* interesting. · is · Each + singular noun. · Every girl and every boy *were* given sweets. · was · Every … and every … → singular. · f · Every man, woman and child ___ given a food packet. · was · were · are · have been · Every → singular even with a list. · qxxjjxk · rule · e · Each of the answers · carry · two marks. · No error · Each of → singular: “carries”. · qe1thp8 · rule

grammar.t: One of + plural noun + singular verb; the + adjective + plural verb
grammar.x: One of + plural noun + singular verb; the + adjective + plural verb · “One of my friends” — the subject is one , so the verb is singular. The noun after “one of” must be plural. · “The + adjective” means a whole class of people: the rich, the poor, the young, the old, the brave. It is plural. · One of + plural noun + singular verb. The rich / the poor → plural verb, “they”. · One of my friends *own* a furniture shop. · owns · Subject: one. · The rich always *looks* down on the poor. · look · The rich = rich people. · When I was in trouble, one of my *friend* lent me money. · friends · From the lecture homework: one of + plural noun. · f · One of the windows ___ broken. · is · are · were · have been · Subject: one. · q7nfxnq · rule · e · The poor · is not always · unhappy. · No error · The poor = poor people: “are not always”. · qnyhonx · rule · f · One of the ___ was absent today. · teachers · teacher · teacher’s · teachers’ · One of + plural noun. · q8uajn · rule

grammar.t: Two articles = two people; one article = one person
grammar.x: Two articles = two people; one article = one person · “ The principal and the secretary” → two different people → plural verb. · “ The principal and secretary” → one person holding both posts → singular verb. · So when the sentence clearly means one person (the Vice-President is also the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha), use only one article. · Count the articles: two articles, two people. Also check “their” / “his” later in the sentence for a hint. · *The host and hostess* of the party were very nice, and they welcomed each guest. · The host and the hostess · Two different people need two articles. · The principal and the secretary of our school *is* coming. · are · Two articles → two people. · The Vice-President and *the* chairman of the Rajya Sabha is elected by an electoral college. · (remove the) · One person holds both posts. · f · The poet and ___ singer has arrived. · (no article) · the · a · an · “Has” shows one person → one article only. · q12qvnj · rule · e · The secretary and · the treasurer · has resigned. · No error · Two articles → two people: “have resigned”. · q1tz3a16 · rule

grammar.t: Gerund or infinitive as subject → singular verb
grammar.x: Gerund or infinitive as subject → singular verb · When an -ing form (gerund) or a to-infinitive is the subject, it names one activity. So the verb is singular. · Writing poems is … To give advice is easy… Don’t be misled by the plural noun inside the phrase. · Writing poems *have* been my hobby since school. · has · Gerund subject → singular. · To give suggestions *are* easy. · is · Infinitive subject → singular. · f · Reading novels ___ my favourite pastime. · is · are · were · have been · Gerund subject → singular. · qvni7hd · rule · e · To make friends · are easy, · but keeping them is hard. · No error · Infinitive subject → “is easy”. · q1tc2biq · rule

grammar.t: Either…or / neither…nor / not only…but also → verb follows the nearer subject
grammar.x: Either…or / neither…nor / not only…but also → verb follows the nearer subject · With these pairs, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (the second one). · Neither Shruti nor her friends are … Either the students or the teacher is … Look at the noun just before the verb. Tip: put the plural noun second. · Neither Shruti nor her friends *is* going. · are · Nearer: friends. · Either Ashish or his colleagues *is* responsible. · are · Nearer: colleagues. · Not only my parents but also my brother *are* coming. · is · Nearer: brother. · Neither the murderer nor his accomplices *was* convicted. · were · From the lecture homework. · f · Either you or he ___ to go. · has · have · are · were · Nearer subject: he. · q11vy1bb · rule · e · Neither the manager · nor his assistants · was present at the meeting. · No error · Nearer: assistants → “were present”. · qo3xm4v · rule

grammar.t: Many + plural, many a + singular
grammar.x: Many + plural, many a + singular · Many + plural noun + plural verb. Many a + singular noun + singular verb (it means “many, one by one”). A great / good many + plural noun + plural verb. · “Many a man has tried.” The “a” is your signal for singular. · Many aspirants preparing for this exam *was* shocked. · were · Many + plural. · Many a man *have* tried to climb Everest without oxygen. · has · Many a → singular. · A great many lives *was* saved by the rescue team. · were · A great many → plural. · f · Many a student ___ failed in this subject. · has · have · are · were · Many a → singular. · q1dhyagz · rule · e · Many a · soldiers · has died for the nation. · No error · Many a + singular noun: “many a soldier has died”. · q4mis6v · rule

grammar.t: A number of vs the number of
grammar.x: A number of vs the number of · A number of = many → plural noun + plural verb. The number of = the count (एक संख्या) → singular verb. · A number of students are … The number of students is … · A number of players *is* still injured. · are · A number of = many. · The number of employees getting laid off *are* increasing. · is · The number = the count. · The number of students using unfair means *are* increasing. · is · From the lecture homework. · f · A number of trains ___ late because of fog. · are · is · was · has been · A number of = many. · q1pnkqkh · rule · e · The number of accidents · have gone up · this year. · No error · The number = the count: “has gone up”. · qe3wlr5 · rule

grammar.t: Collective nouns; none of
grammar.x: Collective nouns; none of · A collective noun (committee, team, jury, family, army, class, government) acting as one unit → singular verb. · When the members act separately or disagree, the idea is plural → plural verb: “The jury have different opinions.” · The lecture treats none of + plural noun as singular (none = not one). · One decision → singular. Different opinions, quarrelling, taking their seats → plural. · The committee *have* agreed to build a park. · has · One decision. · The jury *has* different opinions about the case. · have · Members differ. · None of his friends *were* present at his funeral. · was · None = not one. · Modern English also accepts “none of + plural noun + plural verb”. In SSC questions, follow the lecture and pick singular when you must choose. · f · The team ___ selected its new captain. · has · have · are · were · One decision → singular (note “its”). · q14h2c19 · rule · e · The family · are divided · over the property. · No error · The members disagree → plural verb. Correct. · q1myjawf · rule

grammar.t: Titles and proper names as subject → singular
grammar.x: Titles and proper names as subject → singular · The name of a book, film, series or one thing is singular even if it looks plural: “The Harry Potter series was written by J.K. Rowling.” “The Arabian Nights is a classic.” · A word can change number with its meaning: “Mathematics (the subject) is my favourite.” But “His mathematics (calculation skills) are weak.” · Title or name → singular. Watch for a possessive like “his / her”: it often turns a subject word into “skills”. · The Harry Potter series *were* written by J.K. Rowling. · was · One series (title). · Mathematics *have* always been my favourite subject. · has · Subject name. · I think that his mathematics *is* very weak. · are · Here mathematics = calculation skills. · f · “Great Expectations” ___ written by Charles Dickens. · was · were · are · have been · Title → singular. · q1jbtx8w · rule · e · The United States · have a · presidential system. · No error · Name of one country → “has a”. · q15gjpxh · rule

grammar.t: Right verb form after each helping verb
grammar.x: Right verb form after each helping verb · Each helping verb fixes the form of the main verb after it: · Helping verb · Main verb form · Example · do / does / did · V1 · did not go · is / am / are / was / were (continuous) · V-ing · is playing · has / have / had · V3 · has written · has been / have been / had been · V-ing (active) or V3 (passive) · has been working · will / shall / can / may / must · V1 · will go · “Did went”, “has wrote”, “is play”, “has been worked” are the classic traps. Check the form right after the helping verb. · Abhishek does not *took* the bus to school. · take · Does + V1. · He did not *went* to school yesterday. · go · Did + V1. · Trisha is *play* chess with her friends. · playing · Is + V-ing. · Brian Wiest has already *wrote* three books. · written · Has + V3. · She had not *ate* at such an expensive restaurant before. · eaten · Had + V3. · She has been *worked* on this report since eight o’clock. · working · Has been + V-ing (active). · f · Did you ___ the news last night? · hear · heard · hearing · hears · Did + V1. · q1oefvzh · rule · e · The children have · went to school · by bus. · No error · Have + V3: “have gone”. · q124391 · rule · f · He has been ___ for two hours. · waiting · waited · wait · waits · Has been + V-ing (active). · q1pzas9j · rule

grammar.t: Since / for with a continuing action → present perfect (continuous)
grammar.x: Since / for with a continuing action → present perfect (continuous) · If an action started in the past and is still going on, use the present perfect continuous (has / have been + V-ing) with since / for. · For stative verbs (know, love, own…), use the present perfect instead: “I have known her for 5 years.” · With “since” (from a point in past to now), the main clause is present perfect: “She has not called me since she moved.” · Since 2022 / for the last 10 years → has / have been + V-ing. Never “is working since”. · I *am teaching* English for the last 10 years. · have been teaching · Continuing action. · Shruti *is working* as a content writer since 2022. · has been working · Continuing action. · She *is living* here for the last 20 years. · has been living · Continuing action. · I *have been knowing* her for 5 years. · have known · Stative verb. · Nalini *didn’t call* me even once since she moved. · has not called · Since → present perfect. · I *am waiting* here for you for the last 2 hours. · have been waiting · From the lecture homework. · f · It ___ since morning. · has been raining · is raining · was raining · rains · Since morning and still going on. · q1p8l4sr · rule · e · We are living · in this house · since 2015. · No error · Since 2015 and still → “We have been living”. · q1a88qrn · rule · f · I ___ him since childhood. · have known · am knowing · know · have been knowing · Stative verb with since → present perfect. · q1g8vnwp · rule

grammar.t: Signal words for simple present and present continuous
grammar.x: Signal words for simple present and present continuous · Simple present : habits, facts, proverbs, and words like always, often, daily, every day, regularly, frequently, occasionally, seldom, never, usually. · Present continuous : at this time, at this moment, at present, currently, these days, right now, now, look!, listen!. · Habit or fact → simple present. Happening now → is / am / are + V-ing. · As Rohan lives in the mountains, he *has often gone* for a hike. · often goes · Habit → simple present. · He *is seldom leaving* his home. · seldom leaves · Habit → simple present. · f · Water ___ at 100°C. · boils · is boiling · boiled · has boiled · Scientific fact → simple present. · qguy19a · rule · e · Look! The baby · sleeps · on the sofa. · No error · “Look!” shows it is happening now: “is sleeping”. · q1nbmf7l · rule · f · These days she ___ for the bank exam. · is preparing · prepares · prepared · has prepare · These days → present continuous. · qzqnpmj · rule

grammar.t: Present perfect signals; past perfect with before / after
grammar.x: Present perfect signals; past perfect with before / after · Present perfect signals: yet, so far, already, just, just now*, lately, recently, of late. (*“just now” is often used with the past too.) · Past perfect is for the earlier of two past actions: Past perfect + before + simple past. Simple past + after + past perfect. · Don’t use past perfect for a single past action, or for the later action. · The action that happened first gets “had + V3”. After “after”, the earlier action; before “before”, the earlier action. · I *hadn’t got* any email about the interview yet. · haven’t got · Yet → present perfect. · Her children *hadn’t been* well lately. · haven’t been · Lately → present perfect. · I *never met* anyone from India before I started living with Sangeeta. · had never met · Earlier past action. · The doctor *had arrived* after the patient had died. · arrived · The doctor arrived later. · f · The train ___ before we reached the station. · had left · has left · left · leaves · Earlier past action → past perfect. · qb795un · rule · e · I have finished · my homework · an hour ago. · No error · “Ago” is a past signal: “I finished my homework an hour ago”. · qpikcrq · rule · f · We ___ three chapters so far. · have completed · had completed · completed · complete · So far → present perfect. · q15hevgr · rule

grammar.t: Simple past and simple future signals
grammar.x: Simple past and simple future signals · Simple past : yesterday, ago, in the past, last day / Sunday / week / year, in 2010. · Simple future : tomorrow, next week / year, in the coming days, shortly, presently (= soon), in 2040. · A finished past time word never takes the present perfect (“have gone … last Sunday” is wrong). A future time word needs will / shall. · It *had rained* heavily yesterday. · rained · Single past action. · I *have gone* to the cinema last Sunday. · went · Last Sunday → simple past. · The guests *arrive* shortly. · will arrive · Shortly → future. · We *gather* more information in the coming days. · will gather · Future signal. · The PDF’s printed answer for “the guests arrive shortly” is reversed. The correct form is “will arrive”. · f · She ___ her grandparents next month. · will visit · visited · has visited · had visited · Next month → future. · q57snpr · rule · e · He has left · the company · in 2019. · No error · A past year → simple past: “He left the company in 2019”. · qvdme2w · rule · f · My father ___ me a watch two days ago. · gave · has given · had given · gives · Ago → simple past. · q1y64xym · rule

grammar.t: Sequence of tenses; no future after if / when / until
grammar.x: Sequence of tenses; no future after if / when / until · If the main (reporting) clause is in the past, the dependent clause is also put in the past: “My mother asked me where I was going.” (Exception: universal truths stay present.) · In time and condition clauses after when, while, if, until, unless, as soon as, before, after, provided that, do not use “will”. Use the present for a future meaning. · Asked / wanted to know → was / had. “I will call when I finish.” (not “when I will finish”) · My mother asked me where I *am* going. · was · Past reporting verb. · The teacher wanted to know if the students *have* completed their homework. · had · Past reporting verb. · I will call Shraddha when I *will finish* my presentation. · finish · No future after “when”. · You will get a seat only if someone *will cancel* his ticket. · cancels · No future after “if”. · f · I will wait here until you ___ back. · come · will come · came · had come · No future after “until”. · qdaopbq · rule · e · He said that · he is · very busy that day. · No error · Past reporting verb → “he was very busy”. · qn042nt · rule · e · Our teacher told us · that the earth · revolves round the sun. · No error · A universal truth stays in the present. Correct. · qo96f0h · rule

grammar.t: By the time
grammar.x: By the time · Past : Past perfect + by the time + simple past. “The suspects had escaped by the time the police arrived .” · Future : Future perfect + by the time + simple present. “I will have completed my homework by the time you come back.” · The action right after “by the time” happens later. The other action is already finished: had + V3 / will have + V3. · The suspects already *escaped* by the time the police arrived. · had already escaped · Earlier action. · I *finished* all the chores by the time my mother woke up. · had finished · Earlier action. · By the time you come back, I *will complete* my homework. · will have completed · Future perfect. · He will have held that post for ten years by the time he *will retire*. · retires · No future after “by the time”. · f · By the time we reached the cinema, the film ___. · had started · started · has started · was starting · Earlier action → past perfect. · q1r08s1k · rule · e · By the time the guests arrive, · we will cook · all the dishes. · No error · Future perfect: “we will have cooked”. · q1ylo4un · rule

grammar.t: Keep the tense consistent with the meaning
