grammar.x: Keep the tense consistent with the meaning · Actions in the same time frame keep the same tense: a story in the past stays past; a general habit stays present. · Joining two clauses with “and / but” does not allow a switch of time unless the meaning changes. · Read the whole sentence and find its time frame first, then check every verb against it. · My parents threw me a party and *invite* all my friends. · invited · Past story. · Most people *bought* groceries from the supermarket, but we prefer our local shop. · buy · General present habit. · When I was a kid, every morning we *plucks* flowers. · plucked · Past story. · The judge asked him if he *has* stolen the money. · had · Past reporting verb. · It grew fast as the country *is experiencing* a boom at that time. · was experiencing · Past time frame. · Most children like to rest after they *returned* from school. · return · General habit. · When I was in college, I studied till 10 pm and then I *go* to bed. · went · From the lecture homework. · f · She opened the door and ___ out. · walked · walks · has walked · had walk · Same past time frame. · q58e70d · rule · e · Every day he gets up early · and went · for a walk. · No error · Daily habit → “and goes”. · qt4cxe4 · rule

grammar.t: Question tags
grammar.x: Question tags · A tag = helping verb + pronoun. It uses the same helping verb as the statement (or do / does / did if there is none). · A positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. Never, seldom, hardly, barely, scarcely, no and nothing make a statement negative. · Contracted forms in negative tags: isn’t, doesn’t, won’t, shouldn’t. Special cases: I am → aren’t I; Let’s → shall we; imperative → will you. · Copy the helping verb, flip positive/negative, use a pronoun. “Never” counts as negative. · We have already met each other, *didn’t we*? · haven’t we · Helping verb: have. · Trains in India never come on time, *aren’t they*? · do they · Never → negative; no helping verb → do. · The new HR was late on his first day, *weren’t he*? · wasn’t he · Helping verb: was. · An aspirant should be consistent, *don’t he*? · shouldn’t he · Helping verb: should. · Let’s go for dinner, *will we*? · shall we · Let’s → shall we. · You haven’t seen the film, *did you*? · have you · Helping verb: have. · f · I am your friend, ___? · aren’t I · am not I · isn’t it · don’t I · I am → aren’t I. · q1g13vnh · rule · f · She hardly ever smiles, ___? · does she · doesn’t she · is she · isn’t she · Hardly makes it negative → positive tag. · qxwavc2 · rule · e · Close the window, · isn’t it? · It is very cold. · No error · An imperative takes “will you?”. · qvleppk · rule

grammar.t: Tags after everybody, nobody, none… → they
grammar.x: Tags after everybody, nobody, none… → they · When the subject is everybody, everyone, somebody, someone, nobody, no one, anybody, anyone, none, each, either, neither or all, the tag pronoun is they . · Nobody, no one, none and neither are negative, so the tag is positive. “All of you” → the tag is “you”. · Everybody came, didn’t they? Nobody called, did they? All of you agree, don’t you? · Everybody has come on time today, *hasn’t he*? · haven’t they · Everybody → they. · None of his colleagues came to the party, *have they*? · did they · Past simple → did. · All of you were present there, *weren’t they*? · weren’t you · All of you → you. · None of them objected to this proposal, *did he*? · did they · From the lecture homework. · f · Someone has taken my pen, ___? · haven’t they · hasn’t he · hasn’t it · didn’t they · Someone → they; helping verb has → haven’t they. · qzbk0p9 · rule · e · Nobody knew · the answer, · didn’t they? · No error · Nobody is negative → positive tag: “did they?”. · qd6egdp · rule

grammar.t: Correlatives join words of the same kind (parallelism)
grammar.x: Correlatives join words of the same kind (parallelism) · Either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, both…and must be followed by the same kind of word on each side: verb with verb, noun with noun, clause with clause. · So place the first half just before the first item: “You can either go on a vacation or stay at home.” · Both pairs only with and , never with “as well as”. · Check the word right after each half. Either + verb … or + verb. Not only + verb … but also + verb. · *Either you can* go for a vacation or stay at home. · You can either go · Verb with verb. · The teacher teaches them *not only* mathematics but also provides counselling. · not only teaches them mathematics · Verb with verb. · Both my friend *as well as* I like Hollywood movies. · and · Both…and. · The war *not only caused* destruction and death but also generations of hatred. · caused not only · From the lecture homework: noun with noun. · f · He is ___ intelligent but also hardworking. · not only · not only is · only not · both · Adjective … adjective. · q12383pg · rule · e · She neither · likes tea · nor coffee. · No error · Neither should stand before the first noun: “She likes neither tea nor coffee”. · qzu4v3l · rule · f · Both the teacher ___ the students enjoyed the trip. · and · as well as · or · with · Both…and. · q1j6h9kl · rule

grammar.t: Hardly / scarcely … when; no sooner … than
grammar.x: Hardly / scarcely … when; no sooner … than · Hardly / scarcely / barely + had + subject + V3 … when + simple past. · No sooner + had + subject + V3 … than + simple past. · These start with a negative adverb, so the helping verb comes before the subject (inversion). · No sooner → than (both have “n”). Hardly / scarcely → when. And always “had I”, never “I had”. · Hardly had I started breakfast *than* the bell rang. · when · Hardly…when. · *Scarcely he had* entered the office when everyone laughed. · Scarcely had he · Inversion. · No sooner had the dance ended *when* the audience cheered. · than · No sooner…than. · f · No sooner had he left ___ it started raining. · than · when · then · that · No sooner…than. · q1jifu46 · rule · e · Hardly had we reached · the station than · the train left. · No error · Hardly…when: “the station when”. · qmx25wq · rule

grammar.t: Although…yet; so…as; as…as
grammar.x: Although…yet; so…as; as…as · Although / though pairs with yet or a comma, never with “but”. · As…as is used in positive and negative sentences. So…as is used only in negative sentences. · Although … , yet … (never but). Not so … as ✔. So … as in a positive sentence ✘. · Though there were many people, *but* there was pin-drop silence. · yet · Though…yet. · Radhika is *not so intelligent as* she used to be. · (no error) · So…as in a negative sentence is fine. · Shivam’s car is *so* expensive as mine. · as · Positive sentence → as…as. · f · Although he worked hard, ___ he failed. · yet · but · still but · and · Although…yet. · q3rwxck · rule · e · This box is · so heavy as · that one. · No error · Positive sentence → “as heavy as”. · qn48br0 · rule

grammar.t: So…that; too…to
grammar.x: So…that; too…to · So + adjective + that + clause (result). Too + adjective + to + V1 (too much to allow the action). · “Too” already has a negative sense, so do not add “not” after “too…to”. · Clause after it (subject + verb) → so…that. V1 after it → too…to. · The dumbbells were *too* heavy that he sprained his wrist. · so · A clause follows. · Aryan was *too* tired that he couldn’t attend class. · so · A clause follows. · His marks were *so* low to get admission. · too · An infinitive follows. · He was *so* old to walk on his own. · too · An infinitive follows. · f · The tea is ___ hot to drink. · too · so · very · such · An infinitive follows. · qkb278f · rule · e · He was so · weak that · he could not stand. · No error · So…that with a clause. Correct. · q1yvhybf · rule

grammar.t: Between…and; lest…should
grammar.x: Between…and; lest…should · Between pairs with and , never with “to”: between 9 pm and 10 pm. (From…to is the other pair.) · Lest means “so that … not”. It takes should (or a bare V1), never “will” and never “not”. · Between A and B. From A to B. Lest + should + V1. · British rule lasted *between 1858 to 1947*. · between 1858 and 1947 · Between…and. · The chief guest will arrive *between 9 pm to 10 pm*. · between 9 pm and 10 pm · Between…and. · Study for 10 hours daily, lest you *will* fail. · should · Lest…should. · f · Walk carefully lest you ___. · should fall · will fall · should not fall · fall not · Lest…should (no “not”). · q4kebcd · rule · e · The shop is closed · from 1 pm and 2 pm · for lunch. · No error · From…to or between…and: “between 1 pm and 2 pm”. · qkk7r3j · rule

grammar.t: Such…as vs such…that
grammar.x: Such…as vs such…that · Such…as : “as” works as a relative pronoun (जो / जैसा). It is followed by a clause that is missing its subject or object: “such students as are serious”. · Such…that : “that” is a conjunction showing result (कि). A complete clause follows: “such a bad-tempered person that no one can live with her”. · After “such”, if the next clause is complete by itself → that. If it needs “as” to be its subject → as. Never “such … who”. · I teach only *such students who* are serious. · such students as · As = relative pronoun. · She is such a bad-tempered person *as* no one can live with her. · that · Result clause. · It was such a ferocious animal *as* everyone stayed away. · that · Result clause. · f · He is not such a fool ___ he looks. · as · that · who · which · “As he looks” = relative sense. · q15f64et · rule · e · It was such a · boring film that · we left early. · No error · Result clause → that. Correct. · qp3p3zn · rule

grammar.t: Don’t double conjunctions: as…so, that + what / where
grammar.x: Don’t double conjunctions: as…so, that + what / where · One link is enough. If “as / since / because” begins the sentence, do not add “so” in the other clause. · In reported speech, do not put “that” before a question word (what, where, when, why, how, if, whether): “I asked her where she was going.” · As … so ✘. Asked that where ✘. · As I have lived in Mumbai for a year, *so* I know how expensive it is. · (remove so) · As already joins the clauses. · I asked her *that where* she was going. · where · Remove that. · Her husband asked her *that what* she was doing. · what · Remove that. · He angrily asked me *if* I had met Rajni *or not*. · whether I had met Rajni or not · From the lecture homework: “or not” pairs with whether. · f · Since it was raining, ___ we stayed indoors. · (no word) · so · therefore so · hence so · Since already joins the clauses. · q1ysg9qs · rule · e · The officer asked me · that why · I was late. · No error · Remove that: “asked me why”. · qoqus5 · rule

grammar.t: Until vs unless; no “not” with them
grammar.x: Until vs unless; no “not” with them · Until is about time (जब तक). Unless is about condition (जब तक नहीं / अगर नहीं). · Both already carry a negative idea, so do not add “not” in the same clause. · Wait until I return (time). You won’t pass unless you study (condition). “Unless you do not” ✘. · *Until* you control your diet, you won’t lose fat. · Unless · Condition. · Please wait for me here *unless* I return. · until · Time. · Yash will not go on the trip unless he *does not have* enough money. · has · No double negative. · f · You will not succeed ___ you work hard. · unless · until · if · when · Condition. · q8lw80z · rule · e · Unless you do not · apologise, · I will not talk to you. · No error · No “not” with unless: “Unless you apologise”. · q3k7arl · rule

grammar.t: The reason … is that; no “supposing if”
grammar.x: The reason … is that; no “supposing if” · “Reason” already means “because”. So after “the reason … is / was”, use that , not because. · Supposing already means “if”, so “supposing if” is double. Use one of them. · The reason is that… ✔. The reason is because ✘. Supposing / if — pick one. · The reason she is upset is *because* she broke up. · that · Reason … that. · The reason Payal missed the meeting was *because* she had a headache. · that · Reason … that. · *Supposing if* you are wrong, will you apologise? · Supposing / If · Use only one. · f · The reason for his absence was ___ he was ill. · that · because · why · as · Reason … that. · qhv54p7 · rule · e · Supposing if · he refuses, · what will you do? · No error · Use one: “Supposing he refuses” or “If he refuses”. · q1r8ndsj · rule

grammar.t: Pick the conjunction that fits the meaning
grammar.x: Pick the conjunction that fits the meaning · Many errors are about meaning, not form. Check the logical link between the two clauses: · Contrast (but, yet, although, though) — the second part is unexpected. Result (so, therefore) — the second part follows. Reason (as, because, since). Condition (if, unless). Purpose (so that). · Read both clauses and ask: surprise → yet / but. Effect → so. Cause → because / as. · He has all the skills and money, *and* he dare not start a company. · yet · Contrast. · She wouldn’t have suffered *when* you had helped her in time. · if · Condition. · He has very little money, *so* he offered to pay for her treatment. · yet · Contrast. · Her husband was very loving and caring *although* she left him. · yet · Contrast. · Yamini broke my laptop, *but* I asked her to get it repaired. · so · Result. · I missed my bus *as* I had to book a taxi. · so · Result. · They had shot him thrice *as* he survived. · yet · From the lecture homework: contrast. · She had not seen me for 10 years *but* she was not able to recognise me. · so · From the lecture homework: result. · f · He was tired, ___ he kept working. · yet · so · because · as · Contrast. · q11w1bcw · rule · e · It was raining heavily, · because we cancelled · the picnic. · No error · Result: “so we cancelled”. · qhcdfal · rule

grammar.t: Verbs that take no preposition before the object
grammar.x: Verbs that take no preposition before the object · These verbs are transitive: the object comes right after them, with no preposition. · Meet, join, obey, violate, ask, kid, tell, inform, remind, warn, thank, advise, reach, resist, resemble, attack, afford, demand, comprise, investigate, enter, flee, explain, describe, discuss, disobey, order, stress, emphasise, await, despise, marry, accompany, answer, approach, attend, lack, sign. · Discuss the matter (not discuss about). Enter the room (not enter into). Comprise three parts (not comprise of). Reach Delhi (not reach at). · The play *comprises of* three acts. · comprises · No preposition. · Juhi strongly *resembles of* her grandmother. · resembles · No preposition. · The police are *investigating into* the murder. · investigating · No preposition. · Let’s *discuss about* your situation. · discuss · No preposition. · f · We reached ___ at 10 pm. · Mumbai · at Mumbai · to Mumbai · in Mumbai · Reach takes a direct object. · qmcf6kd · rule · e · The thief entered · into the house · through the window. · No error · Enter takes a direct object: “entered the house”. · qqsnai · rule · f · She married ___ last year. · a doctor · with a doctor · to a doctor · for a doctor · Marry takes a direct object. · qlirrnv · rule

grammar.t: “To” before the person: when it is needed and when it is not
grammar.x: “To” before the person: when it is needed and when it is not · No “to” before the person after: ask, beg, inform, advise, allow, call, assure, apprise, remind, warn, thank, wish, order, request, invite, forbid, welcome, congratulate, compliment. “I asked the cook .” · Use “to” before the person after: propose, announce, apologise, plead, talk, report, suggest, speak, listen, write, pray, complain, describe, explain, appeal, reply, object. “I apologised to my client.” “Explain to me the cause.” · Thank him, tell him, ask him. But explain to him, suggest to him, apologise to him. · I always *ask to* the cook to add extra sauce. · ask · No “to”. · I want to *thank to* Reeta. · thank · No “to”. · My parents *forbade to me* from going. · forbade me · No “to”. · I *apologised my client* for cancelling. · apologised to my client · “To” needed. · He *proposed his parents* that they go to Kerala. · proposed to his parents · “To” needed. · I asked the doctor to *explain me* the cause. · explain to me · “To” needed. · He *suggested his friends* that they invest. · suggested to his friends · From the lecture homework. · f · Please explain ___ how this machine works. · to me · me · for me · with me · Explain + to + person. · q19dskji · rule · e · He congratulated · to me · on my success. · No error · No “to”: “congratulated me”. · qgfp75w · rule · e · She complained · the manager · about the poor service. · No error · “To” needed: “complained to the manager”. · q12zzoou · rule

grammar.t: Because vs because of; in case vs in case of; unless vs without
grammar.x: Because vs because of; in case vs in case of; unless vs without · A conjunction is followed by a clause (subject + verb). A preposition is followed by a noun or pronoun (no verb of its own). · Conjunction (+ clause) · Preposition (+ noun) · because · because of · in case · in case of · unless · without · although / though · despite / in spite of · Look after the word. Subject + verb → because / in case. Only a noun phrase → because of / in case of. · The match was stopped *because* the heavy rain. · because of · A noun follows. · I love spring *because of* the flowers and leaves fill my heart with joy. · because · A clause follows (…fill my heart). · People bought groceries in bulk *in case of* the lockdown gets extended. · in case · A clause follows. · You can call me *in case* any emergency. · in case of · A noun follows. · f · The flight was delayed ___ bad weather. · because of · because · since · as · A noun phrase follows. · q1xnv2mz · rule · e · In case of · it rains, · take an umbrella. · No error · A clause follows: “In case it rains”. · qb88a3z · rule

grammar.t: Instead of, in spite of, despite
grammar.x: Instead of, in spite of, despite · Instead of = in place of (की बजाय). In spite of / despite = regardless of (के बावजूद). · Despite is never followed by “of”. In spite of always is. · Despite the rain ✔. Despite of the rain ✘. In spite of the rain ✔. · *Inspite of* buying a new car, I used my father’s old car. · Instead of · In place of. · *Instead of* the financial difficulties, they never borrowed. · In spite of · Regardless of. · *Despite of* criticism, Tobey kept trying. · Despite · No “of”. · f · ___ his illness, he attended the meeting. · Despite · Despite of · Instead of · In spite · Regardless of → despite (no of). · qtk4eq4 · rule · e · She drank juice · in spite of tea · because she had a cold. · No error · In place of → “instead of tea”. · qqbeq18 · rule

grammar.t: Two words joined by “and” that take different prepositions
grammar.x: Two words joined by “and” that take different prepositions · When two words share one object but need different prepositions, write both prepositions: “superior to but cheaper than yours”, “liable for any loss of or damage to this car”. · Test each word alone with the object. If they need different prepositions, write both. · My bag is *superior* but cheaper than yours. · superior to · Superior takes “to”. · I won’t be liable for any *loss and damage to* this car. · loss of or damage to · Loss takes “of”. · f · He was both interested ___ and good at mathematics. · in · at · for · with · Interested in, good at: both are needed. · q8usjzz · rule · e · She is fond · and devoted · to her pets. · No error · Fond takes “of”: “She is fond of and devoted to her pets”. · q1y8ulx4 · rule

grammar.t: Between vs among
grammar.x: Between vs among · Between is used for two. Among is used for more than two. · Between can be used for more than two when each one has a separate relationship with every other one: an agreement between four countries. · Two → between. A crowd, group or class → among. A treaty / agreement / trade between several parties → between. · My mother stood *among* me and my brother. · between · Two people. · There could be pickpockets *between* the passengers. · among · A crowd. · A peace agreement was signed *among* India, China, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. · between · Mutual agreement. · f · The property was divided ___ the two brothers. · between · among · within · in · Two people. · qc8df1s · rule · e · He distributed · the sweets between · all the children of the village. · No error · More than two → “among”. · q1qqiass · rule

grammar.t: Angry at / with
grammar.x: Angry at / with · Angry, annoyed, vexed and disgusted take at for a thing or situation, and with for a person. · Angry with someone. Angry at something. · I was angry *at* my mother for not telling me. · with · A person. · I was angry *with* my new phone’s performance. · at · A thing. · f · The teacher was annoyed ___ the student for coming late. · with · at · on · about · A person → with. · q1nws6y2 · rule · e · He was vexed · with the delay · in the delivery. · No error · A thing → “at the delay”. · qxqs6t1 · rule

grammar.t: Supply to / with / for
grammar.x: Supply to / with / for · Supply something to somebody. Supply somebody with something. Supply something for a purpose. · Thing first → to the person. Person first → with the thing. Purpose → for. · She supplies stationery *with* all the schools. · to · Thing first → to. · I supplied him *to* food and medicines. · with · Person first → with. · I supply medicines to homeless people *to* their treatment. · for · Purpose. · f · The company supplies the army ___ uniforms. · with · to · for · by · Person / group first → with. · q3vtpuk · rule · e · The NGO supplied · books to · the village school. · No error · Thing first → to. Correct. · qao4as2 · rule

grammar.t: Fixed prepositions
grammar.x: Fixed prepositions · Some words always take the same preposition. SSC asks these often. · Correct · Common mistake · accused of · accused for · cope with · cope up with · dispose of · dispose off · afraid of · afraid from · different from · different than · confident of · confident for · deal in (goods), deal with (people or topics) · deal software · prefer to · prefer than · senior / junior / superior / inferior to · senior than · congratulate on · congratulate for · Learn them as one unit, the way you learn a word’s spelling. · Rohan was accused *for* theft. · of · Accused of. · She is still coping *up with* her mother’s death. · with · Cope with. · Dispose *off* all the extra items. · of · Dispose of. · She is afraid *from* wild animals. · of · Afraid of. · Your curry tastes different *than* the one at your mother’s. · from · Different from. · I am confident *for* my success. · of · From the lecture homework: confident of. · His company *deal with* computer software. · deals in · From the lecture homework: deal in goods, plus singular verb. · f · He is senior ___ me by two years. · to · than · from · over · Senior to. · qy9dk6e · rule · e · We congratulated him · for his success · in the exam. · No error · Congratulate on: “on his success”. · qyb7qf · rule

grammar.t: Infinitive describing a noun needs its preposition
grammar.x: Infinitive describing a noun needs its preposition · When a to-infinitive describes a noun, that noun must be the object of the infinitive. If the verb needs a preposition to take that object, keep the preposition at the end. · “No one to talk” ✘ — you talk to someone → “no one to talk to ”. “Someone to rely” ✘ → “someone to rely on ”. · Turn it around: talk to no one, rely on someone, sit on a chair, write with a pen. The preposition stays. · He had no one *to talk*. · to talk to · Talk to someone. · He needs someone *to rely*. · to rely on · Rely on someone. · They didn’t even offer me a chair *to sit*. · to sit on · From the lecture homework. · f · Give me a pen to ___. · write with · write · write by · writing · Write with a pen. · q2npqna · rule · e · The child · has no toys · to play. · No error · Play with toys: “to play with”. · q1evb127 · rule

grammar.t: Dangling -ing phrase (present participle): wrong subject
grammar.x: Dangling -ing phrase (present participle): wrong subject · An opening -ing phrase (“Walking in the park, …”) borrows its doer from the subject of the main clause. · “Walking in the park, a snake bit him” says the snake was walking. Fix it by making the right person the subject, or by giving the phrase its own subject: “While he was walking in the park, a snake bit him.” · Ask “Who was walking?” The answer must be the first noun after the comma. · *Walking in the park*, a snake bit him. · While he was walking in the park · The snake was not walking. · *Walking down the road*, a car caught Rohit’s attention. · While Rohit was walking down the road · The car was not walking. · *Climbing the mountain*, animals were seen by the hikers. · While the hikers were climbing the mountain · The animals were not climbing. · *Travelling through the metro*, her mobile went missing. · While she was travelling through the metro · The mobile was not travelling. · *While driving to work*, a truck hit her car. · While she was driving to work · From the lecture homework. · f · ___, I saw a rainbow. · Looking out of the window · Looking out of the window, a rainbow · While looking out, the rainbow · Looked out of the window · The subject “I” is the one looking. · q157eur9 · rule · e · Opening the door, · a strange smell · hit me. · No error · The smell did not open the door. The phrase needs its own subject: “When I opened the door, a strange smell hit me.” · q50y237 · rule

grammar.t: Dangling “Being …” phrase
grammar.x: Dangling “Being …” phrase · The same logic applies to “Being + adjective / V3”. The phrase describes the subject of the main clause. · “Being injured, we took him to hospital” says we were injured. Fix: “He being injured, we took him to hospital” (absolute phrase) or “As he was injured, we…”. · Who was injured / sick / strong? That person must be the subject, or must be named at the start of the phrase. · *Being injured*, we took him to hospital. · He being injured · We were not injured. · *Being hospitalised*, Radhika’s parents took care of her. · She being hospitalised · Her parents were not in hospital. · *Being strong*, his mother called him to help with the lifting. · He being strong · His mother is not the strong one. · f · ___, the match was cancelled. · It being a rainy day · Being a rainy day · Been a rainy day · Being rainy day · The phrase needs its own subject “it”. · q1wchc3m · rule · e · Being a hot day, · we stayed · indoors. · No error · We were not a hot day: “It being a hot day”. · q9hz8e0 · rule

grammar.t: Perfect participle: “Having + V3” for the earlier action
grammar.x: Perfect participle: “Having + V3” for the earlier action · When one action is completed before another, use Having + V3 (or After + V-ing) for the first action: “Having played for two hours, he went home.” · A plain -ing form shows two actions at the same time, so it cannot show “first this, then that”. · Passive: Having been + V3 : “Having been caught, the thief confessed.” · First action finished → Having + V3. Subject received the action → Having been + V3. · *Having played* for 2 hours, he went home. · (no error) · Correct perfect participle. · *Completing* the assignment, Suhani lay on the sofa. · Having completed · The earlier action. · *Sleeping* for 2 hours, she woke up. · Having slept · The earlier action. · *Having caught*, the thief admitted his crime. · Having been caught · The thief was caught (passive). · f · ___ his work, he went out to play. · Having finished · Finishing · Finished · Having been finished · The earlier action, done by him. · ql0nexd · rule · e · Having been selected · for the job, · she thanked her teachers. · No error · She was selected (passive), then thanked. Correct. · q57ikxh · rule

grammar.t: “To” as a preposition: + V-ing
grammar.x: “To” as a preposition: + V-ing · In these phrases, “to” is a preposition , so a noun or gerund (V-ing) follows, not V1. · Look forward to, with a view to, in addition to, pay attention to, conducive to, accustomed to, used to (= habit), prone to, vulnerable to, addicted to, devoted to, indifferent to, object to, averse to, opposed to, committed to, prefer … to. · Prefer A to B : “I prefer watching films to reading novels.” Never “prefer … than”. · Check: can you put a noun after this “to”? (look forward to the holidays ✔) Then it takes V-ing: look forward to meeting you. · We are looking forward to *join* his company. · joining · Preposition to. · He was not accustomed to *work* at night. · working · Preposition to. · I prefer watching Hollywood movies *than* reading novels. · to · Prefer … to. · She started yoga with a view to *improve* her health. · improving · From the lecture homework. · f · She is committed to ___ the poor. · helping · help · helped · be help · Committed to + V-ing. · q1wq644o · rule · e · I object to · be treated · like a child. · No error · Object to + V-ing: “being treated”. · qbehlme · rule

grammar.t: Verbs followed by infinitive vs gerund
grammar.x: Verbs followed by infinitive vs gerund · To-infinitive after: seem, appear, decide, desire, want, try, endeavour, hurry, fail, happen, refuse, promise, prove, hope, plan, agree, afford, manage, offer, wish. · Gerund after: enjoy, detest, mind, resent, avoid, excuse, resist, miss, prevent, defer, delay, postpone, consider, appreciate, admire, forgive, recollect, suggest, risk, admit, deny, finish, practise, keep, quit. · Stop, forget and remember take both with a change of meaning: “stop to smoke” (pause in order to smoke) vs “stop smoking” (quit). “Forgot to bring” (did not bring) vs “forgot bringing” (brought but doesn’t recall). · Future or intention → to-infinitive (decide to, want to). Something already happening or general activity → gerund (enjoy, avoid, consider). · He decided *going* on a trip to Manali. · to go · Decide + to. · She failed *meeting* the deadline. · to meet · Fail + to. · She forgot *bringing* her laptop to the meeting. · to bring · She did not bring it. · He detests *to wait* in long queues. · waiting · Detest + gerund. · She avoids *to eat* junk food. · eating · Avoid + gerund. · She is considering *to follow* her dream. · following · Consider + gerund. · The director deferred *to make* the decision. · making · From the lecture homework. · f · I don’t mind ___ for a few minutes. · waiting · to wait · wait · waited · Mind + gerund. · q1adgprk · rule · f · They refused ___ the documents. · to sign · signing · sign · signed · Refuse + to. · q1x7f40t · rule · e · He suggested · to go · for a movie. · No error · Suggest + gerund: “suggested going”. · q1o2ofrm · rule

grammar.t: Bare infinitive after let, make, see, hear…
grammar.x: Bare infinitive after let, make, see, hear… · After let, bid, make, see, notice, feel, hear, watch, have and help (optional), the next verb is a bare infinitive (V1 without “to”): “She lets her brother borrow her car.” · In the passive, “to” comes back: “He was made to work .” “He was seen to enter .” · Let him go. Made me cry. Heard her sing. Saw him cross. No “to” in active voice. · She lets his brother *to borrow* her car. · borrow · Let + bare V1. · We heard him *to say* mean things. · say · Hear + bare V1. · We saw him *to cross* the road. · cross · See + bare V1. · f · The teacher made us ___ the poem twice. · read · to read · reading · reads · Make + bare V1 (active). · qa06rw · rule · e · He was made · work · on Sunday. · No error · Passive brings back “to”: “was made to work”. · qfv5wyk · rule

grammar.t: Causative verbs: make / have / get
grammar.x: Causative verbs: make / have / get · When someone gets a task done by another, look at what follows the object: · Doer after make / have → bare V1: “The coach made the players practise .” “He had the cook prepare dinner.” (With get + doer → to + V1: “She got the mechanic to repair it.”) · Receiver (the thing acted on) after have / get → V3: “She got her car repaired .” “I had my hair cut .” · Can the object do the action? A cook can prepare → bare V1. A car cannot repair itself → V3. · The coach made the players *to practise* every day. · practise · Doer → bare V1. · The director had the actors *rehearsed* their lines. · rehearse · Doer → bare V1. · Ranjan had the cook *prepared* a meal. · prepare · Doer → bare V1. · Anaya got her car *to repair* by the mechanic. · repaired · Receiver → V3. · The chef had the food *tasting* by his assistants. · tasted · Receiver → V3. · I got my presentation *to review* by my supervisor. · reviewed · Receiver → V3. · f · I had my watch ___ yesterday. · repaired · repair · to repair · repairing · The watch is the receiver → V3. · qu1cmrz · rule · e · She had the plumber · fixed · the leaking tap. · No error · The plumber is the doer → bare V1: “fix”. · q1q9osxb · rule

grammar.t: The three conditionals
grammar.x: The three conditionals · Type 1 (possible future) : If + simple present → will + V1. “If you finish on time, the boss will promote you.” · Type 2 (unreal present) : If + V2 / were → would / could / might + V1. “If I were the President, I would help.” Here V2 is not past time; it shows imagination. Use were for all subjects. · Type 3 (unreal past) : If + had + V3 → would / could / might + have + V3. “If Abhishek had completed his degree, they might have hired him.” · Never “will” in the if-clause. Were, not was, for imagination. Had + V3 in the if-clause → have + V3 in the result. · If you *will finish* the project on time, the boss will promote you. · finish · No will after if. · If I *was* the President of the USA, I would help poor countries. · were · Imagination → were. · If Abhishek had completed his degree, they *might hire* him. · might have hired · Type 3. · f · If I ___ wings, I would fly to the mountains. · had · have · will have · had had · Unreal present → V2. · qges0vj · rule · e · If it will rain · tomorrow, · the match will be cancelled. · No error · No will after if: “If it rains”. · qgxp39g · rule · f · If you had left earlier, you ___ the train. · would have caught · would catch · will catch · had caught · Type 3. · qof76ia · rule

grammar.t: Mixed conditionals
grammar.x: Mixed conditionals · Sometimes the time of the “if” part and the result part differ. Then the two halves are mixed. · Unreal state that never changes + past result : If + were / V2 → would have + V3. “If I were his father, I would have taught him a lesson.” You can never become his father, so the condition is a permanent unreal state, not a past event. · Past condition + present result : If + had + V3 → would / could + V1 (now / today). “If Juhi had asked for help that day, she could be alive today.” · A condition that can never be true (being someone else, being from another country) → were. A result about now or today → would / could + V1. · If I *had been* his father, I would have taught him a lesson. · were · A permanent unreal state. · If she *had been* from the USA, she would have got the opportunities she deserved. · were · Where she is from cannot change. · If Juhi had asked for help, she *could have been* alive today. · could be · Result is about today. · We would have adjusted our plans if we *were* informed. · had been informed · From the lecture homework: past condition, past result. · “If I had been his father…” is not a grammar error in general English, and many books accept it. The lecture’s point is about meaning: for a state that can never change, SSC-style answers prefer “were”. · f · If you had taken the medicine yesterday, you ___ better now. · would feel · would have felt · will feel · felt · Past condition, present result. · qsk8ozu · rule · e · If I had won · the lottery last year, · I would be rich now. · No error · Past condition, present result. Correct. · qb399po · rule

grammar.t: I wish
grammar.x: I wish · Wish about the present : I wish + V2 (were for “be”). “I wish I knew the answer.” “I wish I were more fluent.” · Wish about the past : I wish + had + V3. “I wish I had listened to my parents.” · As with conditionals, V2 here is imagination, not past time. · A past clue (when I was…, last year, then) → had + V3. No past clue → V2 / were. · I wish I *know* how to solve this problem. · knew · Present wish → V2. · I wish I *was* more fluent. · were · Imagination → were. · I wish I *listened* to my parents when my company was making profits. · had listened · Past wish. · f · I wish I ___ a car when I was in college. · had had · had · have · would have · Past wish → had + V3. · q1hhroim · rule · f · She wishes she ___ taller. · were · was · is · had been being · Present wish → were. · q1kxrrsp · rule · e · I wish · I have · more free time. · No error · Present wish → V2: “I had”. · qmsu2j2 · rule

bns.x: What replaced what, dates, section counts · Crime → Police → Court · A criminal case always moves in this order, and so do the three laws. 1. BNS — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita What is a crime and its punishment. Substantive law. 2. BNSS — Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita FIR, arrest, investigation, bail, trial. Procedural law. 3. BSA — Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam Which evidence the court accepts. Procedural law. Example: your phone is snatched. BNS §304 says snatching is a crime. BNSS governs the FIR and CCTV collection. BSA decides whether the CCTV footage is valid evidence. · What replaced what · Old law New law Indian Penal Code, 1860 BNS Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973 BNSS Indian Evidence Act, 1872 BSA IPC was a colonial law drafted under Thomas Babington Macaulay , first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council (post created by the Charter Act 1833). CrPC was first made in 1861; independent India replaced it in 1973. Aim of the new laws: modernise and decolonise criminal justice, make it victim-centric, faster and tech-enabled. · Numbers you must know · Law Chapters Sections Act no. BNS 20 358 45 BNSS 39 531 46 BSA 12 170 47 Memory trick 358 : justice ( न्याय ) must be equal, 3 + 5 = 8. 531 : police work backwards and look for odd things: 1, 3, 5 reversed. 170 : the judge wants all evidence एक साथ (1-7), and the accused's chance of escape is 0. 45 · 46 · 47 : act numbers in case order, crime → police → court. · Three dates · 11 Aug 2023 — introduced in Lok Sabha by Home Minister Amit Shah (Ministry of Home Affairs). 25 Dec 2023 — President Droupadi Murmu gave assent. This is the date they were enacted . 1 Jul 2024 — came into force. Exam alert Also on 1 July: GST launched (2017) and National Doctors' Day (Dr B.C. Roy's birthday). All asked in SSC. · Old case or new law? · Crime committed before 1 Jul 2024 → punished under IPC . Trial or investigation already pending on 1 Jul 2024 → continues under the old CrPC , because of the repeal and savings clause (BNSS §531 ). If 25 of 30 witnesses were heard under the old code, switching midway would create chaos. Proceedings that start after 1 Jul 2024 follow BNSS and BSA.

Cognizable, compoundable, courts, Magistrate · Cognizable vs non-cognizable · Cognizable (संज्ञेय) Serious crimes: murder, rape, kidnapping, robbery. Police can arrest without warrant and investigate without the Magistrate's approval (when legal conditions are met). Non-cognizable Less serious. Police need the Magistrate's approval to investigate and a warrant to arrest. · Compoundable, criminal and civil · Compoundable Parties can settle, e.g. out of court or in a Lok Adalat. Small theft in the mohalla. Non-compoundable No settlement allowed: murder, rape. Criminal vs civil Murder, dowry harassment, theft are criminal. Divorce is civil (दीवानी) . · Who is a Magistrate? · A Magistrate is a judge of the lowest criminal court. Court hierarchy: 1 Supreme Court 2 High Court 3 District / Sessions Judge 4 Magistrates (Chief Judicial Magistrate appointed by the High Court) Smaller offences go to Magistrates. They also grant default bail and receive search-and-seizure videos.

Sedition, terrorism, organised crime, mob lynching · Firsts in BNS · Child defined for the first time: below 18 years §2 . All definitions are in section 2. Terrorism, organised crime, petty organised crime and mob lynching defined. Community service added as a punishment §4 . · Sedition is gone · Colonial sedition (राजद्रोह) , IPC §124A , has been removed . In its place: BNS §152 — acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India . · Terrorism and organised crime · §113 Terrorist act Intends to threaten unity, integrity, security of India, intimidate the public or disturb public order. Death or life if death results. Conspiring, organising or assisting: 5 years to life + fine of at least ₹5 lakh. §111 Organised crime Continuing unlawful activity on behalf of a crime syndicate : kidnapping, extortion, contract killing, land grabbing, financial scams, cyber crime. Death or life if anyone dies; otherwise 5 years to life. · Petty organised crime and mob lynching · §112 Petty organised crime Causes general insecurity: chain snatching, pickpocketing, theft by a gang . 1 to 7 years + fine. §103(2) Mob lynching Murder by a group of 5 or more on grounds of race, caste, sex, language, place of birth or belief. Death or life + fine. Memory trick 111 organised (all ones, everyone organised) → 112 petty organised → 113 terrorist → remove the middle 1 from 113 = 103 mob lynching. · More new provisions · §69 Sexual intercourse by deceitful means : false promise of marriage or job. §70(2) Death possible for gang rape of a woman under 18 (IPC: under 12). §106(2) Hit and run : causing death by rash driving and fleeing without informing police/Magistrate → up to 10 years + fine . §95 Hiring a child to commit an offence: 3 to 10 years + fine. §141 Importing a girl under 21 or a boy under 18 for illicit intercourse (boys added).

Chapter V, murder, theft vs snatching · Chapter V: women and children · Sections 63–99 . IPC scattered these; BNS puts them in one chapter. If a question on rape, stalking or cruelty gives an option outside 63–99, eliminate it. §63 Rape definition · §69 deceitful intercourse · §70 gang rape §77 Voyeurism : secretly watching or recording §78 Stalking : following a woman SSC answer for "first time" in sexual offences: gender neutrality in certain offences (child offences now cover boys). · Offences against the body (Ch VI) · 100 Culpable homicide 101/103 Murder / punishment: death or life + fine 108 Abetment of suicide 137/138 Kidnapping / abduction (abduction is by force or deceit) 143 Trafficking of persons (Fundamental Right, Art. 23) · Your phone: theft or snatching? · 303 Theft (चोरी) : taken quietly from your pocket while you slept 304 Snatching (छिनैती) : grabbed from your hand by a biker. New. 308 Extortion : taken by blackmail or threat 309 Robbery (लूट) : taken at knifepoint 310 Dacoity (डकैती) : robbery by 5 or more Memory trick 303 then 304: quiet first, then grab.

Community service, defamation, general exceptions · Community service · §4 lists punishments: death, life, imprisonment, forfeiture, fine and now community service . Unpaid work for society: cleaning, planting trees, helping in orphanages. Only for petty offences (6 offences). Keeps jails from overcrowding. Never for murder, mob lynching or domestic violence. Defined in BNSS §23 . · Defamation and unpaid fines · §356 Defamation : up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or community service . §8(5) Jail for not paying a fine: up to ₹5,000 → 2 months ; up to ₹10,000 → 4 months . Memory trick 356 is also Article 356, President's Rule. The President is quick to feel defamed. · What BNS changed, in numbers · Imprisonment increased 33 offences Fine increased 83 offences Mandatory minimum sentence 23 offences Community service 6 offences · When it's not an offence · §20 Child under 7 : nothing is an offence. §21 Child 7–12 without maturity to understand: no offence. §14 Soldier firing on a mob on a superior's lawful order: no offence. §18 Accident while doing a lawful act with care. §27 Guardian who, in good faith and for the child's benefit, allows a risky surgery: not guilty . §45 Abetment (उकसाना) : instigating, conspiring or aiding. Liable even if not at the scene.

Thana, chowki, e-FIR, zero FIR, CCTNS · Thana vs chowki · A city is divided into areas, each under a thana (police station) with a fixed jurisdiction. Head: SHO / Thanedar (Inspector). Each thana area has several chowkis (police posts) nearby. Head: Daroga (Sub-Inspector). FIR is registered only at a thana. A chowki only writes your complaint in its General Diary (GD) . A real FIR gets you a free copy . A GD entry gives no receipt. · FIR under BNSS §173 · Information on a cognizable offence can be given orally, in writing or electronically . e-FIR : lodge online; sign within 3 days at the station. Offences punishable with 3 to 7 years: police may do a preliminary inquiry (DSP-level permission) first. Memory trick 173 = एक साथ तीन : information can be given 1 (ek) saath 3 ways. e-FIR signed in 3 days. · Zero FIR · You're robbed at knifepoint on a highway. You won't stop to find the local thana; you escape. At the next safe thana, 70 km away, you file an FIR. That is a zero FIR : file at any police station, regardless of where the crime happened . The station transfers it to the right one. "Zero" = zero boundaries. · CCTNS · Crime and Criminal Tracking Network & Systems : a national portal linking every police station. All FIRs and investigation records are on it. A stolen car found near the Nepal border can be matched to an FIR in Bhopal. An unidentified body in Kanpur can be matched to a missing-person report in Uttarakhand. BNSS gives access to FIR through CCTNS. · §530: electronic mode · Trials and all proceedings, including e-summons , e-warrant , witness examination and judgment, may be held in electronic mode . Memory trick 530: your 5 fingers on the keyboard get 3 e-powers (e-FIR, e-summons, e-warrant) with 0 boundaries.

24 hours, 15 days, 60/90 days, bail vs parole · Rights on arrest · §47 Grounds of arrest must be told immediately upon arrest . §58 No detention beyond 24 hours without a Magistrate's order (also Art. 22). §38 Right to meet an advocate of your choice during interrogation (not throughout it). Memory trick "I won't say anything till my lawyer comes." He अड़ जाता है → अड़तीस = 38. · Police custody in parts · Police custody = lock-up; police can question any time. Judicial custody = jail; police need court permission. §187 Police custody is still 15 days max , but it can now be taken in parts (e.g. 8 days, later 7) during the first 40 or 60 days. Effect: the accused may be denied bail for the full 60/90 days , since police can call him back. Memory trick 187: 8 + 7 = 15 days, in two parts. · Default bail · Police must file a charge sheet (motive, weapon, relationship, progress) within: 60 days if the offence carries under 10 years 90 days if 10+ years, life or death If not, the accused gets default bail as a right. It is granted by the Magistrate . · Bail, parole, bail bond · Bail No conviction yet; released while the case continues. Parole Already convicted. Good conduct can earn temporary leave (say 20 days), then back to jail. Bail bond An undertaking for release with a surety : money deposited so you won't run. Abscond and it is forfeited. · Other bail sections · §479 Undertrial cap: first-time offender released on bond after 1/3 of maximum sentence; others after 1/2 . Not for death/life offences. §480 Bail in non-bailable offences · §482 Anticipatory bail (before arrest). §218 Government must decide on sanction to prosecute an officer within 120 days , or sanction is deemed granted .

Video search, forensics, witness protection · §105: video of search & seizure · In films, a corrupt officer plants drugs during a raid. §105 stops this: every search and seizure must be audio-video recorded . Without a warrant, police can't even cross your gate. With one, officers keep cameras on the whole time. Mobile phones are fine. Recording goes to the Magistrate without delay. If police don't record, you may record them. Memory trick 105: the officer holds 1 camera with a round lens ( 0 ) in his 5 fingers. · Forensics and medical reports · §176 For offences punishable with 7 years or more (a "big crime"), forensic experts must visit the crime scene and video-record evidence collection. §184 Medical report of a rape victim goes to the investigating officer within 7 days . §193 Investigation of sexual offences within 2 months ; victim told of progress within 90 days . Memory trick 176 has the 7 inside it: forensics for 7+ years. · Samples, summons, witnesses · §349 Magistrate can order specimen signatures, handwriting, fingerprints and now voice samples . §63 Summons: in duplicate, signed and sealed, or in encrypted electronic form . §398 Witness protection scheme : States must protect witnesses; they can depose by video conferencing. Vulnerable witnesses can have identity concealed. Cyber crimes are investigated by cyber crime cells set up by government . Memory trick 398: the State posts 3 guards from 9 am to 8 pm.

60 days charges, 30/45 days judgment, summary trial · Timeline table · Step Limit § Produce before Magistrate 24 h 58 Sign e-FIR 3 days 173 Rape medical report 7 days 184 Police custody total 15 days 187 Charge sheet (under 10 yrs) 60 days 187 Charge sheet (10+ yrs) 90 days 187 Sexual offence probe 2 months 193 Victim progress update 90 days 193 Sanction to prosecute officer 120 days 218 Frame charges after first hearing 60 days 251 Judgment after arguments 30 (max 45) 258 Plea bargaining application 30 days 290 · Courts · §6 (Chapter II) Classes of criminal courts : Court of Session, Judicial Magistrates, Executive Magistrates. §21 Offences under BNS 64–71 are tried, as far as practicable, by a court presided over by a woman . §258 Judges can't sit on a decision: judgment within 30 days of arguments ending, extendable to 45 . · Special trials · §356 Trial in absentia of a proclaimed offender : accused of an offence punishable with 10+ years, life or death, who absconded to avoid trial. Not "any person", not someone who is ill. §283 Summary trial : quick trial for non-serious offences. Maximum sentence 3 months . §25(1) Several offences proved in one trial: the court may make sentences run concurrently or consecutively . · Plea bargaining · Accused admits guilt in exchange for a lesser punishment. First added to CrPC by the 2005 amendment . §290 Application within 30 days of framing of charges. Exam alert Options that cover every case with commas or brackets ("30 days, extendable to 45") are usually correct. "May" often marks the right legal option.

Document, primary vs secondary, §57, §63 · What BSA changed · Replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (which predates electronics). 12 chapters, 170 sections. Aligns evidence law with forensic science and digital technology . Digital evidence can be primary evidence. Joint trial : a proven confession by one accused that affects others counts against all. · Document now means more · §2 Document includes electronic and digital records: emails, server logs, computer and phone files, messages, websites, location data, voicemails. Someone messages "send ₹500, I'll get you a job" and keeps the money. The WhatsApp chat is evidence; it doesn't need to be on paper. Tip: get any paid promise confirmed on email. What counts as an electronic record is defined by the IT Act, 2000 . · Primary vs secondary · §57 Primary The original itself. A CCTV clip saved at once on the DVR, office computer and cloud: each copy is primary , even if the DVR is destroyed. Same for your WhatsApp backup on Drive. §58 Secondary Proves what the original said: certified copies, counterparts, oral account. You lose your signed agreement; the other party's copy works. · §63: the certificate · A screenshot alone isn't enough; it could be edited or AI-made. Electronic records need a certificate (including from a digital forensic expert) that the device worked properly and the record wasn't tampered with. Memory trick 63 is also the rape definition in BNS. In BSA, 63 is the electronic-record certificate.

Direct evidence, §23, expert opinion · Oral evidence must be direct · §55 Sonam slaps Archana outside the office. In court: Riya "I saw it myself." Direct ✓ Mohan "I wasn't there; Riya told me." Hearsay ✗ Vishal "I didn't see, but she slaps everyone." Assumption ✗ Only what the witness personally saw, heard or perceived counts. · Admission vs confession · §15 Admission Facts that raise an inference , without accepting guilt: "I alone had the computer-room key and opened the paper file at 10 pm, but I didn't leak it." Confession Directly accepting the crime : "I leaked it on Telegram because my raise was refused." · Confession to police: §23 · Rohan tells police "I stole the necklace and hid it in my water tank." In court this cannot be proved against him , because police could beat or threaten a confession out. An SMS confession to a police officer is treated the same. Exception: discovery. Police recover the necklace from the tank. That part is proved by the discovery. A confession recorded before a Magistrate under the proper procedure (BNSS §183 ) can be used. Memory trick Police can't get a confession with 2–3 slaps → §23. · Expert opinion and more · §39 Tea served by Rohan has poison, says the forensic expert. Rohan isn't automatically guilty; the expert answers only the scientific question. Opinion is relevant but not conclusive ; the court decides. §26 Dying declaration : statements of persons who are dead or can't be found. §24 Confession of co-accused in a joint trial. §121 Estoppel : you can't deny what you made someone believe and act on.

IPC 124A, 377, 497, 510 and food safety · IPC provisions in questions · 124A Sedition. Removed; replaced by BNS 152. 377 Criminalised "unnatural offences" incl. consensual same-sex relations. Decriminalised for adults in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) . 497 Adultery. Struck down in Joseph Shine (2018). 510 Drunken misconduct in public: simple imprisonment up to 24 hours or fine up to ₹10 , or both. · Food safety · BNS §274 food adulteration: up to 6 months. The special law with life imprisonment for making or selling unsafe food: Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 .

schemes.x: Every CGL shift asks 1–3 scheme questions. They come in only a few shapes: ministry , launch year / date , launch place , objective , beneficiaries & eligibility , amount (loan, pension, subsidy), outlay , full form , and which one is NOT a feature . Each lesson here is built around those shapes. · Two kinds of central schemes · Type · Money · Examples · Central Sector (CS) · 100% from the Centre; run by central ministries · PM-KISAN, PM SVANidhi, PM-DevINE, VVP-II, PM Vishwakarma, PM-VBRY · Centrally Sponsored (CSS) · Centre + State share; states implement · MGNREGA/VB-G RAM G, PMAY, JJM, PM POSHAN, PM SHRI, Samagra Shiksha, Mission Vatsalya, RKVY · CSS sharing pattern (Centre : State) · States / UTs · Share · General states · 60 : 40 · 8 North-East + Himalayan states (HP, Uttarakhand) + UT of J&K · 90 : 10 · UTs without legislature (Ladakh, Chandigarh, A&N, Lakshadweep, DNH&DD) · 100 : 0 · UTs with legislature (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K) · J&K 90:10; Delhi & Puducherry 60:40 · 6-9-100 : sixty (general), ninety (NE & hills), hundred (UTs without an assembly). Only three UTs have a legislature: D elhi, P uducherry, J &K → “ DPJ ”. · Study schemes as a story, not a list. The second lecture's method: every scheme answers a problem the previous one left behind. No bank account → Jan Dhan → no collateral → MUDRA → SC/ST and women left out → Stand-Up India. Make in India → PLI → ECMS → MPMS → Semiconductor Mission. census.x: Census (जनगणना) is the official count of every person in the country, with details such as age, sex, literacy, religion, language, work, housing and migration. India takes it every 10 years (decennial). The data decides schemes, SC/ST reservation, redrawing of constituencies and sharing of taxes between Centre and states. · Timeline · c. 300 BCE · Kautilya's Arthashastra mentions collecting population data for taxation. · 16th cent. · Ain-i-Akbari (Abul Fazl) records population, industry and wealth under Akbar. · 1824, 1827–28 · James Prinsep counts Allahabad and Banaras. · 1830 · Henry Walter counts Dacca (Dhaka) city → called the Father of Indian Census . · 1872 · First census of India under Lord Mayo . Non-synchronous: regions counted at different times. · 17 Feb 1881 · First synchronous (regular) census under Lord Ripon . Census Commissioner W.C. Plowden . reports.x: Every CGL shift has 1–2 questions on reports & indices. They come in only four shapes : (1) India's rank (most asked), (2) who is #1 , (3) who publishes it , (4) the pillars / indicators of a few famous indices (HDI, MPI, GHI, Gender Gap, WHR, Press Freedom). Sometimes a fifth: did India go up or down from last year? Learn those five things per index and nothing else. · What to learn for each index · Priority · What · Example · ★★★ · India's rank (+ last year) · Press Freedom 157 (151) · ★★★ · Publisher · Press Freedom → RSF (Paris) · ★★ · Top country · Press Freedom → Norway, 10th year · ★★ · Pillars (famous ones only) · HDI → 3 dimensions, 4 indicators · ★ · Bottom country, India's score · Eritrea last; skip scores except a few · The Scandinavian rule. In any 'good-life' index (happiness, peace, gender, press, HDI, SDG, corruption, energy) the #1 is almost always one of the five Nordic countries: Finland, Iceland, Norway, Denmark, Sweden . If only one Nordic country is in the options, that is your best guess. Who owns what: F inland = Happy + SDG · I celand = Peace + Gender + HDI · N orway = Press + Democracy · D enmark = Corruption-free (+ 4th in climate) · S weden = Energy transition. festivals.h: त्योहार के प्रश्न कैसे आते हैं
festivals.x: India has roughly 140 festivals worth knowing — about five per state. The 2025 papers (CGL, CHSL, MTS, CPO, Steno, Delhi Police, Selection Post) asked them in four shapes: (1) which state (most common), (2) which tribe or community , (3) what is worshipped or marked (a deity, a harvest, a new year), and (4) statement / 'best describes' questions on rituals. The lecture's rule: fix the state first; details come second. · Name endings give the state away. -Kut → Mizoram (Chapchar Kut, Mim Kut, Pawl Kut). -Ngai → Manipur (Gaan-Ngai, Lui-Ngai-Ni). Habba → Karnataka (Gowri Habba, Gombe Habba — habba means festival in Kannada). Pooram / Vallam / Aarattu → Kerala. Pongal / Deepam / Attam → Tamil Nadu. Losar / Lochar / Losoong → Tibetan-Buddhist belt (Ladakh, HP, Sikkim, Arunachal). -Sim → Santhal (Erok Sim, Magh Sim). · When the state in your head is missing from the options. Naga people live in Manipur and Mizoram too. So if a -Ngai festival's options lack Manipur, mark Nagaland ; if a -Kut festival's options lack Mizoram, mark Nagaland . Bushu (Dimasa) is Assam and Nagaland — if Assam is absent, Nagaland. · Solve statements with logic. Extreme words — only, exclusively, without any, universally — are usually false. A loose, descriptive statement with no hard fact is usually true. The Rajasthan International Folk Festival 'exclusively showcases Manganiyars and Langas without international artists' — false; the name itself says International . · Hindu months — the calendar every question uses · Month · Roughly · What falls here · Chaitra · Mar–Apr · Most New Years (Ugadi, Gudi Padwa, Cheti Chand, Navreh) · Vaishakh · Apr–May · Baisakhi, Vishu, Bohag Bihu, Buddha Purnima · Jyeshtha · May–Jun · Ganga Dussehra · Ashadha · Jun–Jul · Rath Yatra, Goncha · Shravan (Sawan) · Jul–Aug · Hareli, Teej, Jivati, Pola · Bhadrapada (Bhado) · Aug–Sep · Onam, Karma, Paryushana, Ganesh Chaturthi · Ashwin · Sep–Oct · Navratri, Durga Puja, Bathukamma, Kojagiri · Kartik · Oct–Nov · Diwali, Chhath, Karva Chauth, Pushkar, Kati Bihu · Pausha–Magha · Dec–Feb · Lohri, Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Magh Bihu · Phalguna · Feb–Mar · Holi, Mahashivratri, Yaoshang · Use the season as a clue. A bonfire means winter (Lohri, Bhogi, Magh Bihu's Uruka) — not March or October. Chaitra + 'new year' is almost always right. Rice is a kharif crop: harvested around Oct–Nov , so 'new rice' festivals (Nuakhai, Puthari, Nongkrem, Loku) sit in autumn. · Pre-harvest vs post-harvest. Pre-harvest (or sowing) festivals ask the gods for a good crop; post-harvest festivals thank them. Many PYQs hinge on this one word — Sungremong is pre-harvest, Tokhu Emong post-harvest; Chapchar Kut before sowing, Mim Kut after the maize harvest; Erok Sim at sowing, Magh Sim after harvest. · Fix the state first: -Kut Mizoram, -Ngai Manipur, Habba Karnataka, Pooram Kerala, Losar Tibetan belt. · If Manipur/Mizoram is missing from options for a Ngai/Kut festival → Nagaland. · Extreme words (only, exclusively, without) → usually false. · Chaitra = New Year; bonfire = winter; new rice = Oct–Nov.

festivals.t: New Year & harvest festivals across India
festivals.x: Most regional New Years fall in Chaitra–Vaishakh (Mar–Apr) , when the Sun enters Aries and the rabi harvest is in. The Sun reaches the Tropic of Capricorn at the winter solstice (22 Dec), then begins its northward journey (Uttarayan) ; around 14 January it enters the zodiac Makara (Capricorn) . It is not the longest day (21 June), not monsoon, and not the start of north India's harvest (rabi is cut in March–April). · Lohri is 13 January, the night before Makar Sankranti — not the winter solstice (22 Dec). The PYQ linked Lohri with sugarcane harvesting (rice is cut in Oct–Nov; mangoes are summer). · New Year ↔ harvest pairs. Assam's three Bihus split the year: Bohag (Apr, New Year) → Kati (Oct, lamps for the growing crop) → Magh (Jan, harvest feast). Kerala: Vishu (New Year) vs Onam (harvest). Tamil Nadu: Puthandu (New Year) vs Pongal (harvest). · Chaitra–Vaishakh New Years: Ugadi, Gudi Padwa, Puthandu, Vishu, Poila Boishakh, Bohag Bihu, Baisakhi, Cheiraoba, Navreh, Cheti Chand. · Vishu = Kerala New Year (not harvest); Onam = harvest. · Makar Sankranti = Uttarayan, Sun enters Capricorn; Pongal, Magh Bihu, Lohri/Maghi, Khichdi. · Lohri 13 Jan, a night before Sankranti.

iprplans.x: Industrial Policy Resolutions (IPR) and Five Year Plans are among the least-taught but most-asked economy topics. The 2025 papers (CGL, CHSL, Steno, Selection Post, NTPC) asked them in five shapes: (1) which year / which policy , (2) key feature , (3) 'not associated with' (exclusion), (4) assertion–reason , and (5) matching (4 items vs 5 options). The lecture's rule: learn it as one story — government-controlled (1948) → tighter (1956) → small units (1977) → efficiency (1980) → open up (1991). · Three economic systems · System · Who decides what to produce · Example · Socialist (समाजवादी) · Government decides everything; aim is equal distribution · India before 1991 (mostly PSUs), USSR · Capitalist (पूंजीवादी) · Market/profit decides; state stays out of business · USA, France · Mixed (मिश्रित) · Both sectors; government mostly regulates the market (IRDAI for insurance, SEBI for shares) · India — declared by IPR 1948 · Mixed economy test: private companies run the business, the government writes the rules. Insurance: LIC + ICICI + Bajaj, all regulated by IRDAI . Shares: PSU and private companies, all regulated by SEBI . Public-sector decisions are taken by government; private-sector decisions by individuals — both statements true. · Invisible hand · Given by · Adam Smith — 'Father of Economics' · Book · An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776) · Idea · Each person working for own profit unknowingly benefits society — the baker buys flour → mill workers and farmers earn too · PSU vocabulary · PSU / PSE · Any government company: government owns 51% or more of shares · CPSE · Central Public Sector Enterprise — central government stake ≥ 51% · SPSE · State Public Sector Enterprise — state government stake ≥ 51% · Navratna / Miniratna · Scheme of 1997 · Maharatna · Scheme of 2009 (the biggest CPSEs) · Three solving rules from the lecture. (1) Never use 'mutual friend' logic — A links to B, B to C, so A to C? Economics options are built to trap that. Pick only a direct link you have read. (2) Extreme words — all, entirely, only, complete — are usually false ("reserved list was eliminated entirely " ✗). (3) If the question asks a negative consequence , drop every positive-sounding option first. · Why study IPRs with Five Year Plans? They move together: IPR 1956 ↔ 2nd Plan (Mahalanobis, heavy industry); 1977 statement ↔ Janata rolling plan; 1991 NIP ↔ 8th Plan (first after LPG). · Socialist = government decides; capitalist = market decides; mixed = both, government regulates. · India became a mixed economy through IPR 1948. · Invisible hand = Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations 1776. · PSU = government stake ≥ 51% (CPSE central, SPSE state). · No 'mutual friend' logic; extreme words usually false.

Key facts · Date · 6 April 1948 — first industrial policy of independent India · Presented by · Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee , first Industry (& Supply) Minister · Where · Constituent Assembly (Legislative) — no Lok Sabha yet · Main aim · Promote the public sector ; declared India a mixed economy · Categories · Four · Mookerjee → मुखड़ा : he gave India's industry its first face (मुखड़ा). Patel = first Home Minister; Mahalanobis was never a minister — he was a planner. · The four categories — remember S·B·I·O · Category · Count · What it meant · S · Strategic — exclusive Central monopoly · 3 · Arms & ammunition, atomic energy, railway transport · B · Basic — new units only by the State · 6 · Coal, iron & steel, aircraft, shipbuilding, telephone/telegraph/wireless equipment, mineral oils. Existing private units could continue (reviewed after 10 years) but could not expand freely · I · Important — regulated by government · 18 · Private allowed but centrally regulated: sugar, cement, heavy chemicals, cotton & woollen textiles, etc. · O · Others · rest · Open to private enterprise, individuals, cooperatives · “SBI-O” and 3 × 6 = 18. Strategic 3, Basic 6, Important 18 (3 × 6), then Others. Read it like the bank: SBI + O. · The lecture first said 'six' strategic, then corrected itself to three. Strategic = 3 (arms & ammunition, atomic energy, railways). The six are the basic industries. · Nehru was Prime Minister from 15 August 1947 , not from 1952. What began in 1952 was the first elected Lok Sabha . Until then the Constituent Assembly also worked as the provisional Parliament — which is why the 1948 resolution was placed there. · Why so anti-private? Memories of the East India Company (a trader that became ruler), socialist ideals (DPSP Art. 39(b)–(c): prevent concentration of wealth) and the wish to protect small artisans. The lecture's image: the government behaved like an over-caring parent until 1990. · IPR 1948: 6 April 1948, S.P. Mookerjee, Constituent Assembly. · Four categories SBI-O: Strategic 3 (central monopoly), Basic 6 (new units by State), Important 18 (regulated), Others. · Made India a mixed economy; main aim = promote public sector.

Key facts · Date · 30 April 1956 · Nickname · Economic Constitution of India · Linked plan · 2nd Five Year Plan (1956–61, Mahalanobis model) · Central theme · State control of the 'commanding heights' — public sector to lead heavy and basic industry · Classification · Three schedules — A, B, C · Also said · Support small & cottage industries; reduce regional disparities; fair treatment of labour · Schedules A · B · C · Schedule · Count · Rule · A · 17 · Exclusive responsibility of the State (the old 3 strategic grew to 17) · B · 12 · Progressively State-owned; private sector may supplement (the old 6 basic doubled to 12) · C · rest · Left to private initiative, under licensing (old 18 + Others merged) · “17-12-बाकी” and the growth story: 3 → 17 , 6 → 12 (doubled), 18 + others → C . Two schedules for government, one for private — the state holds the steering wheel. · Decode the economics English. 'State control of the commanding heights of the economy' simply means the government took the top seat in every key decision. That is the 1956 answer. 'Import-led growth', 'consumer goods', 'full privatisation' — all traps. · 1956 was the basis of the 2nd Plan, not the 3rd. In the 'NOT associated' PYQ, 'formed the basis of the Third Five Year Plan' was the odd one out. (Note: the 1956 text did mention reducing regional disparities and helping small industry — but in 'key feature' questions the three-schedule classification is the best answer.) · Licence Raj (लाइसेंस राज) · Meaning · Private firms needed government licences to start, expand, change product or import machines · Law · Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951 · Became densest · After IPR 1956 · Effects · Entry barriers, hindered expansion, inefficiency, red-tapism, corruption · Ended · Largely by NIP 1991 · Freight Equalisation Policy · Introduced · 1952 · Abolished · 1993 · Idea · Minerals (coal, iron) cost the same to transport anywhere in India — to balance industrial growth · Result · Mineral-rich east (Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Bengal) lost its natural advantage; industry clustered in the west (Gujarat, Maharashtra) · Why heavy industry? Poverty goes when jobs come; jobs come from industry. The lecture's logic: the government wanted big industry but did not trust Tata/Birla to lead it — so the State took Schedule A and B itself. · IPR 1956: 30 April 1956, 'Economic Constitution', basis of 2nd Plan. · Three schedules: A 17 (State only), B 12 (State leads, private supplements), C rest. · Commanding heights = State control; Licence Raj densest after 1956. · Freight Equalisation 1952–1993 hurt the mineral-rich east.

The control years · 1969 · MRTP Act — Monopolies & Restrictive Trade Practices (in force 1 June 1970); 14 banks nationalised (19 July) · 1973 · FERA — Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (replaced the 1947 Act); Industrial Policy Statement 1973 (joint sector) · 1977 · Industrial Policy Statement — George Fernandes, Janata govt (23 Dec) · 1978 · District Industries Centres begin (1 May 1978) · 1980 · Industrial Policy Statement (23 July); 6 more banks nationalised (15 April) · MRTP Act 1969 · Aim · Stop concentration of economic power and monopolies · How · Big firms (assets above a limit: ₹20 crore in 1969, ₹100 crore from 1985) needed approval to set up or expand · 1991 · Asset threshold removed · Replaced by · Competition Act 2002 (CCI set up 2003); MRTP repealed 2009 · MRTP threshold was ₹20 crore (later ₹100 crore), not ₹500 crore as one lecture said. And MRTP did not need '75 licences' — that was classroom exaggeration for the paperwork maze. · FERA → FEMA · FERA · 1973 (in force 1974); tightly controlled foreign exchange; violation = criminal offence · FEMA · Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 (in force 1 June 2000); violation = civil offence · Trick · R = Regulation = Rigid; M = Management = Mild · FERA is 1973, not 1971. One lecture said 'FERA 1971 became FEMA 1999' — the year is 1973. Also, MRTP (1969) and FERA (1973) were separate Acts; the 1980 statement did not create them. · Industrial Policy Statement 1977 · By · George Fernandes , Industry Minister, Janata government · Core idea · Decentralisation — take industry to villages and small towns; rural and urban growth together · Small units · Priority to small-scale, cottage and tiny units (tiny sector defined); SSI reserved list raised from ~180 to 500+ items · New body · District Industries Centre (DIC) — single window per district for loans, raw material, training, marketing · Big houses · Restrictions on large business houses tightened · Decentralisation is not disinvestment. One lecture called 1977's decentralisation 'disinvestment' (selling government shares). Disinvestment began in 1991–92 . In 1977, decentralisation meant spreading small industries to districts. · “77 = गांव की ओर” : 1977 took industry to the village — tiny units + DIC. “80 = अच्छा करो” : 1980 tried to make the public sector efficient. · Industrial Policy Statement 1980 · Mood · First softening: competition, modernisation, selective liberalisation ; automatic capacity expansion allowed · Objectives · Optimum use of installed capacity · higher productivity · employment · correct regional imbalance ('nucleus plants') · agro-based industry · promote export-oriented and import-substitution industries · consumer protection against high prices and bad quality · economic federalism · Public sector · Revive its efficiency · NOT an objective · Permitting maximum FDI — that is 1991 · The 1980 PYQ confused even the teacher. Official objectives include promoting export-oriented industries and consumer protection — so those are NOT the odd ones out. The option that does not fit 1980 is 'permitting maximum foreign direct investment' . · US/China vs India on monopoly. The goal — stop wealth piling up with a few — was the same everywhere. The US and China answered with more competitors ; India answered by capping the big firms . The lecture's point: capping killed growth; competition would have grown it. · MRTP 1969 (threshold ₹20 cr → ₹100 cr 1985 → removed 1991) → Competition Act 2002 → repealed 2009. · FERA 1973 (criminal) → FEMA 1999 (civil). · 1977: George Fernandes, decentralisation, tiny units, DIC (1978). · 1980: efficiency of PSUs, selective liberalisation; max FDI is NOT a 1980 objective.

Key facts · Date · 24 July 1991 (same day as the Union Budget) · Trigger · Balance of payments crisis 1990–91 (reserves for ~2 weeks of imports; gold pledged) · Prime Minister · P.V. Narasimha Rao (also held Industry) · Finance Minister · Manmohan Singh · Pillars · L iberalisation · P rivatisation · G lobalisation · Status · Still India's last full industrial policy · What 1991 changed · Area · Change · De-licensing · Compulsory licensing abolished except a short list (18 then; now 4 : cigars & cigarettes, electronic aerospace & defence equipment, industrial explosives, hazardous chemicals) · De-reservation · Public-sector-only list cut from 17 to 8 · FDI · Automatic approval up to 51% in 34 high-priority industries — first time foreigners could hold majority · Technology · Automatic approval for foreign technology agreements · MRTP · Asset threshold removed; no prior approval for big firms · Disinvestment · Sale of part of government's stake in PSUs (from 1991–92) · Trade · Tariffs cut, quantitative restrictions and import licensing phased out · Public-sector reserved list · 1956 · 17 (Schedule A) · 1991 · 8 · 2001 · 3 — defence, atomic energy, railway transport · Today · 2 — atomic energy and railway operations · Dec 2025 · SHANTI Act lets private firms build and run nuclear power plants; sensitive fuel-cycle work stays with government · Numbers the lectures got wrong. 1991 reserved 8 industries (one lecture said 5 'core areas'). FDI up to 51% was in 34 high-priority industries (one lecture said 47). Also, 1991 is the latest industrial policy — the '2002, 2011, 2022 policies' in one lecture were other documents (2011 was the National Manufacturing Policy). · “1991 = undo button.” Whatever 1950–1990 did, 1991 reversed: licence → de-licence; reserved → de-reserved; FERA → (FEMA 1999); MRTP → (Competition Act 2002); closed → FDI. L because licences broke firms, P because PSUs were inefficient, G because we needed money and competition. · Nationalisation is NOT a pillar of 1991. Nationalisation (making companies government-owned) was 1969 and 1980 for banks. Options mixing 'nationalisation' into LPG are wrong. · 1991 → 8th Plan. The 8th Plan (1992–97) was the first plan after LPG and moved India to indicative planning — the government points the direction, the market does the running. · NIP 24 July 1991: BoP crisis; PM Narasimha Rao, FM Manmohan Singh; LPG. · Licensing now only 4 industries; reserved list 17 → 8 → 3 → 2 (atomic energy, railways). · 51% FDI automatic in 34 industries; MRTP threshold removed; disinvestment begins. · Nationalisation ≠ LPG.

iprplans.h: 1991 से पहले बनाम बाद · PYQ पैटर्न
iprplans.x: Two phases in one table · 1947–1990 · After 1991 · Role of state · Over-caring parent; public sector dominant · Regulator and facilitator · Trade strategy · Inward-looking , import substitution, high tariffs · Outward-looking; tariffs cut, QRs removed · Private sector · Licence Raj, MRTP, FERA · De-licensed, competition law, FEMA · Foreign capital · Very limited · FDI welcomed (51% → up to 100% in many sectors) · Result · Protected market → inefficiency, low innovation · Competition → efficiency · Match the period, then the tone. Any 1947–90 question: answer contains inward-looking, import substitution, protection of domestic industry, entry barriers, inefficiency . Any post-1991 question: reduced tariffs, removed licensing, removed quantitative restrictions, prudential norms . · Why public sector got the lead (1947–90) · Correct reason · A tool to achieve social goals , balanced regional development and control of strategic industries · Wrong reasons · 'Public sector was inherently more efficient' · 'private sector had enough capital and technology' · 'no demand for industrial goods' · Banking reforms · Bank nationalisation · 14 banks on 19 July 1969; 6 banks on 15 April 1980 · Narasimham Committee I · 1991 — financial system reforms · Narasimham Committee II · 1998 — banking sector reforms; merge and consolidate strong public sector banks · Prudential norms · Capital adequacy — CRAR = Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (Basel norms) · Assertion–reason on trade reforms. 'Trade reforms removed quantitative restrictions on imports and exports' ✓. 'Trade reforms increased import licensing to support domestic manufacturers' ✗ — increasing licences is the pre-1991 habit. · The lecture's parenting analogy. A child never allowed to fall never learns to stand. 1947–90 India held its industry's hand so tightly that it never learned to compete — and 1991 finally let go. · 1947–90: inward-looking, import substitution, protection → inefficiency. · Post-1991: tariffs cut, licensing and QRs removed, prudential norms (CRAR). · Public sector's lead: social goals, balanced regional development, strategic control. · Banks nationalised 1969 (14) and 1980 (6); Narasimham I 1991, II 1998 (merge & consolidate).

Mahalanobis · Known as · Father of Indian Statistics · Founded · Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata (1931); journal Sankhya · Birthday · 29 June = National Statistics Day · Also · Chaired the National Income Committee (1949) · Harrod and Domar were not both British. Roy Harrod was British; Evsey Domar was American. And the Gadgil formula belongs to the 4th Plan — one lecture put it on the 3rd. · Why the 3rd Plan failed · 1962 · War with China · 1965 · War with Pakistan · 1965–67 · Severe droughts; also rupee devaluation (1966) and inflation · Set up then · IDBI (1964), Food Corporation of India (1965), Agricultural Prices Commission (1965; renamed CACP 1985) · Plan Holiday · Period · 1966–69 — three annual plans (1966-67, 1967-68, 1968-69) · Name · Coined in mockery by the opposition and press · Why · Wars, drought, money shortage after the 3rd Plan · Big event · Green Revolution (HYV seeds) began in 1966 · IPR 1956 + 2nd Plan = one project. The policy reserved heavy industry for the State; the plan funded it — Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur. · 1st 1951–56 Harrod-Domar, agriculture, 2.1→3.6%. · 2nd 1956–61 Mahalanobis, rapid industrialisation, steel: Bhilai–USSR, Rourkela–W. Germany, Durgapur–UK. · 3rd 1961–66 self-reliance first time; failed (1962, 1965 wars, drought). · Plan Holiday 1966–69: three annual plans.
