iprplans.h: आठवीं से बारहवीं योजना · योजना का अंत
iprplans.x: Plans 8 to 12 · Plan · Years · PM · Focus / slogan · Target → Achieved · 8th · 1992–97 · P.V. Narasimha Rao · Human resource development ; first after LPG; indicative planning · 5.6% → 6.8% · 9th · 1997–2002 · A.B. Vajpayee · Growth with social justice and equality · 6.5% → 5.4% · 10th · 2002–07 · Vajpayee → Manmohan Singh · 8% growth; double per-capita income in 10 years · 8.0% → 7.6% · 11th · 2007–12 · Manmohan Singh · Towards faster and more inclusive growth · 9.0% → ~8% · 12th · 2012–17 · Manmohan Singh → Narendra Modi · Faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth · 8.0% (last plan) · 11 → 12 just adds a word. 11th = faster + inclusive. 12th = faster + inclusive + sustainable . 9th = social justice + equality (नौ = न्याय). · Match-type PYQ trap: 'Faster and more inclusive growth' = 11th ; 'Faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth' = 12th . One lecture's quiz gave the 11th slogan to the 12th — read every word. · Highlights · 8th · 73rd & 74th Amendments (1992), PM Rozgar Yojana (1993), MPLADS (1993) · 10th · National Horticulture Mission (2005–06), NREGA (2005), NRHM (2005) · 11th · RTE in force (2010), NRLM (2011) · 12th · Planning Commission replaced by NITI Aayog (1 Jan 2015); plan period ended March 2017 — India's last FYP · Hindu rate of growth · Coined by · Prof. Raj Krishna (1978) · Meaning · India's slow ~3.5% annual growth during 1950–80 · Idea · Low growth accepted as normal · The Hindu rate of growth is not about the 10th Plan. One lecture tied it to 2002–07, when growth was near 8%. The term describes the ~3.5% growth of 1950–80 . · PM trick — Rahul Gandhi's family tree: Plans 1-2-3 = नाना जी (Nehru); 4-5-6 = दादी जी (Indira); 7 = पापा जी (Rajiv); 8 = Narasimha Rao; 9 = Vajpayee; 10 = Vajpayee + Manmohan; 11 = Manmohan; 12 = Manmohan + Modi. · Small print on the family trick. The 3rd Plan also saw Lal Bahadur Shastri (1964–66) after Nehru's death, and the 9th was launched in 1997 before Vajpayee's government took over. In exams, the trick's answer is what is expected. · From plans to NITI. Planning Commission gave money and targets top-down; NITI Aayog gives advice and ranks states (cooperative & competitive federalism) — no plan funds. · 8th 1992–97 HRD, first after LPG (Rao); 9th growth with social justice & equality (Vajpayee). · 10th 8% target, 7.6% achieved; 11th faster & more inclusive; 12th faster, more inclusive & sustainable (last). · Hindu rate of growth: Raj Krishna, ~3.5% in 1950–80.

Income terms · NDP · GDP − depreciation · Personal income (PI) · What you earn · Disposable income (DI) · PI − personal direct taxes — what you can spend · DI splits into · Consumption + Saving (C + S = DI) · So · DI + personal taxes = PI · ₹12 lakh package example: ₹1 lakh a month = personal income. 'निर्मला ताई' takes 20% tax → ₹80,000 = disposable income. Of that, ₹30,000 SIP (saving) + ₹50,000 spent (consumption) = ₹80,000. · Three ways to measure GDP · Method · What is added · Income · Rent + interest + wages + profit · Output / Value-added · Value added at each stage (farmer ₹5 → mill +₹5 → baker +₹5) · Expenditure · C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption, investment, government spending, net exports · 'G' is government expenditure, not subsidy , and 'savings method' is not a GDP method. One lecture read G as 'government subsidy'. · History of national income estimates · First estimate · Dadabhai Naoroji , 1867–68 — per capita ₹20 ( Poverty and Un-British Rule in India ) · First scientific estimate · V.K.R.V. Rao (1931–32) · National Income Committee · August 1949 — Chairman P.C. Mahalanobis ; members D.R. Gadgil and V.K.R.V. folkdances.x: India has roughly 250 folk dances worth knowing, about eight per state. SSC asks them in four shapes: (1) which state (by far the most common), (2) which community or tribe performs it, (3) what it depicts or when it is danced (war, harvest, wedding, a deity), and (4) statement questions (CGL 2024–25 asked these on Jhora, Dangi, Kalbelia, Ghoomar, Tamasha, Jhumair and Dumhal). The lecture's rule: learn the state first; details come second. · The name often gives the state away. Kunitha → Karnataka (Dollu, Suggi Kunitha). Cholom → Manipur (Pung, Dhol Cholom). Lam → Mizoram (Khuallam, Chheih Lam, Tlanglam, Sarlamkai; lam = dance in Mizo). Chham → the Tibetan-Buddhist belt (Ladakh, HP, Sikkim, Arunachal). -attam / -kali / -koothu → Kerala or Tamil Nadu (a double 't' is the clue). Nacha / Nach → Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Bihar (Danda Nacha, Raut Nacha, Launda Nach). Nati / Natti → Himachal (Barada Nati is the Uttarakhand exception). · The eight classical dances (Sangeet Natak Akademi) · Classical dance · State · Hook · Bharatanatyam · Tamil Nadu · Oldest; temple dance of Thanjavur · Kathak · Uttar Pradesh · Katha = story; Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras gharanas · Kathakali · Kerala · Green faces, huge headgear · Mohiniattam · Kerala · Mohini = enchantress; lasya · Kuchipudi · Andhra Pradesh · Village Kuchipudi; Bhamakalapam · Odissi · Odisha · Tribhanga; Gotipua and Mahari are its roots · Manipuri · Manipur · Ras Leela; Jagoi · Sattriya · Assam · Sankardeva's sattras · Classical vs folk. If a question asks for a folk dance of Punjab and the options are Kuchipudi, Yakshagana, Mohiniattam and Bhangra, eliminate the three classical/theatre forms of the south. The Ministry of Culture also counts Chhau as classical (nine in all), but SSC keys follow the Akademi's eight. · Indian dance forms on UNESCO's Intangible Heritage list · Element · State · Year · Koodiyattam · Kerala · Proclaimed 2001 (inscribed 2008) · Ramlila · Uttar Pradesh · Proclaimed 2005 (inscribed 2008) · Baul songs · West Bengal · Proclaimed 2005 (inscribed 2008) · Ramman · Uttarakhand (Chamoli) · 2009 · Chhau · Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal · 2010 · Kalbelia · Rajasthan · 2010 · Mudiyettu · Kerala · 2010 · Sankirtana · Manipur · 2013 · Garba · Gujarat · 2023 · Ghoomar is NOT on the UNESCO list. A CGL statement said 'Ghoomar and Kalbelia are both UNESCO-listed' — only Kalbelia (2010) is. From Rajasthan, only Kalbelia; from Gujarat, only Garba (2023). · Sort by theme when the name rings no bell. Dances fall into a few families: war/martial, harvest/sowing, weddings, unmarried girls, festivals, a deity, and animal mimicry. Revise → Themes groups them this way. If a question says 'depicts victory in war', you only have to scan the martial list. · Dance ↔ festival. Many dances are asked through the festival they belong to: Ponung at Solung, Popir at Mopin, Bagurumba at Bwisagu, Chu Faat at Pang Lhabsol, Wangala and Nongkrem are both festival and dance, Karma at Karma Puja, Garba at Navratri. If you finished the Festivals workbook, half of this is already known. · Statement questions. Extreme words — only, exclusively, solo, women alone — are usually false. That is how two 2024 CGL statements were built: 'Dangi is a solo narrative dance' (false: it is a group dance) and 'women alone perform the Mardani variant of Jhumair' (false). · Learn the state first. · Kunitha → Karnataka; Cholom → Manipur; Lam → Mizoram; Chham → Buddhist Himalaya; -attam/-kali → Kerala/TN. · 8 classical: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Mohiniattam, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Sattriya. · UNESCO: Chhau & Kalbelia & Mudiyettu 2010, Garba 2023; Ghoomar is not listed.

appointments.h: नियुक्ति के प्रश्न कैसे आते हैं
appointments.x: Appointments are pure facts, so there's little to understand and a lot to remember. SSC asks them in four shapes: (1) who has been appointed as… (most common), (2) which number (26th CEC, 53rd CJI), (3) first woman / first from a country , and (4) the static part behind the post — the Article, the Act, the tenure, who appoints and who removes. The lecture's advice: when you read a name, ask which Part and Article is this body in, what is the tenure, and can the person be reappointed? · Three kinds of bodies — know which is which · Type · Made by · Examples · Constitutional · Named in the Constitution · ECI (Art 324), UPSC (315), CAG (148), Finance Commission (280), AG (76), Advocate General (165), NCSC (338), NCST (338A), NCBC (338B) · Statutory · An Act of Parliament · CIC (RTI Act 2005), NHRC (PHRA 1993), NCW (1990 Act), CVC (CVC Act 2003), NGT (NGT Act 2010), SEBI (1992), Lokpal (2013) · Executive / extra-constitutional · A government (cabinet) resolution · NITI Aayog (2015), Planning Commission (1950), Law Commission, CBI (powers from DSPE Act 1946) · Ask “कौन बनाया?” If the Constitution made it → constitutional. If Parliament passed an Act → statutory. If the cabinet just decided → executive. NITI Aayog, Law Commission and CBI are the three favourite traps — none is constitutional, none is statutory. · Which number? — the most-asked ordinals · Post · Holder · Number · Chief Election Commissioner · Gyanesh Kumar · 26th · RBI Governor · Sanjay Malhotra · 26th · Chief Justice of India · Justice Surya Kant · 53rd · Vice-President · C.P. Then 3-27-28-31 : CDS 3rd, Navy 27th, Air 28th, Army 31st. · Appointments link to Polity. Every constitutional post in this workbook has an Article. Learn the name and the Article together — SSC often asks the Article in the same question ("The CAG, presently K. Sanjay Murthy, is appointed under Article…"). · Constitutional = in the Constitution; statutory = Act of Parliament; executive = cabinet resolution. · NITI Aayog, Law Commission, CBI: neither constitutional nor statutory. · Number pairs: 26 CEC & RBI; 15 VP & CAG; 16 AG & FC; CDS 3, Navy 27, Air 28, Army 31; CJI 53.

space.h: अंतरिक्ष की भाषा — पेलोड से रोवर तक
space.x: Every space question uses a small set of words. Learn them once and the long Steno/CGL statement questions become easy to read. A space mission is a complete plan to solve one problem from space — e.g. 'photograph flooded Delhi every hour'. The lecture called its example Mission Aankh : put a camera in the sky. · The building blocks of a mission · Word · What it is · Mission Aankh example · Payload · The main item the mission exists for · The camera / sensor · Satellite bus · Support platform: solar panels, battery, antenna, thermal control, small thrusters, computer · Keeps the camera powered, cool and pointed at Delhi · Spacecraft · Payload + satellite bus together · The whole flying machine · Launch vehicle / rocket · Carries the spacecraft to the right height and path — a 'space taxi' · PSLV, GSLV, LVM3 · Ground segment · Control centre, big antennas and computers on Earth · ISRO's control room that commands and receives images · P + B = S. P ayload + B us = S pacecraft. The rocket is only the bus-to-school; the student (spacecraft) writes the exam. Rocket ≠ satellite. · Spacecraft by job — the spy-movie analogy · Type · What it does · Indian / world example · Orbiter · Circles the body and watches from outside · Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, Mangalyaan · Lander · Lands and works from one spot (soil, temperature, surroundings) · Vikram (Chandrayaan-3) · Rover · Comes out of the lander and moves around · Pragyan; NASA's Curiosity, Perseverance · Flyby · Passes close at high speed, collects data, does not enter orbit · Voyager, Pioneer 10 · Atmospheric probe · Plunges into an atmosphere to measure gases, pressure, temperature · Galileo probe at Jupiter · Crew capsule / module · Pressurised cabin with oxygen, temperature control, safety, re-entry system · Gaganyaan crew module, Orion · Space observatory · A telescope 'lab' placed above clouds and pollution · AstroSat, Hubble, JWST · A satellite is anything that keeps going round another body. Once a spacecraft lands (Vikram on the Moon) it is no longer a satellite — it is just a spacecraft/lander. So: every artificial satellite is a spacecraft, but not every spacecraft is a satellite. · Why doesn't a satellite fall? Not because there is no gravity — gravity is exactly what holds it. The satellite is thrown sideways so fast that while it falls, the round Earth curves away beneath it. It is in continuous free fall . Forward motion + gravity = orbit. No engine has to run; in space there is no friction to slow it (Newton's first law). · Two speeds to remember · Orbital velocity (LEO) · ≈ 7.8 km/s ≈ 28,000 km/h — goes round Earth in ~90 min · Escape velocity (Earth) · 11.2 km/s — leave Earth's gravity for the Moon/Mars · GEO satellite speed · ≈ 3.07 km/s — slower because it is farther out · Rule · Lower orbit → higher speed → shorter period · पहलवान rule. Near a strong wrestler (low orbit, strong gravity) you must run very fast; far away (high orbit) you can stroll past. So low orbit = fast, high orbit = slow. · Rover needs a lander. Chandrayaan-3 = propulsion module (carrier) + Vikram (lander) + Pragyan (rover). Chandrayaan-2 had an orbiter instead of a propulsion module — the orbiter still works. · Payload + bus = spacecraft; rocket only carries it. · Orbiter watches, lander sits, rover moves, flyby passes, probe dives in. · Satellite stays up by continuous free fall; LEO 7.8 km/s, escape 11.2 km/s.

space.t: Orbits: LEO, MEO, GEO, SSO & Lagrange points
space.x: Orbits by height · Orbit · Height · Used for · LEO — Low Earth Orbit · 160–2,000 km · Earth observation (sharp images), ISS (~400 km), Gaganyaan (~400 km), Hubble (~540 km), Starlink-type constellations · MEO — Medium Earth Orbit · Between LEO and GEO (~20,000 km) · Navigation — GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou · GEO — Geostationary · 35,786 km above the equator · Communication, TV broadcast, weather (INSAT, GSAT) · Camera distance rule. Want sharp detail (crop, flood, rooftop)? Stand close → LEO. Want a rough road map? Middle → MEO. Want the whole cloud system or a fixed relay mirror? Stand far → GEO. · Orbits by shape, tilt and timing · Orbit · Key idea · Geosynchronous (GSO) · Period = one sidereal day (~23 h 56 min). Can be tilted or elliptical, so it traces a figure-8 in the sky · Geostationary (GEO) · A special GSO: circular + zero inclination (over the equator) + same direction as Earth's spin → looks fixed · GTO — Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit · Elliptical 'parking-to-GEO' orbit; rockets drop satellites here, satellites raise themselves to GEO · Polar orbit · Passes over both poles; Earth turns beneath it, so it scans the whole globe strip by strip · Sun-synchronous (SSO) · Near-polar; crosses a given place at the same local solar time every day — same shadows, so images can be compared · HEO — Highly Elliptical · Very elongated; spends long time over one high-latitude region · Equatorial orbit · Orbit in the plane of the equator · Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not every geosynchronous orbit is geostationary. A GSO that is tilted or elliptical repeats every 24 h but wanders north–south. Only circular + equatorial + prograde makes it 'stationary'. · Orbit vocabulary · Apogee / Perigee · Farthest / nearest point of an orbit around Earth (P = Paas = Perigee) · Aphelion / Perihelion · Farthest / nearest point around the Sun · Prograde / Retrograde · Same / opposite direction as Earth's rotation (west→east is prograde) · Inclination · Tilt of the orbit plane from the equator · ISS · ~400 km, 51.6° inclination, ~90 min per orbit, ~28,000 km/h, ~16 orbits a day · Lagrange points are five spots where the pull of two big bodies (Sun–Earth or Earth–Moon) plus orbital motion balance, so a small spacecraft can stay in step with them using very little fuel. Gravity is not zero there — net force just matches what the orbit needs. They are also called libration points . · The Sun–Earth Lagrange points · Point · Where · Use · L1 · Between Sun and Earth, ~1.5 million km from Earth · Uninterrupted view of the Sun — Aditya-L1 , SOHO · L2 · Behind Earth, ~1.5 million km away · Deep-space viewing with Sun, Earth, Moon behind — JWST , Gaia · L3 · Opposite side of the Sun · Not used · L4, L5 · 60° ahead / behind Earth on its orbit; form equilateral triangles with Sun and Earth · Only stable points; Trojan asteroids gather here · L1 looks at the Sun, L2 looks away. L1–L2 distance ≈ 3 million km; L2–L3 ≈ 300 million km (asked in CHSL Mains). L1, L2, L3 are unstable — spacecraft keep doing small burns; L4 & L5 are stable. · Orbit → job → satellite name. GEO: INSAT, GSAT, CMS-03. SSO/polar: Cartosat, Resourcesat, EOS, NISAR (747 km). L1: Aditya. LEO: XPoSat, AstroSat (650 km), ISS, Gaganyaan. · LEO <2,000 km (imaging, ISS); MEO ~20,000 km (GPS); GEO 35,786 km (communication, weather). · GEO = GSO + circular + equatorial; SSO = same local time each pass. · L1 Aditya, L2 JWST; L4/L5 the only stable points.

A balloon flies forward when air rushes out behind. A rocket does the same with hot gas: momentum thrown backward pushes the rocket forward — Newton's third law (conservation of momentum). It does not need air to push against, so it works in vacuum. The push is called thrust . · Burning needs oxygen, and space has none. So a rocket carries its own oxidiser along with the fuel ; fuel + oxidiser = propellant . · Propellant types · Type · Fuel + oxidiser · Strength · Weakness · Solid · Pre-mixed grain · Huge thrust, simple, good for lift-off & strap-on boosters · Cannot throttle, stop or restart · Liquid (storable) · e.g. UDMH + N₂O₄ in separate tanks (Vikas engine) · Throttle, shut down, restart — good for manoeuvring · More complex · Cryogenic · Liquid hydrogen (−253 °C) + liquid oxygen (−183 °C) · Highest energy per kg · Super-cold storage; heat and cold side by side · Semi-cryogenic · Refined kerosene (RP-1) + liquid oxygen · Only LOX needs cooling; kerosene is dense and cheap · Kerosene leaves soot (coking) — bad for reuse · Methalox · Liquid methane + liquid oxygen · Clean burn — good for reusable engines · Methane also needs cooling (−162 °C) · 'Semi-cryogenic' does NOT mean half solid, half liquid. It means only the oxidiser (LOX) is cryogenic; the fuel is kerosene at room temperature. Cryogenic = LH₂ + LOX. Semi-cryo = kerosene + LOX. Methalox = methane + LOX. · Fuel family ladder: Hydrogen (cryo, cleanest, hardest) → Kerosene (semi-cryo, sooty like a lantern chimney) → Methane (methalox, clean and reusable). The oxidiser is LOX in all three — the fuel is what changes. · Staging. Carrying empty tanks is like climbing a hill with empty steel tiffins. So a rocket drops each stage when its fuel is spent; the lighter rocket speeds up. Strap-on boosters give extra lift-off thrust. Dropping expensive stages is costly — hence reusable rockets. · Indian engines & stages · Vikas · Liquid engine (UDMH + N₂O₄) — PSLV 2nd stage, GSLV/LVM3 core · CE-7.5 · Indigenous cryogenic engine of GSLV Mk II upper stage (CUS); first success GSLV-D5, Jan 2014 · CE-20 / C25 stage · LVM3's cryogenic upper stage (C25 ≈ 25 t propellant); C32 is the upgraded version · S200 · Solid strap-on booster of LVM3 · SCE-200 · Semi-cryogenic (kerosene–LOX) engine under development · Scramjet · Air-breathing: no compressor fans; very high forward speed compresses incoming air, oxygen from air burns hydrogen. ISRO test 28 Aug 2016 · Mach number · Speed ÷ speed of sound. 1 supersonic, >5 hypersonic · Fuel choice explains ISRO's roadmap. GSLV/LVM3 use hydrogen-cryo upper stages; NGLV moves to methalox for reusable boosters (clean burn), with spark torch igniters for repeated restarts (Lesson 7). · Rocket = Newton's third law; carries its own oxidiser. · Solid = thrust, no restart; liquid = control; cryo = LH₂+LOX; semi-cryo = kerosene+LOX; methalox = methane+LOX. · Stages are dropped to shed dead weight; Vikas liquid, CE-20 cryo, S200 solid.

space.h: भारत की अंतरिक्ष यात्रा — इनकोस्पार से राकेश शर्मा तक
space.x: After the USSR launched Sputnik-1 (4 Oct 1957) , the USA answered by setting up NASA (1958) . In India, Dr Vikram Sarabhai — father of the Indian space programme — convinced Nehru that space technology could reach farmers, teachers and fishermen far away. India first had to learn what space was: hence a research committee before any agency. · Timeline · 1962 · INCOSPAR (Indian National Committee for Space Research) under the Department of Atomic Energy ; set up by Vikram Sarabhai with Homi Bhabha's support · 21 Nov 1963 · First sounding rocket Nike-Apache (US-made) from Thumba (TERLS), Kerala — near the magnetic equator · 1967 · Experimental Satellite Communication Earth Station, Ahmedabad , to train engineers · 15 Aug 1969 · ISRO formed, superseding INCOSPAR · 1972 · Space Commission and Department of Space set up; ISRO brought under DoS (Sept 1972). DoS reports directly to the Prime Minister · 1975–76 · SITE — Satellite Instructional Television Experiment using NASA's ATS-6, TV lessons to ~2,400 villages · 19 Apr 1975 · Aryabhata , first Indian satellite — built in India, launched from Kapustin Yar (USSR) on a Soviet rocket; project led by U.R. Rao · 1977–79 · STEP — Satellite Telecommunication Experiments Project with the P&T department using the Franco-German Symphonie satellite · 1979 & 1981 · Bhaskara-I & II — first Indian experimental remote-sensing satellites (launched by USSR) · 10 Aug 1979 · SLV-3 first flight fails; Prof Satish Dhawan takes the blame publicly · 18 Jul 1980 · SLV-3 puts Rohini RS-1 in orbit from Sriharikota — first Indian satellite on an Indian rocket; project director APJ Abdul Kalam · 1981 · APPLE (Ariane Passenger PayLoad Experiment) — first indigenous experimental communication satellite, launched on Europe's Ariane · 1983 · INSAT-1B — first operational INSAT (1A of 1982 failed): communication + TV + weather on one satellite · 1984 · Rakesh Sharma (IAF) — first Indian in space, Soviet Soyuz T-11 , to Salyut-7 · The very first rocket from Thumba was American. One lecture said the first two rockets came from Russia (M-100) and France (Centaure). Those came later; 21 Nov 1963 was the US-built Nike-Apache . Also: INCOSPAR (1962) is not ISRO — ISRO is 1969. · 62-63-69-72-75-80: समिति (committee) → रॉकेट (Thumba) → ISRO → विभाग (DoS) → उपग्रह (Aryabhata) → अपना रॉकेट (SLV-3 + Rohini). 'Committee, rocket, organisation, department, satellite, own rocket.' · Aryabhata was Indian-made but not Indian-launched. First Indian satellite on an Indian rocket = Rohini RS-1 (1980, SLV-3) . Rohini Technology Payload (RTP) flew on the failed 1979 SLV-3. · People to know · Vikram Sarabhai · Father of Indian space programme; VSSC named after him; Space Applications Centre idea · Homi J. Bhabha · Father of the nuclear programme; INCOSPAR sat under his DAE · Satish Dhawan · ISRO chairman 1972–84; Sriharikota launch centre named after him · U.R. Rao · Led Aryabhata; URSC Bengaluru named after him · APJ Abdul Kalam · SLV-3 project director; 'Missile Man' · Rakesh Sharma · 1984, Soyuz T-11; 'Saare Jahan Se Achha' · Shubhanshu Shukla · 2025, first Indian on the ISS (Axiom-4) · V. Narayanan · Current ISRO Chairman (from 14 Jan 2025) · Failure → fix → retry runs through the whole story: SLV-3 (1979 fail, 1980 success), INSAT-1A → 1B, PSLV-D1 (1993 fail) → D2 (1994 success), Chandrayaan-2 lander → Chandrayaan-3. · 1962 INCOSPAR (DAE) → 1963 Nike-Apache, Thumba → 1969 ISRO → 1972 DoS & Space Commission. · Aryabhata 19 Apr 1975 (USSR launch); Rohini RS-1 on SLV-3, 18 Jul 1980. · SITE 1975 (ATS-6), STEP (Symphonie), APPLE 1981 (Ariane), INSAT-1B 1983, Rakesh Sharma 1984.

space.t: ISRO centres & how space is governed
space.x: Build a mission 'Kheti & Baadh' (farm and flood watch) and each ISRO centre does one job: the camera, the satellite around it, the rocket, the engine, the engine test, the launch, then the data. · Which centre does what · Centre · Place · Job · SAC — Space Applications Centre · Ahmedabad · Payloads (cameras, sensors, transponders) · URSC — U.R. Rao Satellite Centre · Bengaluru · Satellites: design, bus, assembly, testing · VSSC — Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre · Thiruvananthapuram · Launch vehicles (rockets) · LPSC — Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre · Valiamala (Thiruvananthapuram) & Bengaluru · Liquid & cryogenic stages/engines · IPRC — ISRO Propulsion Complex · Mahendragiri, Tamil Nadu · Engine and stage testing · SDSC SHAR — Satish Dhawan Space Centre · Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh · Launch port — two pads, third being built · NRSC — National Remote Sensing Centre · Hyderabad · Receives, processes and distributes Earth-observation data; runs Bhuvan · TERLS · Thumba, Kerala · Sounding rockets since 1963 · PRL — Physical Research Laboratory · Ahmedabad · Space science (PARAS-2 at Mount Abu) · “Ahmedabad aankh, Bengaluru badan, Thiruvananthapuram taxi.” Ahmedabad makes the eye (payload), Bengaluru the body (satellite), Thiruvananthapuram the taxi (rocket); Mahendragiri tests the engine; Sriharikota launches; Hyderabad reads the data. · Why Sriharikota? On the east coast, so rockets fly east over the Bay of Bengal (spent stages fall into the sea, not on towns) and get a free push from Earth's west-to-east spin; close to the equator, where that push is largest. · Who decides, who sells, who permits · Body · Year · Role · Space Commission · 1972 · Policy and priorities · Department of Space · 1972 · Implements; under the PM directly (no ministry) · ISRO · 1969 · Research & development, human spaceflight, frontier tech · Antrix Corporation · 1992 · First commercial arm · NSIL — NewSpace India Ltd · 2019 · PSU commercial arm: sells launches & services, transfers tech to industry · IN-SPACe · 2020 · Single-window autonomous regulator — authorises private and government space activities, levels the playing field · IN-SPACe was announced and set up in June 2020 (one lecture said 2022). Indian Space Policy came in 2023 ; IN-SPACe Norms, Guidelines & Procedures (NGP) in 2024. · FDI in space (2024 amendment) · Activity · Automatic route up to · Satellite components, systems, sub-systems · 100% · Satellite manufacturing & operations, data products, ground/user segment · 74% (beyond: government approval) · Launch vehicles, spaceports · 49% (beyond: government approval) · 100-74-49 = parts-satellite-rocket. The more strategic the item, the lower the automatic limit. · Other governance terms · Indian Space Policy 2023 · Institutionalises the 2020 reforms; ISRO moves to R&D, industry takes mature tech · Space Situational Awareness · Tracking objects and hazards in orbit — Project NETRA ; ISSAR reports · DFSM · Debris-Free Space Missions — all Indian missions to leave no debris by 2030 · SSLV tech transfer · To HAL — agreement 10 Sept 2025 (ISRO, NSIL, IN-SPACe) · Commercial chain: a foreign customer goes to NSIL , not ISRO directly — e.g. Proba-3 for ESA (PSLV-C59) and AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird (LVM3-M6). That earns India foreign exchange. · SAC payload, URSC satellite, VSSC rocket, LPSC liquid engine, IPRC tests, SHAR launches, NRSC data. · Space Commission & DoS 1972; Antrix 1992; NSIL 2019; IN-SPACe 2020; Space Policy 2023. · FDI automatic: 100% components, 74% satellites, 49% launch vehicles.

space.t: India's rockets: SLV-3 to LVM3 and SSLV
space.x: The launch-vehicle family · Vehicle · Stages · Lift-off mass · Payload · Notes · SLV-3 · 4, all solid · 17 t · 40 kg to LEO · First Indian rocket; Rohini 1980; retired 1983 · ASLV · 5, all solid (strap-ons counted) · ~40 t · 150 kg to 400 km LEO · First success ASLV-D3, 1992 · PSLV · 4: Solid–Liquid–Solid–Liquid · 230 t (CA) – 320 t (XL) · ~1,750 kg SSO; ~1,425 kg sub-GTO · 'Workhorse'; first success PSLV-D2, 15 Oct 1994 (IRS-P2); variants CA, DL, QL, XL · GSLV Mk II · 3: Solid–Liquid (Vikas)–Cryogenic · ~420 t · ~2,250 kg GTO · Indigenous cryo stage since GSLV-D5 (2014) · LVM3 (GSLV Mk III) · 3: S200 boosters, L110 core, C25 cryo · ~640 t · 4,000 kg GTO; 8,000 kg LEO · 'Bahubali' / 'Fat Boy'; heaviest Indian rocket · SSLV · 3 solid + liquid VTM (Velocity Trimming Module) · ~120 t · 500 kg to LEO; ~300 kg SSO · Launch-on-demand, low cost; 34 m tall, 2 m wide · HLVM3 · Human-rated LVM3 · — · Gaganyaan crew module to ~400 km · Crew escape system added · Stage count 4-5-4-3-3-3: SLV-3 four, ASLV five, PSLV four, GSLV three, LVM3 three, SSLV three (+VTM). Lift-off mass is the whole loaded rocket (PSLV-XL 320 t); payload is the satellite it can place in orbit (PSLV ~1,750 kg). SSC asks both. · Firsts and failures · 20 Sep 1993 · PSLV-D1 fails (IRS-1E lost) · 15 Oct 1994 · PSLV-D2 succeeds — IRS-P2 in sun-synchronous orbit · 18 Apr 2001 · GSLV-D1 first flight (GSAT-1), partly successful · 8 May 2003 · GSLV-D2 — first successful GSLV flight (GSAT-2) · 5 Jan 2014 · GSLV-D5 — first success with India's own cryogenic stage · Dec 2014 · LVM3-X/CARE suborbital test · 15 Feb 2017 · PSLV-C37 — 104 satellites in one launch (96 from the USA; main satellite Cartosat-2D) · Oct 2022 · LVM3 launches 36 OneWeb satellites · 2025–26 · PSLV-C61 (May 2025) and PSLV-C62 (Jan 2026) both fail in the third stage · GSLV-D2 flew in 2003, not 2004. Also, the PSLV variants are CA, DL, QL and XL — there is no 'KL'. · Launch sites · Sriharikota (SDSC SHAR) · Two pads; Third Launch Pad approved Jan 2025 (~₹3,985 crore, ~4 years) for NGLV & human flight · Kulasekarapattinam, Thoothukudi (TN) · Second spaceport, for SSLV ; foundation 28 Feb 2024. Lets polar launches go straight south, avoiding the fuel-wasting 'dogleg' around Sri Lanka · Thumba (TERLS) · Sounding rockets · Dhanush · Agnikul's private launch pad inside SHAR · Rocket ↔ mission pairs SSC loves: PSLV-C25 → Mangalyaan; PSLV-C37 → 104 satellites; PSLV-C57 → Aditya-L1; PSLV-C58 → XPoSat; PSLV-C60 → SpaDeX; GSLV-F14 → INSAT-3DS; GSLV-F15 → NVS-02 (100th); GSLV-F16 → NISAR; LVM3-M4 → Chandrayaan-3; LVM3-M5 → CMS-03; LVM3-M6 → BlueBird Block-2. · SLV-3 4 solid/40 kg; ASLV 5 solid/150 kg; PSLV 4 (S-L-S-L); GSLV 3 with cryo; LVM3 640 t/4 t GTO; SSLV 3 solid + VTM/500 kg. · PSLV-D1 failed 1993, D2 succeeded 1994; GSLV-D5 2014 first own cryo; C37 104 satellites 2017. · Kulasekarapattinam = SSLV spaceport; third pad at Sriharikota.

space.h: पुनः प्रयोज्य रॉकेट और निजी क्षेत्र
space.x: Throwing away a rocket after every flight is like buying a new bus for every Lucknow–Delhi trip. A Reusable Launch Vehicle (RLV) recovers parts to fly again and cut recurring cost. Two kinds of recovery: the winged top stage lands horizontally on a runway like a plane; the booster lands vertically on its tail like SpaceX's Falcon 9. · ISRO's reusable-tech trail · 23 May 2016 · RLV-TD HEX — winged demonstrator flown to ~Mach 5 on an HS9 solid booster from Sriharikota, splashed into the Bay of Bengal · 28 Aug 2016 · First experimental scramjet engine test (Advanced Technology Vehicle), Sriharikota · 2 Apr 2023 · RLV-LEX-01 — autonomous runway landing, Chitradurga (Karnataka); dropped from a Chinook helicopter · 22 Mar 2024 · RLV-LEX-02 — 'Pushpak' released 4.5 km up, 4 km away; corrected cross-range and landed itself · 23 Jun 2024 · RLV-LEX-03 — third and final landing test under tougher wind and dispersion · LEX = Landing EXperiment, Pushpak = the plane. Ramayana's flying chariot lands on a runway. LEX tests the top stage; booster recovery comes with NGLV. · Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV) · Approved · Sept 2024, ₹8,240 crore · Payload · Up to ~30 t to LEO (expendable), ~10 t to GTO — about 3× LVM3 · Cost · About 1.5× LVM3 · Design · Three stages, partially reusable first stage; ISRO now plans LOX–methane engines · Timeline · First flight targeted early 2030s; needs Sriharikota's third launch pad · Spark torch igniter · Gives reliable ignition and many restarts — essential to bring a booster back · NGLV's fuel changed. The older plan (in one lecture) used semi-cryogenic kerosene boosters; recent PYQs (CGL 2025) state LOX–methane was chosen for clean burn and reuse. If a question offers methalox for NGLV, pick it. · Private rockets · Company · What · Fact to remember · Skyroot Aerospace (Hyderabad) · Vikram-S , 18 Nov 2022, mission 'Prarambh' · India's first private rocket (suborbital) · Skyroot Aerospace · Vikram-1 , 18 Jul 2026, mission ' Aagaman ' · India's first private orbital rocket; 500 km LEO; stages Kalam-1200, Kalam-250, Kalam-100 (solid) + Raman liquid stage. India = 3rd country with private orbital launch after USA & China · Agnikul Cosmos (IIT-Madras incubated) · Agnibaan SOrTeD , 30 May 2024 · From Agnikul's own pad Dhanush ; engine Agnilet — world's first single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine · Space Zone India + Martin Group · RHUMI-1 , Aug 2024 · India's first reusable hybrid rocket (Tamil Nadu) · Vikram-S was Skyroot's, not Agnikul's. The Steno lecture marked Agnikul for 'first private rocket Vikram-S'. The rocket is named after Vikram Sarabhai and built by Skyroot ; Agnikul's rocket is Agnibaan . Also, Agnilet is semi-cryogenic , not cryogenic. · Skyroot = Vikram + Kalam (rocket named after Sarabhai, motors after Kalam). Agnikul = Agni-everything : Agnibaan rocket, Agnilet engine, Dhanush pad. · Reuse needs three things together: clean fuel (methalox, no soot), restartable ignition (spark torch igniter) and autonomous landing (LEX series). That is why all three show up in recent PYQs. · RLV-TD 2016 → LEX-01 (2023) → LEX-02 & 03 (2024, Pushpak, Chitradurga). · NGLV: ₹8,240 cr, ~30 t LEO, 3× LVM3 at 1.5× cost, methalox, reusable. · Skyroot: Vikram-S (2022), Vikram-1 'Aagaman' (18 Jul 2026, first private orbital). Agnikul: Agnibaan, Agnilet, Dhanush.

space.t: Satellites by job: communication, imaging, navigation
space.x: Satellite families · Family · Job · Orbit · Examples · INSAT · 'Bahubali' — communication, TV, weather, disaster warning, search & rescue · GEO · INSAT-1B (1983); INSAT-3D/3DR/3DS = weather only · GSAT / CMS · Pure communication, high-throughput broadband · GEO · GSAT-7 'Rukmini' (Navy, 2013), GSAT-20/N2 (Ka-band), CMS-03 · IRS → EOS · Remote sensing / Earth observation · SSO / polar · IRS-1A (1988), Cartosat (mapping), Resourcesat, Oceansat, RISAT (radar), EOS series · NavIC (IRNSS) · Regional navigation · GEO + inclined GSO · IRNSS-1A (2013) …, NVS-01 (2023), NVS-02 (2025) · IDRSS · Data relay — LEO spacecraft talk to ground in near real time via a high relay satellite · GEO · For Gaganyaan & LEO satellites · 3D = Weather. INSAT is the Bahubali that does everything; the moment you see '3D', '3DR' or '3DS' after it, that Bahubali has been given only weather duty. · Why does navigation need at least four satellites? One satellite tells you only your distance (a circle of possible positions). Two circles cross at two points; three pin one point. The fourth corrects your phone clock against the satellites' atomic clocks — a tiny time error is a big position error. That is why atomic-clock failures crippled NavIC (by March 2026 only a few satellites gave full service) and why NVS replacements matter. · NavIC · Full name · Navigation with Indian Constellation (earlier IRNSS) · Design · 7 satellites: 3 GEO + 4 inclined geosynchronous · Coverage · India plus ~1,500 km beyond its boundary · Second generation · NVS-01 (May 2023, GSLV-F12, first Indian atomic clock); NVS-02 (29 Jan 2025, GSLV-F15) stuck in transfer orbit — oxidiser valve did not open; NVS-03 on GSLV-F18 due Oct 2026 · GAGAN · GPS-Aided GEO Augmented Navigation — ISRO + Airports Authority of India; for aircraft landing; operational 2015 · Remote sensing = learning about the ground without touching it. Passive sensors read reflected sunlight (no data at night/clouds). Active sensors send their own signal — Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) works day, night and through clouds (RISAT, EOS-04, NISAR). Data goes to NRSC, Hyderabad ; the public sees it on Bhuvan ; weather data on MOSDAC ; archives on Bhoonidhi . · NISAR — NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar · Item · Fact · Launch · 30 Jul 2025, GSLV-F16 , Sriharikota (GSLV Mk II) · Mass · ~2,393 kg · Orbit · Sun-synchronous, 747 km , ~100 min period; revisits each spot every 12 days · Radars · L-band (NASA) ~24 cm wavelength; S-band (ISRO) ~9–10 cm · Antenna · 12 m mesh reflector on a 9 m boom · Firsts · First dual-frequency radar Earth-observation satellite; first ISRO–NASA hardware partnership · Phases · Commissioning ~90 days after launch; science phase from Nov 2025 · NISAR's S-band is not 12 cm. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength: L-band 1.25 GHz ≈ 24 cm, S-band 3.2 GHz ≈ 9.4 cm. What matters for the exam: L from NASA, S from ISRO . · Name tells job: Carto-sat = cartography (maps); Resource-sat = resources; Ocean-sat = ocean colour, fish zones; RI-SAT = Radar Imaging; EMISAT = electronic intelligence; HysIS = hyperspectral; Anvesha (EOS-N1) = hyperspectral surveillance. · INSAT = all-rounder; INSAT-3D/3DR/3DS = weather; GSAT/CMS = communication; IRS/EOS = imaging; NavIC = navigation; IDRSS = relay. · Navigation needs 3 satellites for position + 1 for clock; NavIC 7 satellites, 1,500 km beyond India. · NISAR: GSLV-F16, 30 Jul 2025, 747 km SSO, 12-day revisit, L-band NASA, S-band ISRO.

biology.x: The lecturer's #1 topic. “Cell + Plant & Animal Kingdom — these two must never be weak.” SSC asks who discovered what and when : dead cell (Hooke), living cell (Leeuwenhoek), nucleus (Brown), cell theory (Schleiden & Schwann), ‘cells come from cells’ (Virchow). The year often solves a question even when the name is unfamiliar. · Discovery ladder · 1665 · Robert Hooke sees dead cork cells; book Micrographia ; names them ‘cells’ (like monks' rooms) · 1674 · Antonie van Leeuwenhoek sees living cells (pond water, plaque) — ‘animalcules’; also described Spirogyra · 1831 · Robert Brown discovers the nucleus · 1838–39 · Schleiden (plants) & Schwann (animals) — cell theory · 1855 · Rudolf Virchow — omnis cellula e cellula : new cells arise from pre-existing cells · 1931 · Knoll & Ruska — electron microscope · “Hooke ne Cork kaata, Leeuwen ne Living dekha.” Hooke = H for Hollow/dead cork; Leeuwenhoek = L for Living . Then S+S (Schleiden + Schwann) built the theory and V irchow added ‘ V ansh’ — every cell has a parent cell. · What the cell theory says · 1 · All living organisms are made of cells · 2 · The cell is the basic structural & functional unit of life · 3 (Virchow) · All new cells arise from pre-existing cells · Record-holder cells · Record · Cell · Largest cell (world) · Ostrich egg · Largest human cell · Ovum (egg) — visible to the eye · Smallest human cell · Sperm · Longest cell · Neuron (nerve cell) · Smallest cell overall · Mycoplasma (PPLO) · Unicellular organisms do everything with one cell — Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas, bacteria. Multicellular organisms (plants, animals) divide work among many cells → tissues → organs → systems. Biology = bios (life) + logos (study); Aristotle is the father of biology and zoology, Theophrastus the father of botany. · Hooke's law (springs, F ∝ −x) is physics — same Robert Hooke, different chapter. Don't pick ‘Hooke's law’ for a cell question. And Hooke's cells were dead ; only the cell walls were left, so he never saw a nucleus. · Leeuwenhoek's ‘animalcules’ are the bacteria and protozoa of L9. Virchow's idea is what cell division (L6) actually does. · Hooke 1665 dead cork cells, Micrographia. · Leeuwenhoek 1674 living cells. · Brown 1831 nucleus. · Schleiden & Schwann 1838–39 cell theory. · Virchow 1855 cells from cells. · Largest cell ostrich egg; human largest ovum, smallest sperm; longest neuron.
