About one question per CGL shift. Rhombus side + one diagonal → area (Pythagoras on half-diagonals) is the favourite; trapezium 'find the height / other side' is the common CHSL/CPO form. Tier 2 adds parallelogram from sides + diagonal (Heron). · Parallelogram & rhombus · Parallelogram · A = base × height = ab sin θ · θ = angle between sides a, b · Parallelogram diagonals · d₁² + d₂² = 2(a² + b²) · Parallelogram from a, b, diagonal d · A = 2 × Heron(a, b, d) · A diagonal splits it into two equal triangles · Rhombus area · A = ½ d₁ d₂ = a² sin θ = a × h · Diagonals ⊥ and bisect each other · Rhombus side · a = ½√(d₁² + d₂²) · Half-diagonals are the legs · Rhombus perimeter · 4a = 2√(d₁² + d₂²) · Sum of diagonals L, side a · A = ¼[L² − 4a²] · (d₁+d₂)² − (d₁²+d₂²) = 2d₁d₂ · Trapezium, kite, any quadrilateral · Trapezium · A = ½ (a + b) h · a ∥ b, h = gap between them · Isosceles trapezium height · h = √(c² − ((b − a)/2)²) · c = slant side · Kite · A = ½ d₁ d₂ · Diagonals ⊥ · Any quadrilateral · A = ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂) · h₁, h₂ = offsets (perpendiculars) on diagonal d · Where the right angles are · Rhombus: half-diagonals and the side form a right triangle. · Trapezium: ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × gap. · Parallelogram: base × height (not base × slant side). · SSC CGL Tier 2 2017 · 12 Jan · Half-diagonal = 6; side = 10 → other half = √(100 − 36) = 8 · Other diagonal = 16 · Area = ½ × 12 × 16 = 96 cm² · 96 cm² · Spot the triple 6-8-10 at once. · SSC CHSL 2022 · 17 Mar 2023 S3 · 875 = ½ × (21 + 14) × h · h = 1750 ÷ 35 = 50 cm · 50 cm · SSC CPO 2022 · 11 Nov (Morning) · Side = P → d₁² + d₂² = 4P² · (d₁ + d₂)² = L² → 2d₁d₂ = L² − 4P² · Area = ½ d₁d₂ = ¼(L² − 4P²) · ¼(L² − 4P²) · Value-put: d₁ = 6, d₂ = 8 → L = 14, P = 5, area 24 → ¼(196 − 100) = 24 ✓. · Rhombus = four right triangles. Halve both diagonals; side² = (d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)². Triples: (5, 12, 13), (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), (12, 16, 20). · Parallelogram from two sides + a diagonal: the diagonal cuts it into two congruent triangles → area = 2 × Heron. Sides 15, 7, diagonal 20 → Heron = 42 → area 84. · Height, not slant side. Parallelogram area is base × perpendicular height; base × slant side only works for a rectangle. And trapezium uses the sum of the parallel sides, halved. · Rhombus area is ½ d₁ d₂ — forgetting the ½ (or using side × diagonal) is the classic wrong option. · Square vs rhombus on the same base: area ratio = 1 : sin θ (L11). The regular hexagon in L8 is six equilateral triangles — or two trapeziums. · Parallelogram A = bh = ab sinθ · Rhombus A = ½d₁d₂, side = ½√(d₁²+d₂²) · Trapezium A = ½(a+b)h · Kite ½d₁d₂; any quadrilateral ½ × d × (h₁+h₂)

Asked in almost every shift (often inside another shape). Tier 1: circumference ↔ area, semicircle perimeter (πr + 2r), wire bent from square to circle. Tier 2: circle combined with a square/triangle and answers in π. · Circle (radius r, diameter d = 2r) · Circumference · C = 2πr = πd · With π = 22/7: C = 44r/7 · Area · A = πr² = πd²/4 · Area from C · A = C²/(4π) · No need to find r · A and C link · A = ½ × C × r · Like ½ × base × height of an unrolled triangle · C − d · (π − 1)d = (15/7)d · 'Circumference exceeds diameter by…' · Semicircle & quadrant · Semicircle perimeter · πr + 2r = (36/7) r · Arc + diameter · Semicircle area · πr²/2 · Quadrant perimeter · πr/2 + 2r = (25/7) r · Arc + two radii · Quadrant area · πr²/4 · Circle family · C = 2πr, A = πr². · Semicircle: perimeter = πr + 2r (don't forget the diameter). · Quadrant: perimeter = πr/2 + 2r, area = πr²/4. · SSC CHSL 2018 · 17 Mar S2 · πr + 2r = (36/7) r = 72 → r = 14 · Area = ½ × 22/7 × 14 × 14 = 308 cm² · 308 cm² · Semicircle perimeter = 36r/7: 36 in the numerator means r is a multiple of 7 when the perimeter is a multiple of 36. · SSC CHSL 2021 · 13 Apr (Afternoon) · Side = 13 → wire = 52 m · 2πr = 52 → r = 52 × 7/44 = 91/11 m · Area = C²/(4π) = 52² × 7/88 = 215.09 ≈ 215 m² · 215 m² · Use A = C²/4π directly — no need to find r. · SSC CHSL 2024 · 8 Jul S2 · Semicircle area = ½ × π × 8 = 4π · Square side = √(4π) = 2√π · Perimeter = 8√π cm · 8√π cm · Ratios ignore π. Circumference ∝ r, area ∝ r². If circumferences are 3 : 4, areas are 9 : 16. If areas are 4 : 9, radii are 2 : 3. · The 7-multipliers: C = 44r/7, semicircle perimeter = 36r/7, quadrant perimeter = 25r/7, C − d = 15d/7, C − r = 37r/7, C + d = 29d/7. Divide the given number by the multiplier → r at once. · Semicircle perimeter ≠ πr. 'Perimeter' includes the straight diameter: πr + 2r. Only 'length of the arc / curved part' is πr. · Read radius vs diameter carefully — using d in πr² makes the answer 4 times too big (a favourite wrong option). · Fixed wire → circle has the largest area of all shapes (L11). Sectors (L6) are just θ/360 of these formulas. · C = 2πr, A = πr² = C²/4π · Semicircle P = πr + 2r = 36r/7, A = πr²/2 · Quadrant P = πr/2 + 2r = 25r/7, A = πr²/4 · Areas scale as r²; ratios ignore π

Rising fast: three different CGL 2023 shifts asked a sector question. Forms: radius from sector area + angle, sector perimeter (arc + 2r), area from arc length, clock-hand area. Tier 2: segment = sector − triangle and overlapping circles (L10). · Sector of angle θ (in degrees) · Arc length · l = (θ/360) × 2πr · Sector area · A = (θ/360) × πr² · Area from arc · A = ½ × l × r · No θ needed! · Sector perimeter · l + 2r · Arc plus both radii · Angle from fraction · Sector = 1/n of circle → θ = 360/n · Segment & clock · Segment area · Sector − △ = (θ/360)πr² − ½r² sin θ · Region between chord and arc · θ = 90° · (π/4 − ½) r² = (2/7) r² (π = 22/7) · r = 14 → 56 · θ = 60° · (π/6 − √3/4) r² · Minute hand · 6° per minute · 15 min → 90°, 45 min → 270° · Hour hand · 30° per hour = ½° per minute · Sector vs segment · Sector: (θ/360) of the circle. Perimeter = l + 2r. · Segment (shaded) = sector OAB − △OAB. Here ∠AOB = 90°. · SSC CGL 2023 · 26 Jul S2 · (56/360) × 22/7 × r² = 110 · r² = 110 × 360 × 7 / (56 × 22) = 225 · r = 15 cm · 15 cm · SSC CGL 2022 · 12 Dec S1 · 45 minutes → 45 × 6° = 270° = ¾ of a circle · Area = ¾ × 22/7 × 400 = 6600/7 cm² · 6600/7 cm² · Convert minutes to a fraction of the circle: 45/60 = ¾. · SSC CGL 2023 · 27 Jul S1 · Area = ½ × l × r · = ½ × 5r × r = 5r²/2 · 5r²/2 · Arc given → use ½ lr, never find θ. · Fractions, not degrees. 60° = ⅙, 90° = ¼, 120° = ⅓, 45° = ⅛, 72° = ⅕, 36° = 1/10. Multiply the full-circle value (C or A) by that fraction. · Quarter-circle segment = (2/7) r² with π = 22/7: (11/14 − 1/2) r² = (4/14) r². r = 7 → 14, r = 14 → 56, r = 21 → 126. · Sector perimeter = arc + 2r, not just the arc. Segment = sector − triangle; the triangle is ½r² sin θ, not ½r²(θ). · Clock: the minute hand turns 6° per minute; the hour hand only 30° per hour. 'Area swept by the minute hand in 20 minutes' = ⅓ of the circle. · Overlapping circles, leaves and rangoli shapes in L10 are built from sectors and segments. Arcs of wheels and tracks link to L7. · Arc l = (θ/360)2πr; sector A = (θ/360)πr² = ½lr · Sector perimeter = l + 2r · Segment = sector − ½r² sinθ; 90° segment = (2/7)r² · Minute hand 6°/min; hour hand 0.5°/min

Steady 1 question every few shifts. Circular path around/inside a park, width from two circumferences, wheel revolutions/speed. Tier 2: running tracks (rectangle + semicircles) and two wheels of different radii. · Ring (annulus) · Ring area · π(R² − r²) = π(R + r)(R − r) · R outer, r inner · Path of width w outside circle r · π[(r + w)² − r²] = πw(2r + w) · R = r + w · Path of width w inside circle R · π[R² − (R − w)²] · r = R − w · Width from circumferences · w = (C out − C in )/(2π) · Difference of C = 2πw · Wheels & tracks · One revolution · Distance = circumference = 2πr · n revolutions · Distance = n × 2πr · Revolutions = distance ÷ 2πr · Speed · Speed = (rev per unit time) × 2πr · Then convert cm/min → km/h · Two wheels, same distance · n₁ r₁ = n₂ r₂ · Bigger wheel turns fewer times · Track (rectangle + 2 semicircles) · Perimeter = 2l + 2πr; area = 2rl + πr² · Two semicircles = one circle · Ring and running track · Ring = πR² − πr²; width w = R − r. · Track: 2 straights + 2 semicircles → P = 2l + 2πr. · SSC CGL 2022 · 6 Dec S1 · 2πR − 2πr = 2π(R − r) = 144 · R − r = 144 × 7/44 = 22.9 · Width ≈ 23 cm · ≈ 23 cm · Difference of circumferences ÷ 2π = width directly. · SSC MTS 2019 · 13 Aug S3 · Circumference = πd = 22/7 × 56 = 176 cm · Speed = 7 × 176 = 1232 cm/s · 1232 cm/s · πR² = 1386 → R = 21 · Inner radius = 21 − 7 = 14 → inner area 616 · Path = 1386 − 616 = 770 m² · 770 m² · Inside path → subtract w from the radius; outside path → add w. · Ring in one product: π(R + r)(R − r). With R − r = width w, ring area = π × w × (R + r) = width × mean circumference. · Wheel units: 1 km = 1,00,000 cm. A wheel of radius 35 cm has circumference 220 cm → 500 revolutions per 1.1 km. Speed in km/h = (cm per minute) × 60 ÷ 1,00,000. · Inside vs outside path: inside → inner radius = R − w; outside → outer radius = r + w. Mixing them gives 1078 instead of 770 for the park above — both appear in options. · Revolutions use the circumference (2πr), not the area. And if the diameter is given, C = πd — don't double it again. · Same as rectangular paths in L3, just with circles. Distance/speed questions link to the Time & Distance app. · Ring = π(R² − r²) = π(R+r)(R−r) · Width = (C_out − C_in)/2π · Distance = revolutions × 2πr; n₁r₁ = n₂r₂ · Track: P = 2l + 2πr, A = 2rl + πr²

Occasional but predictable. Tier 1 asks hexagon area from side (CGL 2017 had it in two shifts) and simple angle/side facts. Tier 2 asks a triangle cut from a hexagon (△ABC, △ACE) or an octagon cut from a square. · Any regular n-gon (side a) · Exterior angle · 360°/n · Sum of exterior angles = 360° · Interior angle · (n − 2) × 180°/n · Hexagon 120°, octagon 135° · Area · ½ × perimeter × apothem · Apothem = inradius (centre to side) · Area (trig form) · (n a²/4) cot(180°/n) · Gives the special cases below · Hexagon and octagon · Regular hexagon area · (3√3/2) a² = 6 × (√3/4) a² · Six equilateral triangles · Hexagon radii · Circumradius R = a, inradius = (√3/2) a · Hexagon diagonals · Long = 2a, short = √3 a · △ABC (adjacent vertices) · (√3/4) a² = ⅙ of hexagon · ½ a² sin 120° · △ACE (alternate vertices) · ½ of hexagon · Equilateral with side √3 a · Regular octagon area · 2(1 + √2) a² · Octagon from square of side L · a = L(√2 − 1); corner cut x = a/√2 · x + a + x = L · Hexagon = 6 triangles; octagon = square − 4 corners · Six equilateral triangles of side a; apothem (accent) = (√3/2)a. · Cut four right-isosceles corners: x√2 = a, so a = L(√2 − 1). · SSC CGL 2017 · 23 Aug S3 · A = (3√3/2) a² · = (3√3/2) × 81 = 243√3/2 cm² · 243√3/2 cm² · Six times the equilateral triangle: 6 × (√3/4) × 81. · SSC CGL Tier 2 2022 · 8 Aug · AB = BC = 36, ∠ABC = 120° · Area = ½ × 36 × 36 × sin 120° = 648 × √3/2 · = 324√3 cm² · 324√3 cm² · △ABC = ⅙ of the hexagon = one equilateral triangle of side a: (√3/4) × 1296 = 324√3. · Corners are right isosceles triangles with legs x and hypotenuse a = x√2 · x + a + x = 18 → a(1 + √2) = 18 → a = 18(√2 − 1) · Area = 2(1 + √2) a² = 2(1 + √2) × 324(√2 − 1)² = 648(√2 − 1) cm² · a = 18(√2 − 1) cm, area = 648(√2 − 1) ≈ 268.4 cm² · Some websites cut equilateral corners and get 36(9 − √3) — wrong: a regular octagon needs 45° corner cuts. · Hexagon = 6 triangles. Any hexagon question → work with one equilateral triangle of side a (area (√3/4)a²) and multiply. △ABC = 1 piece, △ACE = 3 pieces, quadrilateral ABCD = 3 pieces. · Angles: exterior = 360/n. Interior = 180 − exterior. Exterior 30° → 12 sides; interior 140° → exterior 40° → 9 sides. · Hexagon area is (3√3/2)a², not (√3/4)a² × 3 or (3√3/4)a². Write it as 6 × (√3/4)a² to avoid slips. · An octagon trimmed from a square is not made by cutting equilateral triangles; the cuts are 45° right isosceles triangles. · Hexagon in a circle: circumradius = side (L9). The equilateral triangle formulas come from L2. · Exterior angle 360/n; interior = 180 − 360/n · Hexagon = (3√3/2)a²; R = a; apothem (√3/2)a · △ABC = ⅙ hexagon; △ACE = ½ hexagon · Octagon = 2(1+√2)a²; from square L: a = L(√2 − 1)

A Tier 2 favourite; Tier 1 asks it every few shifts. Forms: circle in a square / square in a circle, incircle and circumcircle of an equilateral triangle (1 : 4 areas), inradius of a right triangle from its sides, and chains (circle in triangle → square in that circle). · Inscribed = drawn inside, touching. Circumscribed = drawn outside, through the corners. Every question reduces to one link: which length of the inner figure equals which length of the outer one (side = diameter, diagonal = diameter, hypotenuse = diameter …). · Square and circle · Circle in a square (side a) · r = a/2, area = πa²/4 · Diameter = side · Square in a circle (radius r) · side = r√2, area = 2r² · Diagonal = diameter · Rectangle in a circle · Diagonal √(l² + b²) = 2R · Any rectangle; R = d/2 · Largest circle in a rectangle · r = b/2 (smaller side) · Not the length! · Outer circle : inner circle · Areas 2 : 1 · Square between them · Outer square : inner square · Areas 2 : 1 · Circle between them · Triangles and their circles · Any triangle · r = A/s, R = abc/(4A) · s = semi-perimeter · Equilateral (side a) · r = a/(2√3), R = a/√3 · R = 2r; h = 3r = r + R · Equilateral areas · Incircle : circumcircle = 1 : 4 · Because R = 2r · Right triangle · R = c/2 (half the hypotenuse) · Hypotenuse = diameter · Right triangle inradius · r = (a + b − c)/2 · a, b legs; c hypotenuse · Right triangle area · A = r × s = r(r + 2R) · s = r + 2R · Hexagon in a circle · side = R · Six equilateral triangles · Circle in a rhombus · r = (height)/2 = d₁d₂/(4a) · Rhombus area = 2ar · Square ↔ circle · Circle in a square: diameter = side, r = a/2. · Square in a circle: diagonal = diameter, side = r√2, area = 2r². · Incircle and circumcircle · Equilateral: R = 2r, so the circle areas are 1 : 4. · Right triangle: the corner square at C has side r, so a + b − c = 2r. · SSC CPO 2019 · 12 Dec S1 · Inradius r = a/(2√3) = 24/(2√3) = 4√3 cm · Square in a circle: area = 2r² = 2 × 48 · = 96 cm² · 96 cm² · r² = a²/12 = 576/12 = 48 → area 2r² = 96. · SSC CHSL 2020 · 5 Aug 2021 S3 · R = c/2 → hypotenuse c = 25 · s = r + 2R = 3 + 25 = 28 · Area = r × s = 3 × 28 = 84 cm² · 84 cm² · It is the 7-24-25 triangle: (7 + 24 − 25)/2 = 3 ✓. · s = 21, Heron area = 84 · r = A/s = 84/21 = 4 cm · R = abc/(4A) = 2730/336 = 65/8 cm · r = 4 cm, R = 65/8 cm · Equilateral ladder: r : R : h = 1 : 2 : 3. Know any one → the other two. Side 6√3 → h = 9, R = 6, r = 3. · Right-triangle radii in 5 seconds: 3-4-5 → r = 1, R = 2.5; 5-12-13 → r = 2, R = 6.5; 6-8-10 → r = 2, R = 5; 8-15-17 → r = 3; 7-24-25 → r = 3; 20-21-29 → r = 6. · Nesting halves the area. Circle → square inside → circle inside: each step halves the area (2 : 1). Two steps → 4 : 1. · Square in a circle: the diagonal (not the side) equals the diameter. Taking side = 2r gives area 4r², double the true 2r². · For a right triangle, r = (a + b − c)/2 — the minus goes on the hypotenuse. (a + b + c)/2 is the semi-perimeter, not r. · r = A/s and R = abc/4A use the triangle areas of L2. The hexagon (side = R) is L8. Shaded leftovers (circle minus square, triangle minus incircle) continue in L10. · Circle in square: r = a/2; square in circle: side r√2, area 2r² · Equilateral: r = a/(2√3), R = a/√3, r : R : h = 1 : 2 : 3 · Right triangle: R = c/2, r = (a + b − c)/2 · Any triangle: r = A/s, R = abc/(4A) · Hexagon in circle: side = R

Tier 2 loves these; Tier 1 asks one every few shifts. Fixed patterns: four circles at the corners of a square, three touching circles (area between them / string around them), the 'leaf' made by two quadrants, grazing animals and rangoli petals. Answers often come as (a√3 − bπ) or a multiple of 1/7. · Never integrate — subtract. Shaded = (whole simple figure) − (pieces you can name). The pieces are always squares, triangles, sectors, quadrants or segments from L2–L6. Corner pieces of a polygon add up: their angles sum to the polygon's angle sum. · Standard shaded shapes (π = 22/7 values) · Square minus inscribed circle · a²(1 − π/4) = (3/14) a² · Same as square minus 4 corner quadrants of radius a/2 · Square minus one quadrant (radius a) · a²(1 − π/4) = (3/14) a² · Corner left outside the arc · Leaf (two quadrants in a square) · (π/2 − 1) a² = (4/7) a² · = 2 × (90° segment) · Four-petal rangoli (semicircles on 4 sides) · (π/2 − 1) a² = (4/7) a² · Same as the leaf! · 4 touching circles (radius r) · (4 − π) r² = (6/7) r² · Square of side 2r − 4 quadrants · 3 touching circles (radius r) · (√3 − π/2) r² · Equilateral △ of side 2r − three 60° sectors · Circle minus inscribed square · (π − 2) r² = (8/7) r² · Circle in a quadrant (radius R) · r = R(√2 − 1) · r√2 + r = R · Belts, ropes and grazing · Belt round n equal touching circles · Perimeter of centre-polygon + 2πr · Arcs always add up to one full circle · 3 circles in a triangle · 6r + 2πr · 4 circles in a square · 8r + 2πr · Grazing at a corner of angle θ · (θ/360) πr² · Square corner → quadrant · Animals at all corners of a polygon (n sides) · (n − 2) × 180/360 × πr² · Triangle → semicircle; quadrilateral → full circle · Leaf and touching circles · Leaf: quadrants centred at A and C. Leaf = 2 × segment = (π/2 − 1)a². · Four touching circles: (2r)² − 4 quadrants = (4 − π)r². · Three touching circles: shaded = △ − 3 × 60° sectors. Belt (blue) = 3 × 2r + 2πr. · SSC CGL Tier 2 2016 · 1 Dec · r = 140/2 = 70 cm · Four quarter-circles = one full circle = 22/7 × 4900 = 15,400 · Square − circle = 19,600 − 15,400 = 4200 cm² · 4200 cm² · (3/14) × side² = (3/14) × 19,600 = 4200. · SSC CHSL 2022 · 10 Mar 2023 S3 · Centres form an equilateral triangle of side 14 → area (√3/4) × 196 = 49√3 · Three 60° sectors = half a circle = ½ × 22/7 × 49 = 77 · Enclosed area = 49√3 − 77 cm² · (49√3 − 77) cm² · Angles of the triangle add to 180° → the three sectors make exactly one semicircle. · SSC CGL 2022 · 5 Dec S4 · Straight parts: three, each equal to 2r = 8 → 24 cm · Curved parts: each 120° → total 360° = one circumference = 2π × 4 = 8π · Length = 24 + 8π cm · (24 + 8π) cm · Each quadrant = ¼ × 22/7 × 196 = 154 · Triangle ABD (half the square) = 98 → one segment = 154 − 98 = 56 · Leaf = 2 × 56 = 112 cm² · 112 cm² · (4/7) × a² = (4/7) × 196 = 112. · The 1/7 family (π = 22/7): square − circle = 3/14 a²; leaf or 4-petal rangoli = 4/7 a²; four touching circles = 6/7 r²; circle − square = 8/7 r²; 90° segment = 2/7 r². One multiplication and done. · Corner sectors add up. Equal circles at the corners of a triangle → sectors total 180° = ½ circle; at the corners of any quadrilateral → 360° = 1 full circle; pentagon → 1.5 circles. · Belt length: the straight parts equal the distances between centres (2r each), not the diameters around the outside, and the curved parts make one full circle in total — not one per circle. · Leaf vs leftover: the leaf is the overlap (4/7 a²); the two corner pieces outside both quadrants are a² − 4/7 a² = 3/7 a². Read which part is shaded. · Every piece here comes from L5 (quadrants), L6 (sectors and segments) and L9 (inscribed figures). Rangoli and petals are popular in Tier 2 picture questions. · Shaded = whole − named pieces · Square − inscribed circle = (3/14)a²; leaf = rangoli = (4/7)a² · 4 touching circles (4 − π)r²; 3 touching circles (√3 − π/2)r² · Belt = centre-polygon perimeter + 2πr · Corner sectors of a polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°

mensuration2d.h: क्षेत्रफल में प्रतिशत परिवर्तन और अनुपात
mensuration2d.x: About one question every two CGL/CHSL shifts — and it is the fastest mark in mensuration. Forms: side/radius +x% → area?; length +x%, breadth −y% → area?; keep the area constant; similar figures; equal perimeters → which area is bigger. Tier 2 adds 'area +44% → side?'. · Area is length × length , so every length change is applied twice. That is why +10% on every side gives +21% area, not +20%. Perimeter and circumference are single lengths, so they change by the same % as the sides. · Percentage change · Two changes (rectangle) · x + y + xy/100 % · Use −x for a decrease · Every length +x% (square, circle, any similar figure) · 2x + x²/100 % · +10% → +21%, +20% → +44% · +x% and −x% · Always a fall of x²/100 % · +20, −20 → −4% · Keep area constant · Other side falls by 100x/(100 + x) % · +25% length → −20% breadth · Area +k% → side · Side +[√(1 + k/100) − 1] × 100 % · +21% → 10%, +44% → 20%, +69% → 30% · Perimeter / circumference · Same % as the side or radius · Linear, not squared · Ratios and equal perimeters · Similar figures · Area ratio = (side ratio)² · Perimeter ratio = side ratio · Circles · A₁ : A₂ = r₁² : r₂² = C₁² : C₂² · Equal perimeter: circle vs square · Areas 4 : π = 14 : 11 · Circle wins · Equal perimeter: square vs equilateral △ · Areas 9 : 4√3 (≈ 1.3 : 1) · Equal perimeter, all rectangles · Square has the largest area · l = b · Equal area · Circle has the least perimeter · Square and circle of equal area · side : radius = √π : 1 · Why x + y + xy · New area = old + x% strip + y% strip + the small corner xy/100. · Same perimeter: triangle 0.77 : square 1 : circle 1.27 (areas). More sides → more area. · SSC CGL 2019 · 3 Mar 2020 S1 · x + y + xy/100 with x = 40, y = −20 · 40 − 20 − 800/100 = 20 − 8 = 12 · 12 · Multiply factors: 1.4 × 0.8 = 1.12 → +12%. · SSC MTS 2021 · 7 Jul 2022 S1 · 2x + x²/100 = 50 + 625/100 · = 56.25% · 56.25% · 1.25² = 1.5625. · New length = 5/4 of old → breadth must become 4/5 of old · Decrease = 1/5 = 20% · 20% · 100x/(100 + x) = 2500/125 = 20. · 2πr = 4a → a = πr/2 · Circle : square = πr² : π²r²/4 = 4 : π · = 4 : 22/7 = 28 : 22 = 14 : 11 · 14 : 11 · Use fractions as factors. +25% = ×5/4, −20% = ×4/5, +50% = ×3/2, −33⅓% = ×2/3, +12.5% = ×9/8. Multiply the factors; the product minus 1 is the change. · Perfect squares give the side change: area ×1.21 → side ×1.1; ×1.44 → ×1.2; ×1.69 → ×1.3; ×2.25 → ×1.5; ×0.81 → ×0.9; ×0.64 → ×0.8. · +x% then −x% is never 'no change'. The area always falls by x²/100 %. +20%/−20% → −4%; +50%/−50% → −25%. · 'Doubled' means +100%, not +200%. Radius doubled → area ×4 → increase of 300%. Radius tripled → ×9 → +800%. · This is L1's scaling rule (lengths × k → area × k²) written in percent. The same x + y + xy/100 rule is used in the Percentage app (successive change) and, cubed, in Mensuration 3D for volumes. · Two changes: x + y + xy/100 % · All lengths +x%: area 2x + x²/100 %; +x/−x: fall of x²/100 % · Constant area: other side −100x/(100+x) % · Similar figures: area ratio = (side ratio)² · Equal perimeter: circle > square > triangle (circle : square = 14 : 11)

mensuration3d.x: Tier 1: almost every shift has one cube/cuboid question — longest rod, volume from three face areas, TSA from (l+b+h) and diagonal, or a room/wall/brick count. Tier 2: the same ideas inside 2–3 step problems (painting cost, wood thickness, tank capacity in litres). · Cuboid l × b × h · Volume · V = l·b·h · 1 m³ = 1000 litres · Total surface area · TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl) · All 6 faces · Lateral SA (4 walls) · LSA = 2(l + b)·h · Perimeter of floor × height · Diagonal (longest rod) · d = √(l² + b² + h²) · Room / box diagonal · Volume from 3 face areas · V = √(xyz) · x = lb, y = bh, z = hl · (l+b+h) and d given · TSA = (l+b+h)² − d² · Because (l+b+h)² = d² + 2(lb+bh+hl) · Cube of edge a · Volume · V = a³ · TSA · 6a² · LSA = 4a² · Diagonal · a√3 · Face diagonal = a√2 · From TSA S · a = √(S/6) · then V = a³ · Cuboid with its body diagonal · AG = √(l² + b² + h²) is the longest rod that fits. Dashed edges are hidden. · SSC CGL 2022 · 12 Dec S3 · Floor = a² = 64 ⇒ a = 8 m · Longest rod = cube diagonal = a√3 · 8√3 m · Cube diagonal is always edge × √3 — only find the edge. · SSC CHSL 2024 · 9 Jul S3 · (lb)(bh)(hl) = (lbh)² = V² · V = √(120 × 72 × 60) = √518400 · 720 cm³ · Factorise: 120·72·60 = (12·10)(12·6)(6·10) = (12·10·6)² ⇒ V = 720. · (l+b+h)² = l²+b²+h² + 2(lb+bh+hl) · 441 = 169 + TSA · 272 cm² · Square-then-subtract: TSA = (sum of edges-of-a-corner)² − diagonal². No need to find l, b, h. Three faces → volume: multiply the three areas and take the square root; pair factors to avoid big numbers. · Walls ≠ room surface. “Four walls” = 2(l+b)h only. Add the ceiling (lb) if it is painted too; the floor is almost never painted. And 1 m³ = 1000 L, not 100 L. · Inner volume of a box with thickness t: subtract 2t from each outer dimension (both sides), not t. An open box (no lid) loses 2t only from l and b and t from h. · Cuboid: V = lbh, TSA = 2(lb+bh+hl), walls = 2(l+b)h · Diagonal = √(l²+b²+h²); cube diagonal = a√3 · V = √(product of 3 adjacent face areas) · TSA = (l+b+h)² − d² · 1 m³ = 1000 litres; box thickness t ⇒ inner = outer − 2t

Tier 1: 1 question in many shifts — find r from CSA, then the volume; hollow pipe metal; ratio of two cylinders. Tier 2: cylinders appear inside melting, water-flow and combined-solid problems (L7–L9), so the basic formulas must be instant. · Right circular cylinder (radius r, height h) · Curved surface area · CSA = 2πrh · Unroll it: a rectangle 2πr × h · Total surface area · TSA = 2πr(r + h) · CSA + two circular ends · Volume · V = πr²h · Base area × height · Hollow cylinder (pipe) · V = π(R² − r²)h · R outer, r inner; R² − r² = (R+r)(R−r) · Hollow: total surface · 2πRh + 2πrh + 2π(R² − r²) · Outer + inner + two rings · Shortcut · V ÷ CSA = r/2 · So r = 2V/CSA · Solid and hollow cylinder · CSA unrolls into a rectangle 2πr × h. · Metal in a pipe = π(R² − r²)h. · SSC CGL 2023 · 25 Jul S3 · 2πr × 12 = 2640 ⇒ r = 2640 × 7 ÷ (2 × 22 × 12) = 35 cm · V = (22/7) × 35² × 12 · 46200 cm³ · V = CSA × r/2 = 2640 × 35/2 = 46200. · SSC MTS 2024 · 16 Oct S2 · R = 7, r = 6 · V = π(R² − r²)h = (22/7)(49 − 36)(21) · = 22 × 13 × 3 · 858 cm³ · R² − r² = (R + r)(R − r) = 13 × 1. · V ∝ r²h · (2² × 5) : (3² × 3) = 20 : 27 · 20 : 27 · r = 2V ÷ CSA. Whenever both CSA and volume are given, divide — no π needed. Ratios: V ∝ r²h, CSA ∝ rh. Write the powers, then multiply the ratio parts. · Diameter given? Halve it first — using d as r makes the volume 4 times too big. Closed vs open: a tank open at the top has CSA + one base = πr(2h + r), not 2πr(r + h). · Rolling a sheet: the side that is rolled becomes the circumference 2πr, the other side becomes h. Rolling along the length and along the breadth give different volumes. · Cylinder volume is the base of L7 melting (wires are long thin cylinders) and L8 water flow (water in a pipe in 1 s = πr² × speed). · CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r+h), V = πr²h · Pipe: V = π(R² − r²)h = π(R+r)(R−r)h · r = 2V/CSA · V ∝ r²h, CSA ∝ rh for ratios · Open tank: πr² + 2πrh

Tier 1: regular — get l from l² = r² + h², then CSA or volume; Pythagorean triplets (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 7-24-25, 20-21-29) are planted on purpose. Tier 2: ratio-based cones (l : r = 29 : 20, CSA = 5 × base), % change in r and h, and sector ↔ cone conversions. · Right circular cone (radius r, height h, slant l) · Slant height · l = √(r² + h²) · Right triangle: h, r, l · Curved surface area · CSA = πrl · Uses l, never h · Total surface area · TSA = πr(l + r) · CSA + base πr² · Volume · V = ⅓πr²h · One-third of the cylinder on the same base · CSA ÷ base area · l / r · CSA = k × base ⇒ l = kr · Sector ↔ cone · Sector radius · = slant height l · Arc length · = base circumference 2πr · θ/360 × 2πl = 2πr · Angle of sector · θ = 360° × r / l · Area of sector · = CSA of cone = πrl · Cone and the sector it unrolls to · l² = r² + h². CSA uses l; volume uses h. · Fold the sector: its radius becomes l, its arc becomes the base circle. · SSC CHSL 2024 · 10 Jul S2 · πrl = 20π ⇒ l = 5 · h = √(25 − 16) = 3 · V = ⅓π × 16 × 3 · 16π cm³ · r = 4, l = 5 ⇒ the 3-4-5 triplet gives h = 3 instantly. · SSC CGL 2024 Tier 2 · 18 Jan 2025 · πrl = 5πr² ⇒ l = 5r · h² = l² − r² = 24r² ⇒ r² = 63² ÷ 24 = 165.375 · V = ⅓ × (22/7) × 165.375 × 63 = 22 × 165.375 × 3 · 10914.75 cm³ · SSC CGL Tier 2 · 29 Jan 2022 · l = 29k, r = 20k ⇒ h = 21k (20-21-29 triplet) · ⅓π(400k²)(21k) = 2800πk³ = 4838.4π · k³ = 1.728 ⇒ k = 1.2 ⇒ r = 24 · 24 cm · Triplets save time: (r, h, l) = (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (7,24,25), (8,15,17), (20,21,29), (9,40,41) and their multiples. If CSA = k × base, then l = kr. · πrh is not the CSA. Cone CSA uses the slant height l. Many wrong options are built with h. Also do not forget the ⅓ in the volume — the option 3 × the answer is always there. · A cone is ⅓ of a cylinder with the same base and height; a hemisphere is ⅔ of it. So cone : hemisphere : cylinder = 1 : 2 : 3 when h = r (used in L9 ). · l = √(r² + h²); CSA = πrl; TSA = πr(l + r); V = ⅓πr²h · Sector → cone: sector radius = l, arc = 2πr, θ = 360r/l · CSA = k × base ⇒ l = kr · Cone = ⅓ cylinder of same base & height · Watch triplets 3-4-5, 7-24-25, 20-21-29

Tier 1: frequent — hemisphere CSA vs TSA (2πr² vs 3πr²) is the favourite trap; volume ↔ surface area conversions; spherical shell. Tier 2: spheres are melted into cones/cylinders/wires (L7) and dropped into water (L8). · Sphere (radius r) · Surface area · 4πr² · = CSA of the cylinder that just encloses it · Volume · V = (4/3)πr³ · Spherical shell (hollow) · V = (4/3)π(R³ − r³) · R outer, r inner · V ÷ SA · = r/3 · So r = 3V/SA · Hemisphere (radius r) · Curved surface area · CSA = 2πr² · Bowl, inside or outside · Total surface area · TSA = 3πr² · CSA + flat circle πr² · Volume · V = (2/3)πr³ · Half of the sphere · Hemispherical shell (bowl of thickness) · V = (2/3)π(R³ − r³) · Sphere, hemisphere, shell · SA = 4πr², V = (4/3)πr³. · Curved part 2πr² + flat top πr² = 3πr². · Shell: (4/3)π(R³ − r³) — subtract cubes, not radii. · SSC CHSL 2021 · 26 May 2022 S1 · 3πr² = 16632 ⇒ r² = 16632 × 7 ÷ 66 = 1764 ⇒ r = 42 · V = (2/3)(22/7)(42³) = (2/3)(22/7)(74088) · 155232 cm³ · 16632 ÷ 3 = 5544 = 154 × 36, and 154 = π·7² ⇒ r = 7 × 6 = 42. · SSC CGL 2025 · 17 Sep S1 · (2/3)πr³ = 4 × 2πr² · r/3 = 4 ⇒ r = 12 · 12 cm · V/CSA for a hemisphere = r/3 (same as sphere). · SSC CGL 2020 · 17 Aug 2021 S2 · V = (4/3)π(3³ − 2³) · = (4/3)π × 19 · 76π/3 cm³ · 2-3-4 ladder: hemisphere CSA = 2πr², hemisphere TSA = 3πr², sphere = 4πr². Sphere : cylinder (h = 2r) : volume 2 : 3 and surface (sphere vs CSA) 1 : 1 — Archimedes. · “Surface area of a hemisphere” — if the solid is closed (solid hemisphere, paperweight) use 3πr²; a bowl's inside or outside is 2πr². Read the word solid / bowl . · Shell volume: (4/3)π(R³ − r³), not (4/3)π(R − r)³. With R = 3, r = 2: 19 vs 1 — huge difference. · Sphere: 4πr², (4/3)πr³ · Hemisphere: CSA 2πr², TSA 3πr², V (2/3)πr³ · Shell: (4/3)π(R³ − r³) · V ÷ SA = r/3 for sphere and hemisphere (CSA) · Sphere : circumscribed cylinder volume = 2 : 3

Tier 1: about one question in every few shifts — direct volume of a frustum or bucket, or “a cone is cut parallel to its base, find the ratio of volumes”. Tier 2: frustum CSA/TSA with slant height, buckets in litres, and cone cut into 3 parts. · Frustum (radii R and r, height h) · Slant height · l = √(h² + (R − r)²) · Right triangle with legs h and R − r · Volume · V = (πh/3)(R² + r² + Rr) · Big cone − small cone · Curved surface area · CSA = π(R + r)l · Total surface area · π(R + r)l + πR² + πr² · Closed both ends · Bucket (open top) · π(R + r)l + πr² · Only the bottom is closed · Cone cut parallel to its base · Small cone ∼ whole cone · r/R = h/H = l/L · Similar cones · Volume ratio · (h/H)³ · Cut at half height ⇒ 1/8 · CSA ratio · (h/H)² · Cut at half height ⇒ 1/4 · Small cone : frustum · k³ : (1 − k³) where k = h/H · ½ ⇒ 1 : 7; ⅓ ⇒ 1 : 26 · Frustum and the cone it comes from · l² = h² + (R − r)². · Top cone ∼ whole cone: volumes in ratio (h/H)³. · SSC CGL 2022 · 12 Dec S2 · V = (πh/3)(R² + r² + Rr) · = (22/7)(7/3)(25 + 9 + 15) = (22/3)(49) · 359.3 cm³ · h = 7 cancels the 7 of 22/7 — SSC chooses h = 7, 14, 21 for this. · SSC CGL 2025 · 19 Sep S1 · Top cone is similar with scale k = 1/3 · Top : whole = 1 : 27 · Top : bottom = 1 : (27 − 1) · 1 : 26 · Whole cone: l = 26. Frustum: R = 10, r = 5, slant = 13 · CSA = π(10 + 5)(13) = 195π · TSA = 195π + 100π + 25π · 320π cm² · Cube trick for cuts: cuts at heights k, 2k, 3k… from the apex give cone volumes 1 : 8 : 27 : 64…, so the slices are 1 : 7 : 19 : 37 (differences of cubes). For surface areas use squares: 1 : 3 : 5 : 7. · “Cut at ⅓ of height from the top” means the small cone has height H/3 — ratio 1 : 26. “Cut at ⅓ of height from the base” leaves a cone of height 2H/3 — ratio 8 : 19. Read which end. · Frustum slant ≠ h. Use √(h² + (R − r)²). Using h in π(R + r)l is the planted wrong option. Diameters given? Halve both. · V = (πh/3)(R² + r² + Rr) · l = √(h² + (R − r)²); CSA = π(R + r)l · Bucket metal = π(R + r)l + πr² (bottom only) · Cut cone: volumes ∝ k³, areas ∝ k² · Half-height cut ⇒ 1 : 7; one-third from top ⇒ 1 : 26

Tier 1: occasional (a few shifts per exam) — prism with equilateral or right-triangle base, square pyramid with slant height. Tier 2 / CHSL Tier 2: more common — LSA and volume together, hexagonal prism, regular tetrahedron. · Right prism (base perimeter P, base area B, height h) · Volume · V = B × h · Like a cylinder · Lateral surface area · LSA = P × h · Rectangles round the side · Total surface area · TSA = P·h + 2B · Equilateral base side a · B = (√3/4)a², P = 3a · Regular hexagon base side a · B = 6 × (√3/4)a² = (3√3/2)a² · Pyramid (base area B, height h, slant height l of faces) · Volume · V = ⅓ × B × h · ⅓ of the prism on the same base · Lateral surface area · = ½ × P × l · l = height of each triangular face · Square base side a · l² = h² + (a/2)² · Slant from apex to mid-edge · Regular tetrahedron edge a · V = (√2/12)a³ · 4 equilateral faces · Tetrahedron surface / height · TSA = √3 a², height = √(2/3) a · Euler · F + V − E = 2 · Cube 6 + 8 − 12 = 2 · Triangular prism, square pyramid, tetrahedron · Prism: V = base area × h; LSA = perimeter × h. · Square pyramid: l² = h² + (a/2)². · Regular tetrahedron: V = (√2/12)a³, TSA = √3a². · SSC CHSL 2023 Tier 2 · 10 Jan 2024 S1 · LSA = 3 × 4 × h = 120 ⇒ h = 10 · Base = (√3/4)(16) = 4√3 · V = 4√3 × 10 · 40√3 cm³ · SSC CGL 2025 · 16 Sep S3 · h² = l² − (a/2)² = 100 − 36 ⇒ h = 8 · V = ⅓ × 144 × 8 · 384 cm³ · 6-8-10 triplet: half-side 6, slant 10 ⇒ height 8. · SSC CGL Tier 2 · 29 Jan 2022 · 16² + 30² = 34² ⇒ right triangle, area = ½ × 16 × 30 = 240 · LSA = (16 + 30 + 34) × 32 = 2560 · V = 240 × 32 = 7680 · 2560 cm² and 7680 cm³ · Prism behaves like a cylinder, pyramid like a cone: V = Bh and ⅓Bh; lateral = P·h and ½·P·l. Learn one pair, get the other free. · Height vs slant height of a pyramid: volume uses the vertical height h; lateral area uses the slant height l of the faces. l² = h² + (a/2)² for a square base — use half the side. · Base areas come from 2D mensuration: equilateral (√3/4)a², hexagon (3√3/2)a², Heron's formula for scalene bases. Right-triangle bases (16-30-34, 5-12-13) are planted to make the area easy. · Prism: V = Bh, LSA = Ph, TSA = Ph + 2B · Pyramid: V = ⅓Bh, LSA = ½Pl · Square pyramid: l² = h² + (a/2)² · Tetrahedron: V = (√2/12)a³, TSA = √3a² · Hexagon base = (3√3/2)a²

Tier 1 favourite: sphere → small balls, cylinder → sphere, sphere → wire. Almost every exam has one. Tier 2: hollow shells recast into cones, mixed units (wire radius in mm, length in m), and “maximum number” (floor the answer). · One law: volume never changes when metal is melted and recast (no wastage unless stated). So volume of old solid = n × volume of each new solid . Surface area is NOT conserved — it increases when you make many small pieces. · Set up the equation · Number of pieces · n = V(old) ÷ V(one new piece) · Cancel π and common factors before multiplying · Sphere → n small spheres · n = (R/r)³ · R = 6, r = 3 ⇒ 8 balls · Sphere → wire (cylinder) · (4/3)R³ = r²·L · Convert mm and m to cm first · Cylinder → sphere · r²h = (4/3)R³ · Cone ↔ cylinder (same r) · h(cyl) = h(cone)/3 · Hollow solid · use (R³ − r³) or (R² − r²) · Only the metal is recast · Several cubes → one cube · A³ = a³ + b³ + c³ · 3, 4, 5 ⇒ 6 · Volume is conserved · Sphere drawn into a wire: equate volumes, cancel π. · SSC CHSL 2020 · 16 Apr 2021 S1 · π(16²)(9) = (4/3)πR³ · R³ = 256 × 9 × 3/4 = 1728 · R = 12 · 12 cm · SSC CGL Tier 2 · 12 Sep 2019 · L = 2400 cm · (4/3)(512) = r² × 2400 ⇒ r² = 0.2844 · r = 0.533 cm = 16/3 mm · 5⅓ mm · Keep fractions: r² = 2048/7200 = 64/225 ⇒ r = 8/15 cm. · SSC CPO 2024 · 28 Jun S2 · Metal = (4/3)π(5³ − 3³) = (4/3)π(98) · Cone: ⅓π(25)h · h = 4 × 98 ÷ 25 = 15.68 · 15.68 cm · Cancel first: π always cancels; (4/3) against ⅓ leaves 4. Sphere → cone of the same radius: h = 4R. Sphere → cylinder of the same radius: h = (4/3)R. Many cubes → one: add the cubes of the edges. · Units: wire radius in mm and length in m — convert everything to cm before equating. Diameter vs radius of coins and balls is the commonest planted mistake (gives an answer 4× or 8× off). · “Maximum number” of balls: take the floor (166.4 ⇒ 166), never round up. · Volume is conserved; surface area is not · n = V(old)/V(new piece); spheres: n = (R/r)³ · Sphere → wire: (4/3)R³ = r²L (same units!) · Cubes melted together: A³ = a³ + b³ + c³ · Hollow: use R³ − r³ (sphere) or R² − r² (pipe)

Tier 1: about one question per few shifts — rise in water level when a ball is dropped, or time to fill a tank through a pipe. Tier 2: rectangular channels/canals, rain on a roof collected in a tank, mixed units (km/h, cm, hectare, litres). · Flow through a pipe or channel · Water per unit time · = cross-section area × speed · A water column of length v·t · Circular pipe radius r · Q = πr² × v · Use radius, not diameter · Rectangular channel · Q = width × depth × v · Time to fill · t = tank volume ÷ Q · Keep the same units everywhere · Canal irrigation · area = (water in time t) ÷ standing depth · Displacement & rain · Solid fully dropped in · rise × base area of vessel = volume of solid · Archimedes · Cylindrical vessel · h(rise) = V(solid) ÷ πR² · n balls · n × (4/3)πr³ = πR² × rise · Rain · volume = area × rainfall depth · 1 hectare = 10000 m² · Units · 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 km/h = 1000 m per hour · 5 km/h = 5000 m in 1 h · Flow column and displacement · In time t the pipe delivers a cylinder of water πr² × (v·t). · πR² × h = (4/3)πr³: the rise h depends on the vessel's radius R. · SSC CHSL 2020 · 14 Oct S2 · Flow per hour = 1.2 × 0.75 × 15000 = 13500 m³ · Needed = 180 × 140 × 4 = 100800 m³ · t = 100800 ÷ 13500 = 7.467 h = 7 h 28 min · 7 hours 28 minutes · SSC CGL 2025 · 17 Sep S2 · Displaced water = volume of the ball · (4/3)π(4³) = 256π/3 · 256π/3 cm³ · The container's size is extra data — only needed if they ask the rise in level. · Rain = 22 × 20 × 0.02 = 8.8 m³ · Tank base = π × 1² = 22/7 m² · Rise = 8.8 ÷ (22/7) = 2.8 m · 2.8 m · Rise = V(solid) ÷ base area of the vessel. For a sphere in a cylinder: rise = 4r³ / (3R²). For n identical balls multiply by n. Speed in km/h: water column length in 1 hour = speed in metres × 1000. · Unit soup: pipe diameter in cm, speed in km/h, tank in m, answer in minutes. Convert everything to metres (or cm) before dividing. 1 hectare = 10000 m², not 1000. · A ball floating or only partly submerged does not displace its full volume — SSC always says “completely immersed/submerged” when it wants the full volume. · Flow per unit time = cross-section × speed · Time = tank volume ÷ flow (same units) · Rise in level = volume of immersed solid ÷ base area · Rain volume = area × depth; 1 ha = 10000 m² · 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 km/h ⇒ 1000 m per hour

Tier 1: about one question in a few shifts — toy (cone on hemisphere), capsule, tent (cylinder + cone roof), hemispherical depressions in a cube. Tier 2: regular — the CGL Tier 2 paper of 18 Jan 2025 had a toy TSA. Marks are won or lost on which surfaces count . · Two rules. Volume: just add the parts (subtract a cavity). Surface area: add only the surfaces you can touch from outside . Where two solids are glued, the joining circle disappears from both. Where a piece is scooped out, you lose a flat circle but gain the inner curved surface. · Common combinations (same radius r) · Toy: cone on hemisphere · TSA = πrl + 2πr² = πr(l + 2r) · V = ⅓πr²h + ⅔πr³ = ⅓πr²(h + 2r) · Capsule: cylinder + 2 hemispherical ends · TSA = 2πrh + 4πr² = 2πr(h + 2r) · V = πr²h + (4/3)πr³; h = cylinder part only · Tent: cylinder + cone roof · Canvas = 2πrh + πrl · No floor, no joining circle · Ice cream: cone + hemisphere on top · V = ⅓πr²h + ⅔πr³ · Cylinder with cone cavity (same r, h) · V = ⅔πr²h; TSA = 2πrh + πr² + πrl · Lose one end circle, gain the cone's CSA · Cylinder, hemisphere scooped from each end · TSA = 2πrh + 4πr² · Each hollow adds 2πr² and removes πr² · Cube with a hemispherical depression on a face · SA = 6a² + πr² · −πr² (hole) + 2πr² (bowl) · Hemisphere placed on a cube face · SA = 6a² + πr² · Same change: −πr² + 2πr² · Toy, capsule, cylinder with a conical cavity · Toy: πrl + 2πr². The dashed joining circle is inside — not counted. · Capsule: 2πr(h + 2r). h is the cylinder part; total length = h + 2r. · Cone hollowed from below: lose the base circle, gain the inner cone surface πrl. · SSC CGL 2024 Tier 2 · 18 Jan 2025 · l = √(36² + 105²) = √12321 = 111 · Exposed: cone CSA + hemisphere CSA (joining circle hidden) · πr(l + 2r) = π × 36 × (111 + 72) = 36 × 183π · 6588π cm² · 36 = 3 × 12, 105 = 3 × 35 and 12-35-37 is a triplet ⇒ l = 3 × 37 = 111. · SSC CGL 2021 · 18 Apr 2022 S1 · Cube: 6 × 10² = 600 · Each face: lose πr² (hole), gain 2πr² (bowl) ⇒ net +πr² = 4π · Six faces: 600 + 24π = 600 + 528/7 · 675 3/7 cm² · Hemisphere height = r = 7 ⇒ cone height = 32 − 6 − 7 = 19 · Write each part as πr² × (height-equivalent): 6 + 19/3 + 2(7)/3 = 6 + 11 = 17 · V = (22/7)(49)(17) = 154 × 17 · 2618 cm³ · Cylinder → h, cone → h/3, hemisphere → 2r/3: add, then multiply by πr² once. · Height-equivalents: write every part as πr² × (something): cylinder → h, cone → h/3, hemisphere → 2r/3, sphere → 4r/3. Add the brackets, multiply once. 1 : 2 : 3: a cone, a hemisphere and a cylinder with the same r and height r have volumes 1 : 2 : 3. · Never add whole TSAs. Toy ≠ TSA(cone) + TSA(hemisphere): the two base circles are glued inside. Use CSAs only. A tent has no floor canvas unless the question asks for it. · Lengths of the parts: if the total length of a capsule is given, subtract 2r to get the cylinder part. Toy total height = cone height + r (the hemisphere is r tall). · Every piece is a formula from L2 (cylinder), L3 (cone), L4 (hemisphere) . Combined solids melted into something else are L7 ; dropped into water, L8 . · Volume: add the parts, subtract cavities · Surface: only exposed faces — glued circles vanish · Toy: πr(l + 2r); capsule: 2πr(h + 2r); tent: 2πrh + πrl · Scooped hemisphere or hemisphere on a face: net +πr² · Cone : hemisphere : cylinder (height r) = 1 : 2 : 3

mensuration3d.x: Tier 1: common and quick — “radius increased by x%, find the % change in volume / surface area”, or “volume kept the same, by what % must h fall”. Tier 2: two changes at once (r up, h down), ratios of two solids, and equal-volume comparisons (cone vs sphere, cone vs hemisphere). · Why it works: every area is length × length and every volume is length × length × length. So if all lengths scale by k, every area scales by k² and every volume by k³ — whatever the shape. If only some lengths change, multiply the factors of the lengths that appear in the formula. · Scale factors · All lengths × k · Area × k², Volume × k³ · Sphere, cube, or r and h together · Sphere / hemisphere · SA ∝ r², V ∝ r³ · Cylinder · CSA ∝ rh, V ∝ r²h · Change r and h separately · Cone · V ∝ r²h · CSA ∝ rl (l changes with r and h) · Two changes x% and y% · Net % = x + y + xy/100 · Use −x for a decrease · Square of (1 + x%) · (1 + x/100)² − 1 · r +10% ⇒ area +21%, volume +33.1% · Ratios and equal volumes · Similar solids, length ratio a : b · Area a² : b², volume a³ : b³ · Volume ratio → take cube root first · Equal volume, cylinder r changes · h ∝ 1/r² · r +25% ⇒ h × 16/25 (36% less) · Keep V same after r grows x% · h falls by 1 − 1/(1 + x/100)² · Cone = cylinder (same r, V) · h(cone) = 3 h(cyl) · Cone = sphere (same r, V) · h(cone) = 4r · Cone = hemisphere (same r, V) · h(cone) = 2r · Ready multipliers (memorise) · Change in length · Area factor · Volume factor · +10% · 1.21 (+21%) · 1.331 (+33.1%) · +20% · 1.44 (+44%) · 1.728 (+72.8%) · +25% · 1.5625 (+56.25%) · 1.953 (+95.3%) · +50% · 2.25 (+125%) · 3.375 (+237.5%) · +100% (doubled) · 4 (+300%) · 8 (+700%) · −10% · 0.81 (−19%) · 0.729 (−27.1%) · −20% · 0.64 (−36%) · 0.512 (−48.8%) · −50% (halved) · 0.25 (−75%) · 0.125 (−87.5%) · Double the edge · Scale every length by k: faces grow k², volume grows k³. trigonometry.x: Almost every CGL Tier 1 shift has 1–2 trigonometry questions, and the easiest one is usually this type: one ratio is given (e.g. 7 cot P = 24) and you must find another ratio or an expression. Tier 2 asks the same idea with bigger expressions. Expect 30–60 seconds per question once the triangle is drawn. · Take a right triangle and one acute angle θ. The side opposite θ is the Perpendicular (P) , the side next to θ (not the hypotenuse) is the Base (B) , and the longest side is the Hypotenuse (H) . Every trigonometric ratio is just a ratio of two of these sides, so it depends only on θ, not on the size of the triangle. · Naming the sides for angle θ · For θ at C: P = AB (opposite), B = BC (adjacent), H = AC (hypotenuse). If the angle moves to A, P and B swap. · The six ratios · sin θ · P / H · opposite ÷ hypotenuse · cos θ · B / H · adjacent ÷ hypotenuse · tan θ · P / B · opposite ÷ adjacent · cosec θ · H / P = 1/sin θ · reciprocal of sin · sec θ · H / B = 1/cos θ · reciprocal of cos · cot θ · B / P = 1/tan θ · reciprocal of tan · Reciprocal & quotient relations · Reciprocal pairs · sin θ·cosec θ = 1, cos θ·sec θ = 1, tan θ·cot θ = 1 · each pair multiplies to 1 · Quotient · tan θ = sin θ / cos θ · (P/H) ÷ (B/H) = P/B · Quotient · cot θ = cos θ / sin θ · reciprocal of the above · Range (acute θ) · 0 1 · H is the longest side · tan, cot · any positive value · P and B can be in any ratio · Pythagorean triplets that SSC loves · Triplet (P, B, H) · Typical given · Then · 3, 4, 5 · tan θ = 3/4 · sin = 3/5, cos = 4/5 · 5, 12, 13 · cos θ = 5/13 or sec θ = 13/5 · sin = 12/13, tan = 12/5 · 8, 15, 17 · sin θ = 8/17 · cos = 15/17, tan = 8/15 · 7, 24, 25 · cot θ = 24/7 · sin = 7/25, cos = 24/25 · 20, 21, 29 · tan θ = 20/21 · sin = 20/29 · 9, 40, 41 · sin θ = 9/41 · cos = 40/41 · 12, 35, 37 · cos θ = 35/37 · cot = 35/12 · 11, 60, 61 · tan θ = 11/60 · sin = 11/61 · Draw the triangle from one ratio · tan θ = 3/4 → P = 3k, B = 4k, H = 5k. So sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5. · 7 cot P = 24 → cot P = B/P = 24/7 → H = 25, sin P = 7/25. · SSC CGL 2023 · 27 Jul S3 · cot P = 24/7 = Base/Perpendicular → B = 24, P = 7 · H = √(24² + 7²) = √625 = 25 (7-24-25 triplet) · sin P = P/H = 7/25 · 7/25 · Spot the triplet 7-24-25 at once; no need to square. · SSC CGL Tier-I · 3 Mar 2020 S1 · Every term has degree 1 in sin/cos, so divide top and bottom by cos A · = (8 tan A − 4)/(1 − 2 tan A), with tan A = 5/6 · = (20/3 − 4)/(1 − 5/3) = (8/3)/(−2/3) = −4 · −4 · Homogeneous expression → divide by cos and put tan. Never find sin and cos separately. · SSC Selection Post · 9 Nov 2020 S2 · sec θ = H/B = 13/5 → B = 5, H = 13, P = 12 · tan θ = 12/5, cosec θ = 13/12, sin θ = 12/13 · Numerator = 24 + 26 = 50; Denominator = 36 − 26 = 10 · Answer = 50/10 = 5 · 5 · Memory hook: “ S ome P eople H ave, C urly B rown H air, T hrough P roper B rushing” → sin = P/H, cos = B/H, tan = P/B. The other three are just upside down. Divide trick: if every term of an expression has the same degree in sin and cos (like a sin θ + b cos θ over c sin θ + d cos θ), divide by cos θ (or cos²θ) and use tan θ directly. · tan θ = 3/4 does not mean the sides are 3 and 4 — they are 3k and 4k. Ratios never change, so this does not matter for ratio answers, but it matters if a length is asked. sin²θ means (sin θ)² , not sin(θ²). And sin θ cannot exceed 1 (P < H); an option like sin θ = 5/4 is impossible. · Once you can read any ratio from one ratio, L3 (identities) lets you do the same without drawing the triangle, and L10 (heights & distances) is nothing but tan θ = height / distance. · sin = P/H, cos = B/H, tan = P/B; cosec, sec, cot are their reciprocals · Given one ratio → draw the triangle, use a triplet (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25) to get H · Same-degree expression in sin and cos → divide by cos θ and put tan θ · sin θ, cos θ ≤ 1 and sec θ, cosec θ ≥ 1 for every acute θ

Asked in nearly every Tier 1 shift. Either directly (“cosec 30° − cos 60° = ?”) or hidden inside a longer expression with squares of 30°, 45°, 60°. Tier 2 adds 15°, 75°, 18°, 36° and 22.5°. These are pure-memory marks — the table below must be automatic. · The master table · θ · 0° · 30° · 45° · 60° · 90° · sin θ · 0 · 1/2 · 1/√2 · √3/2 · 1 · cos θ · 1 · √3/2 · 1/√2 · 1/2 · 0 · tan θ · 0 · 1/√3 · 1 · √3 · not defined · cot θ · not defined · √3 · 1 · 1/√3 · 0 · sec θ · 1 · 2/√3 · √2 · 2 · not defined · cosec θ · not defined · 2 · √2 · 2/√3 · 1 · Square-root method: write 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 under 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°. In L5 these values are used to test options by putting θ = 30°, 45°, 60°. · sin: √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2 for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°; cos is the same row reversed · Squares to memorise: sin²30 = ¼, sin²45 = ½, sin²60 = ¾, tan²30 = ⅓, tan²60 = 3, sec²60 = 4 · tan 15° = 2 − √3, tan 75° = 2 + √3, tan 22.5° = √2 − 1 · sin 18° = (√5 − 1)/4, cos 36° = (√5 + 1)/4; tan 90°, sec 90°, cot 0°, cosec 0° are not defined

About one question every 2–3 Tier 1 shifts, and a regular in Tier 2. Typical forms: “cot 13° cot 27° cot 60° cot 63° cot 77° = ?”, “if sin 3A = cos(30° − A) find A”, or a long fraction where every angle pairs up to 90°. If the angles look ugly (38°, 52°, 67°), the question is from this lesson. · Why sin of one acute angle = cos of the other · The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°. The side opposite θ is adjacent to (90° − θ), so the ratios swap. · Complement rule: change the angle, add/remove “co” · sin ↔ cos · sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ · e.g. sin 27° = cos 63° · tan ↔ cot · tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, cot(90° − θ) = tan θ · e.g. tan 23° = cot 67° · sec ↔ cosec · sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ, cosec(90° − θ) = sec θ · e.g. sec 52° = cosec 38° · If A + B = 90° (both acute) · Equal ratios · sin A = cos B, tan A = cot B, sec A = cosec B · and the reverse: sin A = cos B ⇒ A + B = 90° · Products = 1 · tan A·tan B = 1, sin A·sec B = 1, cos A·cosec B = 1 · cot A·cot B = 1 · Squares · sin²A + sin²B = 1, cos²A + cos²B = 1 · sec²A − cot²B = 1 · Equation type · sin xA = cos yA ⇒ xA + yA = 90° · also tan 2A = cot(A − 18°) ⇒ 3A − 18° = 90° · Long products and sums · tan 1°·tan 2°·…·tan 89° · = 1 · pairs (1°, 89°)… multiply to 1, middle tan 45° = 1 · cos 1°·cos 2°·…·cos 100° · = 0 · contains cos 90° = 0 · sin²1° + sin²2° + … + sin²89° · = 44½ = 89/2 · 44 pairs (= 1 each) + sin²45° = ½ · sin²5° + sin²10° + … + sin²85° · = 8½ · 8 pairs + sin²45°; add sin²90° = 1 if the series runs to 90° · Rule for n terms · sum of sin² over angles symmetric about 45° = n/2 · n terms, each pair = 1 · SSC CHSL 2023 · 2 Aug S2 · 13° + 77° = 90° → cot 13°·cot 77° = cot 13°·tan 13° = 1 · 27° + 63° = 90° → cot 27°·cot 63° = 1 · Left: cot 60° = 1/√3 · 1/√3 · Pair first, then the leftover standard angle is the answer. · SSC CGL Tier 2 · 15 Nov 2020 · sin 3A = cos(30° − A) ⇒ 3A + 30° − A = 90° ⇒ A = 30° · 2 cosec 30° = 4, tan²60° = 3, cot²30° = 3 · 4 + 3 − 3 = 4 · 4 · SSC CGL Tier 2 · 15 Nov 2020 · sec 52° = cosec 38° → 2 sin²38°·cosec²38° = 2 · sin 26° = cos 64° → cos²64° + sin²64° = 1 → numerator = 3 · sec 67° = cosec 23°, cosec 67° = sec 23° → (tan²23° − sec²23°) + (cot²23° − cosec²23°) = −1 − 1 = −2 · 3/(−2) = −3/2 · −3/2 · Convert every angle above 45° into its complement below 45°; then identities finish it. · Scan for pairs that add to 90° before doing anything else (13 + 77, 27 + 63, 38 + 52, 23 + 67). Write the bigger angle as 90° − (smaller) and switch sin↔cos, tan↔cot, sec↔cosec. Equation trick: sin(…) = cos(…) or tan(…) = cot(…) with acute angles → the two angles add to 90°. · sin²1° + … + sin²89° is 44½, not 45 — the middle term sin²45° is only ½. Count the terms: 89 terms = 44 pairs + 1. A product that includes cos 90° (or tan 0°, sin 0°) is 0; one including tan 90° is undefined — read the range of angles carefully. · This is the 90° case of allied angles (L7): sin(90° + θ) = cos θ too, but with sign rules. In triangles (L9), B + C = 90° when A = 90°, so the same rules apply. · sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ (and vice versa) · A + B = 90° ⇒ tan A tan B = 1, sin²A + sin²B = 1, sin A sec B = 1 · sin xA = cos yA (acute) ⇒ xA + yA = 90° · tan 1°…tan 89° = 1; sin²1° + … + sin²89° = 44½; product with cos 90° = 0

1 question in most Tier 1 shifts, 2–3 in Tier 2. “1/(cosec θ − cot θ) − 1/sin θ is equal to?” or “(2 cos³θ − cos θ)/(sin θ − 2 sin³θ) = ?”. The options are ratios like tan θ, cot θ, sec θ — perfect for value putting , which solves most of them in under 30 seconds. · An identity is true for every angle. So if the question says “A is equal to which option”, put any convenient angle into the question and into each option — only the correct option matches. Choose an angle where all terms are defined and the options give different numbers. · Which angle to put · 45° is the worst choice when options mix tan/cot or sin/cos — they become equal there. · Algebra moves that finish most simplifications · Convert · write everything in sin and cos · tan = s/c, sec = 1/c, cosec = 1/s · Conjugate · (1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ) = cos²θ · also (sec − tan)(sec + tan) = 1 · Rationalise · 1/(cosec θ − cot θ) = cosec θ + cot θ · multiply by the conjugate · Factor · 2 cos³θ − cos θ = cos θ(2 cos²θ − 1) · and sin θ − 2 sin³θ = sin θ(1 − 2 sin²θ) = sin θ(2 cos²θ − 1) · a² − b² · sec⁴θ − tan⁴θ = sec²θ + tan²θ · because sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 · Common results · (sec θ − cos θ)(cosec θ − sin θ)(tan θ + cot θ) = 1 · √(sec²θ + cosec²θ) = tan θ + cot θ · Test values at 30° and 60° (to separate options) · θ · sin · cos · tan · cot · sec · cosec · 30° · 1/2 · √3/2 · 1/√3 · √3 · 2/√3 · 2 · 60° · √3/2 · 1/2 · √3 · 1/√3 · 2 · 2/√3 · SSC CGL 2024 · 23 Sep S2 · Algebra: 1/(cosec θ − cot θ) = cosec θ + cot θ (product of the pair = 1) · So the expression = cosec θ + cot θ − cosec θ = cot θ · Check by θ = 60°: 1/(2/√3 − 1/√3) − 2/√3 = √3 − 2/√3 = 1/√3 = cot 60° ✓ · cot θ · At θ = 60° the options tan, cosec, cot, sec are √3, 2/√3, 1/√3, 2 — all different, so one put is enough. · SSC CGL 2024 · 10 Sep S2 · 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ and cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1 · Expression = sec θ·cosec²θ·1/cosec³θ = sec θ/cosec θ = tan θ · tan θ = 3/4 · 3/4 · Simplify first, substitute last. · SSC CGL 2024 · 13 Sep S2 · tan x/sec x = (sin x/cos x)·cos x = sin x = 1/2 → x = 30° · (1/2 + √3/2)² = (1 + √3)²/4 = (4 + 2√3)/4 · = (2 + √3)/2 · (2 + √3)/2 · Value putting checklist: (1) Options are numbers → put θ = 0°, 45° or 90° (whichever keeps every term defined). (2) Options are tan/cot/sec… → put θ = 30° or 60°, never 45°. (3) A condition fixes θ (sin θ + cos θ = √2 ⇒ θ = 45°) → use that θ. (4) Two options still equal → test them at a second angle. · When value putting fails: at θ = 45°, tan θ = cot θ = 1 and sin θ = cos θ, so several options tie; at 0° or 90°, tan, sec, cot or cosec may be undefined; and when the question has a variable condition (sec θ + tan θ = p), you must use algebra. Also, a constant answer at one angle is not proof unless the options are constants. · Value putting also kills Tier 2 questions from L8 (compound angles) and L9 (A + B + C = 180°: put A = B = C = 60°, or A = 90°, B = C = 45°). · Identity questions: put a convenient angle into the question and the options · Number options → θ = 0°, 45°, 90°; ratio options → θ = 30° or 60° (avoid 45°) · Algebra moves: convert to sin/cos, use conjugates, factor a² − b² · 1/(cosec θ − cot θ) = cosec θ + cot θ; (1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ) = cos²θ · Value putting fails with variable conditions or when options tie — then simplify

About one question every 2–3 Tier 1 shifts; more common in Tier 2. Forms: “maximum value of 5 sin θ + 12 cos θ”, “minimum value of 9 tan²θ + 4 cot²θ”, “greatest value of sin¹²θ + cos²⁰θ”. Each is a one-line formula — the only danger is a trap where the formula’s value cannot actually be reached. · sin θ and cos θ always stay between −1 and 1, so every expression built from them has a range . Three tools find it: (1) combine a sin θ + b cos θ into one sine of size √(a² + b²); (2) use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 to turn a sin²θ + b cos²θ into a + (b − a)cos²θ; (3) use AM ≥ GM when a product of two terms is constant (tan θ·cot θ = 1). · Range formulas · a sin θ + b cos θ · from −√(a² + b²) to +√(a² + b²) · 5 sin θ + 12 cos θ: −13 to 13 · a sin θ ± b cos θ + c · from c − √(a² + b²) to c + √(a² + b²) · the constant just shifts the range · a sin²θ + b cos²θ · between a and b · = a + (b − a)cos²θ, and 0 ≤ cos²θ ≤ 1 · a tan²θ + b cot²θ · minimum 2√(ab) · AM ≥ GM, product ab is constant; no maximum · a sec²θ + b cosec²θ · minimum (√a + √b)² · = (a + b) + a tan²θ + b cot²θ ≥ a + b + 2√(ab) · sin θ·cos θ · maximum ½, minimum −½ · = ½ sin 2θ · sin θ + cos θ · maximum √2 (at 45°) · a = b = 1 → √(1 + 1) · sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ · from ½ to 1 · = 1 − 2 sin²θ cos²θ = 1 − ½ sin²2θ · Why √(a² + b²) · Take out R = √(a² + b²): the bracket becomes sin θ cos α + cos θ sin α = sin(θ + α), which lies between −1 and 1. · The combined wave never goes above +R or below −R, so max = √(a² + b²), min = −√(a² + b²). · SSC CGL 2023 · 20 Jul S3 · 0 ≤ sin²θ ≤ 1, so higher powers are never larger: sin¹²θ ≤ sin²θ and cos²⁰θ ≤ cos²θ · So sin¹²θ + cos²⁰θ ≤ sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 · At θ = 0°: 0 + 1 = 1 → the bound is reached · 1 · Put θ = 0° and θ = 90° — both give 1; any angle in between gives less. · √(3² + 4²) = 5 · 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ lies between −5 and 5 · Maximum = 7 + 5 = 12 (minimum 7 − 5 = 2) · 12 · Constant stays; add/subtract √(a² + b²). · AM ≥ GM: 9 tan²θ + 4 cot²θ ≥ 2√(9 tan²θ·4 cot²θ) · tan²θ·cot²θ = 1 → 2√36 = 12 · Reached when 9 tan²θ = 4 cot²θ, i.e. tan²θ = 2/3 — possible · 12 · 2√(ab) — multiply the coefficients, root, double. · Three one-liners: a sin + b cos → ±√(a² + b²) ; a sin² + b cos² → between a and b ; a tan² + b cot² → ≥ 2√(ab) . Triplets save time: (3, 4) → 5, (5, 12) → 13, (8, 15) → 17, (7, 24) → 25. · AM ≥ GM needs the equality case to be possible. 2 cos²θ + 8 sec²θ ≥ 2√16 = 8 would need cos⁴θ = 4 — impossible. Since 8 > 2, the true minimum is at cos²θ = 1: 2 + 8 = 10 . Rule: a cos²θ + b sec²θ has minimum 2√(ab) only when b ≤ a, else a + b. Same idea: sin²θ + cos²θ + tan²θ + cot²θ + sec²θ + cosec²θ is 7 (1 + 2 + 4), not 6 from a blind AM-GM on six terms. Max of sin θ cos θ is ½ , not 1. · sin θ cos θ = ½ sin 2θ and R sin(θ + α) both come from L8 (compound and double angles). L3’s identities (sec² = 1 + tan²) turn a sec² + b cosec² into the tan² + cot² form. · a sin θ + b cos θ (+ c): c ± √(a² + b²) · a sin²θ + b cos²θ lies between a and b · a tan²θ + b cot²θ ≥ 2√(ab); a sec²θ + b cosec²θ ≥ (√a + √b)² · sin θ cos θ ≤ ½, sin θ + cos θ ≤ √2, sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ ≥ ½ · AM–GM minimum must be reachable — check a cos²θ + b sec²θ when b > a

Tier 1: an occasional direct value (“cos 120° = ?”, “sin 330° = ?”). Tier 2 and long expressions: angles like 150°, 225°, 300°, 420° or negative angles hidden inside a sum. Every such angle reduces to 0°–90° in two steps: pick the rule, then fix the sign. · An angle beyond 90° is measured from the positive x-axis, anti-clockwise. Its ratios equal the ratios of its reference angle (the acute angle it makes with the x-axis) — only the sign changes, and the sign depends on the quadrant where the angle ends. · Signs in the four quadrants · ASTC — “Add Sugar To Coffee”: All, Sin, Tan, Cos are positive in quadrants I, II, III, IV (with their reciprocals). · 150° = 180° − 30°. P is (cos 150°, sin 150°) = (−√3/2, ½): sin stays +½ in quadrant II, cos becomes negative. · Reduction rule in two steps · Step 1 — function · 90° ± θ or 270° ± θ → change: sin↔cos, tan↔cot, sec↔cosec · 180° ± θ or 360° ± θ → keep the same function · Step 2 — sign · sign of the ORIGINAL ratio in the quadrant where the angle lies · treat θ as acute for this · Negative angle · sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ · only cos and sec are even · Beyond 360° · remove full turns: sin 420° = sin 60° · ratios repeat every 360° (tan every 180°) · The standard reductions · Angle · sin · cos · tan · 90° − θ · cos θ · sin θ · cot θ · 90° + θ · cos θ · −sin θ · −cot θ · 180° − θ · sin θ · −cos θ · −tan θ · 180° + θ · −sin θ · −cos θ · tan θ · 270° − θ · −cos θ · −sin θ · cot θ · 270° + θ · −cos θ · sin θ · −cot θ · 360° − θ (= −θ) · −sin θ · cos θ · −tan θ · Values to know beyond 90° · θ · sin · cos · tan · 120° · √3/2 · −1/2 · −√3 · 135° · 1/√2 · −1/√2 · −1 · 150° · 1/2 · −√3/2 · −1/√3 · 210° · −1/2 · −√3/2 · 1/√3 · 225° · −1/√2 · −1/√2 · 1 · 240° · −√3/2 · −1/2 · √3 · 300° · −√3/2 · 1/2 · −√3 · 315° · −1/√2 · 1/√2 · −1 · 330° · −1/2 · √3/2 · −1/√3 · SSC CGL 2023 · 18 Jul S4 · 120° = 180° − 60° → same function, cos · 120° is in quadrant II, where cos is negative · cos 120° = −cos 60° = −½ = −0.5 · −0.5 · Or 90° + 30° → cos changes to sin: −sin 30° = −½. Both routes agree. · SSC CHSL 2017 · 22 Jan (morning) · 330° = 360° − 30° → keep sin · Quadrant IV: sin is negative · sin 330° = −sin 30° = −½ · −1/2 · sin 420° = sin 60°, cos 390° = cos 30° · cos(−300°) = cos 300° = cos 60°; sin(−330°) = −sin 330° = sin 30° · = sin 60° cos 30° + cos 60° sin 30° = ¾ + ¼ = 1 · 1 · It is sin(60° + 30°) = sin 90° (L8). · “Add Sugar To Coffee” for signs (I All, II Sin, III Tan, IV Cos). Vertical axis (90°, 270°) → change the function; horizontal axis (180°, 360°) → keep it. Nod your head up-down at 90°/270° (“yes, change”), side-to-side at 180°/360° (“no change”). · Take the sign from the ORIGINAL ratio , not the new one: cos(90° + θ) is in quadrant II where cos is negative → −sin θ (not +sin θ). tan(180° + θ) = +tan θ (quadrant III, tan positive) — students often write −tan θ. cos(−θ) = cos θ , but sin(−θ) = −sin θ. · L4’s complementary rule is the 90° − θ row of this table. In triangles (L9), A + B = 180° − C gives sin(A + B) = sin C and cos(A + B) = −cos C — the 180° − θ row. · ASTC: All, Sin, Tan, Cos positive in quadrants I–IV · 90°/270° ± θ → change function; 180°/360° ± θ → same function · Sign = sign of the original ratio in that quadrant (θ acute) · sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ; remove 360° turns first · cos 120° = −½, sin 150° = ½, tan 135° = −1, sin 330° = −½

Mainly Tier 2 (1–2 questions), occasionally Tier 1. Forms: “A + B = 45°, find (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B)”, “3 sin x + 4 cos x = 2, find 3 cos x − 4 sin x”, “find cos 2θ if tan θ = 3/4”, or a hidden formula like 3 sin 20° − 4 sin³20° (= sin 60°). Recognising the formula is the whole question. · Sum and difference formulas · sin(A ± B) · sin A cos B ± cos A sin B · sign stays the same · cos(A ± B) · cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B · sign flips · tan(A ± B) · (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B) · tan 15° = (1 − 1/√3)/(1 + 1/√3) = 2 − √3 · cot(A + B) · (cot A cot B − 1)/(cot A + cot B) · reciprocal of the tan formula · Product forms · sin(A + B) sin(A − B) = sin²A − sin²B · cos(A + B) cos(A − B) = cos²A − sin²B · Double and triple angles · sin 2θ · 2 sin θ cos θ = 2 tan θ/(1 + tan²θ) · put B = A in sin(A + B) · cos 2θ · cos²θ − sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2sin²θ = (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ) · four forms — pick the one that matches · tan 2θ · 2 tan θ/(1 − tan²θ) · Half-angle squares · 1 + cos 2θ = 2cos²θ, 1 − cos 2θ = 2sin²θ · so (1 − cos 2θ)/(1 + cos 2θ) = tan²θ · sin 3θ · 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ · “3 sin − 4 sin³” · cos 3θ · 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ · “4 cos³ − 3 cos” (order reversed) · tan 3θ · (3 tan θ − tan³θ)/(1 − 3 tan²θ) · SSC special results · A + B = 45° · (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 2 · also (cot A − 1)(cot B − 1) = 2 · a sin x + b cos x = c · a cos x − b sin x = ±√(a² + b² − c²) · square both and add: sum of squares = a² + b² · tan A = 1/2, tan B = 1/3 · A + B = 45° · (½ + ⅓)/(1 − ⅙) = 1 · sin θ·sin(60° − θ)·sin(60° + θ) · = ¼ sin 3θ · cos version: ¼ cos 3θ; tan version: tan 3θ · Why sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ · Isosceles triangle, equal sides 1, apex 2θ. Area = ½·1·1·sin 2θ. The altitude (cos θ) splits the base into 2 sin θ, so area = ½·2 sin θ·cos θ. Equate: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ. · SSC CGL Tier 2 · 18 Nov 2020 · Let 3 cos x − 4 sin x = y · Square and add: (3 sin x + 4 cos x)² + (3 cos x − 4 sin x)² = 9 + 16 = 25 (the cross terms cancel) · 4 + y² = 25 → y² = 21 → y = √21 (the options give the positive root) · √21 · Direct: √(a² + b² − c²) = √(9 + 16 − 4). · tan(A + B) = tan 45° = 1 → (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) = 1 · tan A + tan B = 1 − tan A tan B → tan A + tan B + tan A tan B = 1 · (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 1 + (tan A + tan B + tan A tan B) = 1 + 1 = 2 · 2 · Check with A = 0°, B = 45°: (1 + 0)(1 + 1) = 2. So (1 + tan 20°)(1 + tan 25°) = 2 instantly. · cos 2θ = (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = (1 − 9/16)/(1 + 9/16) = 7/25 · sin 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 + tan²θ) = (3/2)/(25/16) = 24/25 · Check: (7/25)² + (24/25)² = 1 ✓ · cos 2θ = 7/25, sin 2θ = 24/25 · Spot a formula in disguise: 2 sin x cos x → sin 2x; cos²x − sin²x → cos 2x; 3 sin x − 4 sin³x → sin 3x; 4 cos³x − 3 cos x → cos 3x; (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) → tan(A + B). Value check: any identity in A and B can be tested at A = 0° or A = B. · sin 2θ ≠ 2 sin θ (sin 60° = √3/2, but 2 sin 30° = 1). cos(A + B) has a MINUS : cos A cos B − sin A sin B. sin keeps the sign, cos flips it. sin 3θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ, but cos 3θ = 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ — the order is reversed. · These formulas produce the L2 values (sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°), tan 22.5° from tan 2θ) and the L6 range: a sin θ + b cos θ = R sin(θ + α). In L9 they meet A + B + C = 180°. · sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B; cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B · tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B) · sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ; cos 2θ = 1 − 2sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1; tan 2θ = 2t/(1 − t²) · sin 3θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ; cos 3θ = 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ · A + B = 45° ⇒ (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 2

Equation type: about one question every few Tier 1 shifts, regular in Tier 2. “If 2 sin²θ + 3 cos θ = 3 (0° < θ < 90°), find sec²θ + cot²θ” — solve for θ, then evaluate. Triangle type (mostly Tier 2): “In △ABC, tan((A + B)/2) = ?” or “tan A + tan B + tan C = ?”. Both reward one idea: find the angle first. · In any triangle: A + B + C = 180° · Pair of angles · A + B = 180° − C · then use the 180° − θ row of L7 · sin, cos, tan · sin(A + B) = sin C, cos(A + B) = −cos C, tan(A + B) = −tan C · sin keeps sign, cos and tan flip · Half angles · (A + B)/2 = 90° − C/2 · sin((A + B)/2) = cos(C/2), tan((A + B)/2) = cot(C/2) · Tan sum = product · tan A + tan B + tan C = tan A·tan B·tan C · from tan(A + B) = −tan C · Cot products · cot A cot B + cot B cot C + cot C cot A = 1 · divide the tan result by tan A tan B tan C · Right angle at C · A + B = 90° · complementary rules of L4: sin²A + sin²B = 1 · The angle sum drives every result · Replace A + B by 180° − C (or the half-sum by 90° − C/2) and apply the allied-angle rules. · Solving a simple trig equation (SSC style) · Step 1 · write everything in ONE ratio · sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ, cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ · Step 2 · solve the quadratic · 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0 → (2 sin θ − 1)(sin θ − 1) = 0 · Step 3 · keep only roots in the given range · 0° < θ < 90° rejects sin θ = 1 (θ = 90°) and any value outside −1 to 1 · Step 4 · evaluate the asked expression at that θ · usually 30°, 45° or 60° · a sin θ + b cos θ = c · divide by √(a² + b²) and use L8 · √3 cos θ + sin θ = 1 → cos(θ − 30°) = ½ · x + 1/x = 2 · forces x = 1 · sin θ + cosec θ = 2 ⇒ sin θ = 1 ⇒ any power sum = 2 · SSC CGL 2021 Tier 1 · 18 Apr 2022 S3 · 2(1 − cos²θ) + 3 cos θ = 3 → 2 cos²θ − 3 cos θ + 1 = 0 · (2 cos θ − 1)(cos θ − 1) = 0 → cos θ = ½ (cos θ = 1 gives θ = 0°, not allowed) · θ = 60°: sec²60° + cot²60° = 4 + ⅓ = 13/3 = 4⅓ · 4⅓ · Try the option angles: θ = 60° gives 2(¾) + 3(½) = 3 ✓. · SSC CGL Tier 2 · 13 Sep 2019 · 2(1 − sin²θ) + 3 sin θ = 3 → 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0 · sin θ = ½ (sin θ = 1 rejected) → θ = 30°, 2θ = 60° · ¾ + ¾ + 3 + 4/3 = 35/6 · 35/6 · tan C = −tan(A + B) = −(tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) · = −(1 + 2)/(1 − 2) = 3 · Check: tan A + tan B + tan C = 6 = 1·2·3 ✓ · 3 · Equilateral value put for identities: A = B = C = 60° → tan A + tan B + tan C = 3√3 = tan A tan B tan C. · Equation questions: test the options. Put 30°, 45°, 60° into the given equation — the one that satisfies it is θ. Then evaluate. Triangle identities: value put A = B = C = 60°, or A = 90°, B = C = 45° — then compare with the options. · Reject roots outside the range: in 0° < θ < 90°, cos θ = 1 (θ = 0°) and sin θ = 1 (θ = 90°) are not allowed; sin θ = 2 or −2 is never possible. In a triangle, cos(A + B) = −cos C , not cos C. And tan(A + B) = − tan C. · The triangle results are L7’s allied angles with 180° − C; the equation step uses L3’s identities to reach one ratio. Angles of elevation in L10 are also solved by finding the angle first. · A + B = 180° − C: sin(A + B) = sin C, cos(A + B) = −cos C, tan(A + B) = −tan C · (A + B)/2 = 90° − C/2: sin ↔ cos, tan ↔ cot · tan A + tan B + tan C = tan A tan B tan C; cot A cot B + cot B cot C + cot C cot A = 1 · Equation: one ratio → quadratic → keep the root in range → evaluate · Option-testing with 30°, 45°, 60° is often fastest

About one question in most Tier 1 shifts and 1–2 in Tier 2. Forms: tower + one angle (find height/distance), observer moving towards the tower (30° → 60°), two ships seen from a lighthouse, shadow longer by x m when the sun’s altitude drops, building and tower (elevation + depression). Nearly every one uses only 30°, 45° and 60°. · The angle of elevation is measured UP from the horizontal to the line of sight; the angle of depression is measured DOWN from the horizontal. Because the two horizontals are parallel, the depression seen from the top equals the elevation seen from the bottom (alternate angles). Every problem is one or two right triangles with tan θ = height ÷ horizontal distance . · The two standard pictures · Observer walks from C (30°) to D (60°). BD = h/√3, BC = h√3, so x = CD = 2h/√3 = 2d. Height h = x/(cot 30° − cot 60°) = (√3/2)x. · Depression from the top T to the ship S = elevation of T seen from S (alternate angles, horizontals parallel). · Working formulas · One angle · h = d·tan θ, d = h·cot θ · 30°: h = d/√3; 45°: h = d; 60°: h = √3 d · Two angles, same side · h = x/(cot α − cot β) · x = distance between the two points, α < β · 30° → 60° walk · distance walked = 2 × remaining distance · h = (√3/2) × distance walked · Two angles, opposite sides · total distance = h(cot α + cot β) · two ships on either side of a lighthouse · Complementary angles · α + β = 90° from distances a and b → h = √(ab) · tan α·tan β = 1 → (h/a)(h/b) = 1 · Shadow · shadow = h·cot θ · shadow = h → 45°; shadow = √3 h → 30°; shadow = h/√3 → 60° · Observer’s height · add the eye height to the tower part above the eye · h_tower = d·tan θ + eye height · 30-45-60 side ratios (height : distance : line of sight) · Angle · h : d · h : line of sight · 30° · 1 : √3 · 1 : 2 · 45° · 1 : 1 · 1 : √2 · 60° · √3 : 1 · √3 : 2 · SSC CGL 2021 Tier 1 · 11 Apr 2022 S1 · Present height = 78 tan 30° = 78/√3 = 26√3 · Finished height = 78 tan 60° = 78√3 · Raise by 78√3 − 26√3 = 52√3 · 52√3 m · tan 60° = 3 × tan 30°, so the finished tower is 3 times as tall: raise = 2 × 26√3. · SSC CHSL 2023 Tier 2 · 10 Jan 2024 S1 · Shadows: h cot 30° = h√3 and h cot 45° = h · h√3 − h = 40 → h = 40/(√3 − 1) · Rationalise: h = 40(√3 + 1)/2 = 20(√3 + 1) m · 20(√3 + 1) m · Near ship (45°): distance = 60 cot 45° = 60 · Far ship (30°): distance = 60 cot 30° = 60√3 · Gap = 60√3 − 60 = 60(√3 − 1) ≈ 43.9 m · 60(√3 − 1) m · Same side → subtract the cot values; opposite sides → add them. · Draw first, then use only tan. For 30°/45°/60°, write sides straight from the ratio table — no calculation. 30° → 60° walk: the walked distance is twice the remaining distance and the height is (√3/2) × walked. Approximation: √3 ≈ 1.732, so 60(√3 − 1) ≈ 43.9 and 20(√3 + 1) ≈ 54.6 — use this to pick options quickly. · Eye height: if a 1.5 m tall person sees the top at 45° from 28.5 m, the tower is 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m , not 28.5 m. Depression is measured from the horizontal , not from the vertical tower — the angle inside the triangle at the top is 90° − depression. Same side vs opposite sides: subtract distances for the same side, add them for opposite sides. · Uses only L2’s standard values (tan 30°, 45°, 60°) and L1’s tan = P/B. Shadow and ladder problems are the same triangle as the 30-60-90 triangle of Geometry. · tan θ = height ÷ horizontal distance; depression from the top = elevation from the bottom · Same side: h = x/(cot α − cot β); opposite sides: distance = h(cot α + cot β) · 30° → 60°: walked = 2 × remaining, h = (√3/2) × walked · Complementary angles from a and b: h = √(ab) · Add the observer’s eye height; √3 ≈ 1.732 for approximate options

Rare as a pure question in CGL Tier 1 , but the ideas appear inside other topics: arc length and sector questions in CHSL/CGL mensuration (“an arc subtending 22.5° is 16.5 cm, find r”), the occasional “75° = ? radians”, and clock-hand angles (reasoning and maths). Cheap marks once the two conversions are automatic. · A degree is 1/360 of a full turn (1° = 60′, 1′ = 60″). A radian is the angle at the centre when the arc length equals the radius. A full circle has arc 2πr, so it contains 2π radians: 2π rad = 360° , i.e. π rad = 180° . 1 radian ≈ 57.3° (57°16′ with π = 22/7). · Radian and the clock face · Arc length equal to the radius → angle of 1 radian (≈ 57.3°). In general arc l = rθ with θ in radians. · At 3:40 the hour hand (blue, short) is at 90° + 40 × 0.5° = 110° from 12; the minute hand (accent) is at 240°. Angle = 130° = |30 × 3 − 5.5 × 40|. · Conversions and circle measures · Degree → radian · multiply by π/180 · 75° = 75π/180 = 5π/12 · Radian → degree · multiply by 180/π · 3π/5 = 108°; 1 rad = 180/π ≈ 57.3° (57°16′ with π = 22/7) · Arc length · l = rθ (θ in radians) = (θ°/360)·2πr · θ must be in radians in l = rθ · Sector area · A = ½ r²θ = ½ l r · = (θ°/360)·πr² · Sub-units · 1° = 60′, 1′ = 60″ · 40°20′ = 40⅓° · Clock hands · Minute hand · 6° per minute · 360° in 60 min · Hour hand · 0.5° per minute (30° per hour) · 360° in 12 h · Angle at H:M · θ = |30H − 5.5M| · if θ > 180°, the smaller angle is 360° − θ · Relative speed · 5.5° per minute · hands coincide every 65 5/11 min (11 times in 12 h) · Common angles · Degrees · Radians · Degrees · Radians · 30° · π/6 · 135° · 3π/4 · 45° · π/4 · 150° · 5π/6 · 60° · π/3 · 180° · π · 90° · π/2 · 270° · 3π/2 · 120° · 2π/3 · 360° · 2π · SSC CHSL 2023 · 8 Aug S4 · 22.5° is 1/16 of 360° · Arc = (1/16) × 2 × (22/7) × r = 11r/28 · 11r/28 = 16.5 → r = 16.5 × 28/11 = 42 cm · 42 cm · 22.5/360 = 1/16 — spot the fraction of a full turn first. · θ = |30 × 3 − 5.5 × 40| = |90 − 220| = 130° · 130 < 180, so it is already the smaller angle · 130 × π/180 = 13π/18 rad · 130° = 13π/18 · Sum = 180° = π rad, parts = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 · Largest = 4/9 × π · = 4π/9 (= 80°) · 4π/9 · π = 180° : replace π by 180° and simplify (5π/12 = 5 × 15° = 75°). Clock: “30H − 5.5M” , take the absolute value; if above 180°, subtract from 360°. Fractions of a turn: 22.5° = 1/16, 45° = 1/8, 60° = 1/6, 72° = 1/5, 120° = 1/3 of 360°. · l = rθ needs θ in radians. With θ = 60° it is r × π/3, not 60r. 1 radian ≠ 1° ; 1 rad ≈ 57.3°. Clock hour hand moves during the minutes: at 3:40 it is not at the 3 but 20° past it — that is where the 5.5 (not 6) comes from. · Arc length and sector area are core 2D-mensuration results; the clock formula is also asked in reasoning. Radians are just a different unit — every ratio in L1–L10 is the same: sin(π/6) = sin 30° = ½. · π rad = 180°; degree → radian ×π/180, radian → degree ×180/π · 1 rad ≈ 57.3° (57°16′ with π = 22/7); 1° = 60′, 1′ = 60″ · Arc l = rθ and sector area ½r²θ (θ in radians) · Clock angle = |30H − 5.5M| (use 360° − θ if above 180°) · Minute hand 6°/min, hour hand 0.5°/min

voice.x: Active–passive voice is one of the most reliable marks in SSC English. In CGL Tier 1 (25 English questions, +2 / −0.5) it usually appears as one question in most shifts. In CGL Tier 2 (Paper 1, Module II: 45 English questions, +3 / −1) expect one to three. CHSL, CPO and Selection Post ask it in the same format. Once the method is automatic, a voice question takes 20–30 seconds. · Where voice is asked in SSC exams · Exam · English section · Voice questions (usual) · Marking · CGL Tier 1 · 25 questions · 0–1 per shift, mostly 1 · +2 / −0.5 · CGL Tier 2 (Paper 1, Module II) · 45 questions · 1–3 · +3 / −1 · CHSL Tier 1 · 25 questions · 0–1 · +2 / −0.5 · CPO Paper 1 · 50 questions · 1–2 · +1 / −0.25 · Selection Post / Stenographer · 25–200 (by level) · 1–2 · Varies · The question is almost always worded the same way: “Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice” (or “in active voice”). Four full sentences are given. Usually only the helping verb, the pronoun or the word order differs between options, so you are really checking four things: tense, subject/object swap, the third form (V3) of the verb, and the pronoun case after “by”. · Recent pattern (2023–2025 shifts): what the sentences test · Type · How often · Typical sentence · Simple present / past / future · Very often · The gardener waters the plants every morning. · Continuous (is being / was being) · Very often · The workers were repairing the road. · Perfect (has been / had been) · Very often · She has completed the project. · Modals (can be / must be / should have been) · Often, rising · You must submit the form by Monday. · Interrogative (By whom / Who) · Often · Who wrote this novel? · Imperative (Let … be / You are requested) · Regular · Please close the window. · Passive → active · Regular (about 1 in 4) · The thief was caught by the police. · Two objects, ‘It is said that’, infinitives · Tier 2 favourite · People say that he is honest. · The 30-second elimination. (1) Find the tense from the helping verb and strike out options with the wrong tense — usually two go at once. (2) Check the new subject: the old object must come first, in subject form (him → he, them → they). (3) Check that the main verb is in V3. (4) Check “by + object form” at the end and that no word has been dropped or added (time words like every day, yesterday stay). · SSC distractors are built from tiny tense slips: is vs was, was vs was being, has been vs had been, will be vs would be. Read the helping verb of each option before reading anything else. · Meaning check. Voice change never changes the meaning, the tense or the time words. If an option changes yesterday to today, drops not, or changes can to could, it is wrong — even if the grammar looks fine. · Voice and narration (direct–indirect speech) are asked side by side in SSC papers and use the same skill: keeping tense under control. Revise them together on the last day. · In CGL Tier 1, which step usually eliminates two options at once in a voice question?

voice.t: The rules: object, V3 and pronouns
voice.h: मूल नियम · कर्म, V3 और सर्वनाम
voice.x: Every voice question uses these rules. If you know them by heart, the tense lessons are just tables to remember. · In the active voice the doer (agent) is the subject: Ravi wrote a letter. In the passive voice the receiver of the action becomes the subject: A letter was written by Ravi. Only sentences with an object (transitive verbs) can be changed. She sleeps has no object, so it has no passive. · Four steps of active → passive · 1. Swap · Object → new subject; subject → after “by” · Ravi … a letter → A letter … by Ravi · 2. Helping verb · Add the correct form of “be” for the tense · is / was / will be / is being / has been … · 3. Verb · Main verb always in V3 (past participle) · write → written, sing → sung · 4.
