Agree · Helping verb agrees with the NEW subject · Letters were written; a letter was written · Pronoun change (subject ↔ object form) · Subject form · Object form (after “by”) · I · me · we · us · you · you · he · him · she · her · it · it · they · them · who · whom · V3 forms SSC uses again and again · V1 · V2 · V3 · write · wrote · written · sing · sang · sung · teach · taught · taught · catch · caught · caught · steal · stole · stolen · break · broke · broken · speak · spoke · spoken · choose · chose · chosen · bite · bit · bitten · hide · hid · hidden · lay (put down) · laid · laid · tear · tore · torn · draw · drew · drawn · forgive · forgave · forgiven · sow · sowed · sown · shake · shook · shaken · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. She invited us to the party. · Tense: simple past (invited) → was/were + V3 · Object “us” becomes subject “we” → plural → were · Subject “she” goes after “by” in object form → by her · We were invited to the party by her. · Change the pronoun first (us → we), then the helping verb agrees with it. · Agreement with the new subject. The teacher praised the students → The students were praised, not was. The helping verb follows the new subject, not the old one. · Not every object makes a passive. Verbs of state such as have (own), resemble, lack, suit, fit are not changed: She has a car → ✗ A car is had by her. · Write the V3 column on your rough sheet once a week: half the wrong options in SSC use V2 (was wrote, is spoke) or a misspelt V3 (was teached). · Which of these sentences cannot be changed into passive voice? · In passive voice, “by they” should be written as:

Present tenses appear in roughly one voice question in six. The present continuous (is being) and the present perfect (has been) are the ones SSC likes most, because the distractors are easy to build. · Present tense table · Simple present · V1 / V5 → is / am / are + V3 · He writes a letter → A letter is written by him · Present continuous · is / am / are + Ving → is / am / are + being + V3 · He is writing a letter → A letter is being written by him · Present perfect · has / have + V3 → has / have + been + V3 · He has written a letter → A letter has been written by him · Present perfect continuous · has been + Ving → usually no passive · SSC rarely asks it · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. The gardener waters the plants every morning. · Simple present (waters) → is/are + V3 · Plants (plural) → are watered · “every morning” stays at the end · The plants are watered by the gardener every morning. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. The committee is reviewing the new proposal. · Present continuous (is reviewing) → is/are being + V3 · Proposal (singular) → is being reviewed · The new proposal is being reviewed by the committee. · If the active has “-ing”, the passive must have “being”. · Continuous ↔ being, perfect ↔ been. “-ing” in the active → “being” in the passive. “has/have” in the active → “has/have been” in the passive. Options that drop these words are wrong. · Is being written (present continuous) vs has been written (present perfect) vs was being written (past continuous): SSC puts all three in the options. Match the time of the active verb exactly. · Passive of: “They have painted the walls.”

Past tenses are the single most common voice type in recent SSC shifts — about one question in five. The simple past (was/were + V3) is the easiest mark in the English section. · Past tense table · Simple past · V2 → was / were + V3 · She sang a song → A song was sung by her · Past continuous · was / were + Ving → was / were + being + V3 · She was singing a song → A song was being sung by her · Past perfect · had + V3 → had + been + V3 · She had sung a song → A song had been sung by her · Past perfect continuous · had been + Ving → usually no passive · Not asked · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. The workers were repairing the road. · Past continuous (were repairing) → was/were being + V3 · Road (singular) → was being repaired · The road was being repaired by the workers. · The verb agrees with “road”, not with “workers”. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. The police had arrested the thief before sunset. · Past perfect (had arrested) → had been + V3 · “before sunset” stays · The thief had been arrested by the police before sunset. · “had” never changes to “has”. had been stays past perfect. Options with has been or was for a past perfect sentence are traps. · Simple past is one word in the active (V2). If the active has only one verb word in the past, the answer is just was/were + V3 — no being, no been. · Passive of: “The cat was chasing the mice.”

Modal verbs (can, must, should, may, have to) have become more frequent since 2023, and modal + have + V3 (should have been done) is a Tier 2 favourite. · Future and modal table · Simple future · will / shall + V1 → will / shall + be + V3 · He will help me → I will be helped by him · Future perfect · will have + V3 → will have + been + V3 · He will have finished it → It will have been finished by him · Future continuous · will be + Ving → usually no passive · Rarely asked · Modal + V1 · can / could / may / might / must / should / would + V1 → modal + be + V3 · You must obey the rules → The rules must be obeyed by you · Modal perfect · modal + have + V3 → modal + have been + V3 · She should have sent it → It should have been sent by her · Going to · is going to + V1 → is going to be + V3 · They are going to sell the house → The house is going to be sold by them · Have to / used to / ought to · to + V1 → to be + V3 · We have to finish it → It has to be finished by us · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. You should have informed the police. · Modal perfect (should have informed) → should have been + V3 · police → subject · The police should have been informed by you. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. We have to finish this work today. · have to + V1 → has/have to be + V3 · “this work” is singular → has to be finished · This work has to be finished by us today. · “have to” agrees with the new subject: it has to, they have to. · Modals do not change. can stays can, may stays may. An option with could for can or would for will changes the tense and is wrong. · Modal + be + V3 is the whole rule. Never can being, never must been (without have). · Passive of: “Someone must clean the kitchen.”

Imperatives (orders, requests, advice) come up in about one question in eight. SSC accepts two forms: Let + object + be + V3, and You are requested / ordered / advised + to + V1. · Imperative patterns · Order with object · Let + object + be + V3 · Shut the door → Let the door be shut · Negative order · Let + object + not + be + V3 · Don’t touch the wire → Let the wire not be touched · Request (please / kindly) · You are requested to + V1 · Please help me → You are requested to help me · Order (no object / strong) · You are ordered to + V1 · Get out → You are ordered to get out · Advice · You are advised to + V1 · Work hard → You are advised to work hard · Warning · You are warned (not) to + V1 · Don’t smoke here → You are warned not to smoke here · Let + person + V1 + object · Let + object + be + V3 + by + person · Let him do the work → Let the work be done by him · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. Please lend me your pen. · “Please” → request · Request → You are requested to + V1 · Keep the rest of the sentence unchanged · You are requested to lend me your pen. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. Let her sing a song. · Let + person + V1 + object → Let + object + be + V3 + by + person · song → Let a song be sung by her · Let a song be sung by her. · Let us play cricket is a suggestion: its passive is Let cricket be played by us — not We are requested to play cricket. · Look at the first word. Please / kindly → requested. A bare verb with an object → Let … be …. Don’t → Let … not be … or You are warned/forbidden …. · Passive of: “Do not waste your time.”

Questions in the passive are asked often, and the options are designed to catch mistakes in word order. The Who → By whom rule appears in some form almost every month. · Question patterns · Do / does + V1 · Is / am / are + subject + V3 · Does he sing songs? → Are songs sung by him? · Did + V1 · Was / were + subject + V3 · Did she write the letter? → Was the letter written by her? · Has / have + V3 · Has / have + subject + been + V3 · Have you finished it? → Has it been finished by you? · Is / are + Ving · Is / are + subject + being + V3 · Is he writing a book? → Is a book being written by him? · Modal question · Modal + subject + be + V3 · Can you solve this? → Can this be solved by you? · Who …? · By whom + helping verb + subject + V3 · Who broke the vase? → By whom was the vase broken? · Whom …? · Who + helping verb + subject + V3 · Whom did you call? → Who was called by you? · Why / when / where / how · Wh-word + helping verb + subject + V3 + by … · Why did he beat the dog? → Why was the dog beaten by him? · What + V (what is object) · What + helping verb + V3 + by … · What are you doing? → What is being done by you? · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. Who wrote this novel? · Who → By whom at the start · Simple past → was + V3 · this novel → subject · By whom was this novel written? · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. Why did they postpone the meeting? · Wh-word stays first · did + V1 → was + V3 · by them at the end · Why was the meeting postponed by them? · The passive of a question is still a question. Options that end with a full stop or have statement word order (The letter was written by her?) are wrong in SSC answers. · Who and whom swap. Who (doer) → By whom. Whom (receiver) → Who. Remember: by + whom, because after “by” we need the object form. · Passive of: “Whom did the manager praise?”

voice.h: दो कर्म, इन्फ़िनिटिव और 'It is said'
voice.x: These are Tier 2 favourites: sentences with two objects, sentences with that-clauses (People say that …) and infinitives (to be + V3). Expect one in Tier 2 and occasionally one in Tier 1. · Two objects (give, show, tell, teach, offer, send …) · Person as subject (preferred) · Person + was/were + V3 + thing + by … · He gave me a book → I was given a book by him · Thing as subject · Thing + was + V3 + to + person + by … · He gave me a book → A book was given to me by him · Saying and believing verbs (say, believe, know, think, report) · It-form · It + is/was + V3 + that + clause · People say that he is honest → It is said that he is honest · Subject-form (same time) · Subject + is/was + V3 + to be … · → He is said to be honest · Subject-form (earlier time) · Subject + is + V3 + to have + V3 · People believe that he stole it → He is believed to have stolen it · Infinitives · to + V1 with object · to be + V3 · It is time to close the shop → It is time for the shop to be closed · want / ask + object + to V1 · object + to be + V3 · I want you to do this → I want this to be done by you · Nothing / no time + to V1 · to be + V3 · There is no time to waste → There is no time to be wasted · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. People say that honesty is the best policy. · “People say” → agent is general, so drop it · It + is + said + that + clause · It is said that honesty is the best policy. · With say / believe / know, SSC usually wants the It-form. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. The teacher taught us grammar. · Two objects: us (person), grammar (thing) · Person first: us → We were taught grammar by the teacher · We were taught grammar by the teacher. · With the thing as subject, add to before the person: A book was given to me. A book was given me is old-fashioned and SSC treats it as wrong. · If both “person-first” and “thing-first” forms appear in the options, check the other parts (tense, pronoun). Only one option will be fully correct. · Passive of: “They offered him a job.”

voice.t: Prepositions other than ‘by’, phrasal verbs & gerunds
voice.x: About one question in sixteen, but these are the ones most students get wrong. The fixed prepositions below are tested both in voice and in error-spotting. · Verbs that take a preposition other than “by” · Active · Passive · I know him. · He is known to me. · The news surprised us. · We were surprised at the news. · Smoke filled the room. · The room was filled with smoke. · Snow covered the hills. · The hills were covered with snow. · His work pleased the boss. · The boss was pleased with his work. · The result satisfied her. · She was satisfied with the result. · Music interests me. · I am interested in music. · The jar contains honey. · Honey is contained in the jar. · His rudeness annoyed me. · I was annoyed at his rudeness. · The accident shocked us. · We were shocked at the accident. · Phrasal verbs and gerunds · Phrasal verb · Keep the particle after V3 · They looked after the child → The child was looked after by them · Laugh at / send for / put off · V3 + particle + by · We sent for the doctor → The doctor was sent for · Gerund (-ing) with object · being + V3 · I remember my father taking me there → I remember being taken there by my father · need / want + -ing · = need to be + V3 · The room needs cleaning → The room needs to be cleaned · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. Everybody laughed at the joker. · Phrasal verb “laugh at” – keep “at” · Simple past → was + V3 · Everybody → by everybody · The joker was laughed at by everybody. · Never drop the particle: “The joker was laughed by everybody” is wrong. · The room was filled by smoke and I am known by him are classic SSC distractors. Learn the table above. · Passive of: “The answer surprised the teacher.”

Negative words and unknown agents appear in about one question in sixteen. They are quick marks once you know three rules. · Negatives · not · stays in the same place after the first helping verb · I did not see her → She was not seen by me · Nobody / No one · → not … by anybody / anyone · Nobody saw him → He was not seen by anybody · Never · stays: was never + V3 · She never tells lies → Lies are never told by her · Nothing (as object) · → Nothing … / not anything · He did nothing → Nothing was done by him · When to drop “by …” · Unknown / general agent · someone, somebody, people, they (general), one · Someone has stolen my bag → My bag has been stolen · Obvious agent · the police arrest, the court sentences · He was arrested (by the police) – may be dropped · Keep it · when the agent is a named person or a pronoun like he, she, us · She cooked dinner → Dinner was cooked by her · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice. Nobody can solve this puzzle. · Nobody → not … by anybody · Modal → can not be + V3 · This puzzle cannot be solved by anybody. · This puzzle can be solved by nobody is grammatical but SSC keys cannot be solved by anybody. If both appear, choose the not … anybody form. · No passive: intransitive verbs (sleep, go, come, die), verbs of state (have, resemble, lack, fit, suit) and perfect continuous tenses. If the question asks for one, look for the option that keeps the meaning without inventing a strange verb. · Passive of: “Someone has stolen my purse.”

About one SSC voice question in four asks for the active voice. Tier 2 also uses longer sentences with two clauses, causatives and modal perfects. · Passive → active: reverse the steps · 1. Agent first · The word after “by” becomes the subject (object → subject form) · by him → he · 2. Remove “be” · Drop the be-form and rebuild the tense on the main verb · was written → wrote; has been written → has written · 3. Object · The old subject becomes the object (subject → object form) · I → me, they → them · 4. No agent? · Use a general subject: someone, people, they · The shop was robbed → Someone robbed the shop · Let … be … · Back to a bare imperative · Let the door be shut → Shut the door · You are requested to … · Please + V1 · You are requested to sit → Please sit · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice. The match was won by India. · Agent India → subject · was won → simple past → won · India won the match. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice. The documents are being checked by the clerk. · Agent the clerk → subject (singular) · are being checked → present continuous → is checking · The clerk is checking the documents. · The helping verb now agrees with the new subject (clerk → is). · Tier 2 tricky types · Causative have/get · Already passive in meaning · I had my car repaired = Someone repaired my car for me · Two clauses · Change the clause that has the object, keep the rest · He said that he would finish the task → He said that the task would be finished by him · Modal perfect · must / might / could + have been + V3 · They might have sold the house → The house might have been sold by them · Question with tag · Change the main clause and the tag agrees with it · He cleaned it, didn’t he? → It was cleaned by him, wasn’t it? · In passive → active, the commonest trap is wrong tense: was being repaired → were repairing (not repaired), had been finished → had finished (not has finished). · Active of: “A new bridge will be built by the government.”

voice.h: नवीन पैटर्न अभ्यास · अंतिम दिन के सुझाव
voice.x: This lesson’s question bank is a mixed set modelled on recent CGL, CHSL and CPO shifts (2023–2025): everyday sentences (office, school, government, sport, environment), all tense types, and both directions. Do it in one sitting with a 30-second limit per question. · What changed recently. Sentences are longer and more formal (The ministry has launched a new scheme for farmers), modals and perfect tenses appear more often, and passive → active is asked more than before. The four steps from L2 still answer every one. · Last-day checklist · Tense first · is/was/will + being/been — match it exactly · Pronoun case · subject form at the start, object form after “by” · V3 spelling · written, chosen, stolen, taught, laid · Agreement · helping verb agrees with the new subject · Nothing lost · not, never, time words and modals stay · Special · Who → By whom; Please → requested; Let … be …; known to; filled with · Time budget: voice and narration should take under 30 seconds each in Tier 1. Use the saved time on reading comprehension and cloze, which take longer. · If two options look correct, compare them word by word. The difference is usually one helping verb or one pronoun — and only one of them matches the tense and case rules. · Error-spotting questions sometimes hide a voice error: The letter was wrote by him (V2 for V3) or The room was filled by smoke (wrong preposition). The rules here earn marks there too.

narration.x: Narration (direct–indirect speech) is asked in almost every SSC English section. CGL Tier 1 (25 questions, +2 / −0.5) usually has one narration question in a shift. CGL Tier 2 (Paper 1, Module II: 45 questions, +3 / −1) has one to three. CHSL, CPO and Selection Post ask it in the same format. With the method below it takes 25–35 seconds. · Where narration is asked in SSC exams · Exam · English section · Narration questions (usual) · Marking · CGL Tier 1 · 25 questions · 0–1 per shift, mostly 1 · +2 / −0.5 · CGL Tier 2 (Paper 1, Module II) · 45 questions · 1–3 · +3 / −1 · CHSL Tier 1 · 25 questions · 0–1 · +2 / −0.5 · CPO Paper 1 · 50 questions · 1–2 · +1 / −0.25 · Selection Post / Stenographer · 25–200 (by level) · 1–2 · Varies · The wording is fixed: “Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech” (or “in direct speech”). Four full sentences are given. They usually differ in only one or two places, so you are checking five things: the reporting verb, the joining word, the pronouns, the tense, and the time/place words. · Recent pattern (2023–2025 shifts): what the sentences test · Type · How often · Typical sentence · Statements with tense change · Very often · He said, “I am writing a letter.” · Questions (asked if / asked wh-) · Very often · She said to me, “Where do you live?” · Commands and requests · Often · The teacher said to us, “Do not make a noise.” · Time and place words · Often · He said, “I will come tomorrow.” · Exclamations, wishes, greetings · Regular · She said, “What a lovely view!” · Indirect → direct · Regular (about 1 in 4) · He told me that he was busy. · Exceptions (universal truth, past perfect, modals) · Tier 2 favourite · The teacher said, “The sun rises in the east.” · The 30-second elimination (RJPTW). (1) Reporting verb: said to → told / asked / ordered / requested. (2) Joining word: that / if / whether / wh-word / to. (3) Pronouns: SON rule. (4) Tense: one step back if the reporting verb is past. (5) Words of time and place: now → then, tomorrow → the next day. Most distractors fail at T or W. · SSC distractors are built from one wrong change: is left as is, will left as will, tomorrow left as tomorrow, a question left in question order (asked where did I live), or said me instead of told me. · Narration and active–passive voice appear side by side and both test tense control. Revise them together; the Voice mini app uses the same layout. · Which check usually removes the most wrong options in a narration question?

narration.h: मूल नियम · रिपोर्टिंग वर्ब और सर्वनाम
narration.x: Every narration question uses these rules. Pronoun mistakes are the second most common SSC distractor after tense. · In direct speech the exact words are inside inverted commas: Ram said, “I am tired.” In indirect speech we report them in our own words: Ram said that he was tired. The verb outside the commas (said) is the reporting verb; the words inside are the reported speech. · Five steps of direct → indirect · 1. Reporting verb · said → said; said to + person → told + person · He said to me → He told me · 2. Joining word · statement → that; question → if/whether or wh-word; order → to · told me that … · 3. Pronouns · SON rule (below) · “I” → he / she · 4. Tense · one step back if the reporting verb is in the past · am → was, will → would · 5. Time / place · near words → far words · now → then, here → there · SON rule for pronouns · Person inside the commas · Changes to match · Example · 1st person (I, me, my, we, us, our) · Subject of the reporting verb · He said, “I am ill.” → He said that he was ill. · 2nd person (you, your) · Object of the reporting verb · She said to me, “You are late.” → She told me that I was late. · 3rd person (he, she, it, they) · No change · He said, “She is clever.” → He said that she was clever. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. Rita said to me, “You have done your work well.” · said to me → told me · Statement → that · you (2nd person) → object of reporting verb = me → I; your → my · has/have done → had done · Rita told me that I had done my work well. · said me and told that are both wrong. told must have a person after it (told me that); said must not (said that, or said to me that — rare). · Do pronouns before tense. Once I has become he, the verb agreement (was, not were) follows easily. · He said to her, “I like your dress.” Indirect:

Tense is tested in nearly every SSC narration question. If the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked), the tense inside goes one step back. · Backshift table · Simple present → simple past · V1 / V5 → V2 · “I write” → he wrote · Present continuous → past continuous · is / am / are + Ving → was / were + Ving · “I am writing” → he was writing · Present perfect → past perfect · has / have + V3 → had + V3 · “I have written” → he had written · Present perfect continuous → past perfect continuous · has been + Ving → had been + Ving · “I have been writing” → he had been writing · Simple past → past perfect · V2 → had + V3 · “I wrote” → he had written · Past continuous → past perfect continuous · was + Ving → had been + Ving · “I was writing” → he had been writing · Past perfect · no change · “I had written” → he had written · will / shall → would · will / shall + V1 → would + V1 · “I will write” → he would write · can / may → could / might · modal + V1 · “I can write” → he could write · When the tense does NOT change · Reporting verb in present / future · says, will say → no backshift · He says, “I am busy” → He says that he is busy · Universal truth / scientific fact · stays in present · The sun rises in the east · Habitual fact still true · may stay in present · She said that she goes for a walk daily · Past perfect, would, could, might, should, ought to, used to · no change · “I could swim” → he could swim · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. He said, “I am writing a letter.” · said → said that · I → he · am writing → was writing · He said that he was writing a letter. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. She said, “I bought this car last year.” · bought (simple past) → had bought · this → that; last year → the previous year · She said that she had bought that car the previous year. · Simple past → past perfect, not simple past. “I saw him” → he had seen him. SSC options often keep saw. · Think of each helping verb moving one step: is → was, has → had, was → had been, will → would, can → could, may → might. Past perfect is already at the back: it stays. · She said, “I have finished my homework.” Indirect:

Exceptions are a Tier 2 favourite and appear in Tier 1 about once a month. The universal-truth exception is the one SSC asks most. · Modal changes · will / shall · → would · “I shall go” → he would go · can · → could · “I can help” → he could help · may (possibility / permission) · → might · “It may rain” → it might rain · may (wish) · → might (in a wish) / prayed that … might · “May you live long!” → prayed that I might live long · must (obligation) · → had to (or must) · “I must go” → he had to go · must (deduction / permanent rule) · → no change · “He must be tired” → he must be tired · would, could, might, should, ought to, used to, had better · → no change · “You should rest” → I should rest · No-change cases · Universal truth · present stays · The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun · Historical fact · simple past may stay · He said that Akbar ruled India for many years · Unreal past (wish / if only / it is time) · past stays · He said that he wished he were rich · Conditional type 2 / 3 · no change · He said that if he had money he would buy a car · Past perfect · no change · She said that she had already eaten · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. The teacher said, “The earth revolves around the sun.” · Universal truth → tense does not change · said → said that · The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun. · An option with revolved is a trap for universal truths. But a personal present fact (“I live in Delhi”) does backshift → he lived in Delhi. · Modals already in the past form never move: would, could, might, should, ought to. If the option changes should to should have, it is wrong. · He said, “You should take some rest.” Indirect (he said this to me):

Time words decide about one SSC narration question in three: often two options are identical except for one time word. · Near → far words · Direct · Indirect · now · then · today · that day · tonight · that night · yesterday · the previous day / the day before · tomorrow · the next day / the following day · last night · the previous night / the night before · last week / year · the previous week / year · next week / month · the following week / month · ago · before · this · that · these · those · here · there · hence · thence · thus · so / in that way · come · go (when the place changes) · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. He said, “I will come here tomorrow.” · will → would · here → there · tomorrow → the next day · He said that he would come there the next day. · ago → before (not back), yesterday → the previous day (not the last day), and this → that only when it is a time/place pointer, not inside a fixed name. · If the reporting verb is present (says) or the speech is reported the same day and place, time words need not change. SSC almost always uses said, so change them. · She said, “I met him two days ago.” Indirect:

Questions come up very often. SSC tests three things: asked (not said/told), if / whether or the wh-word, and statement word order without a question mark. · Question patterns · Reporting verb · said / said to → asked / enquired of · He said to me → He asked me · Yes/no question · asked + if / whether + statement order · “Are you ready?” → asked if I was ready · Wh-question · asked + wh-word + statement order · “Where do you live?” → asked where I lived · do / does / did · drop it and change the main verb · “Do you like tea?” → asked if I liked tea · End · full stop, no question mark · … where I lived. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. She said to me, “Where do you live?” · said to → asked · Keep “where”, statement order: where + I + verb · do you live → I lived · She asked me where I lived. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. He said to her, “Have you seen my keys?” · Yes/no → asked her if · have you seen → she had seen · my → his · He asked her if she had seen his keys. · He asked me where did I live and He asked me that where I lived are the classic wrong options: no question order and no that before a wh-word. · Look at the end of each option: one that still ends with ? is wrong in indirect speech. · He said to me, “Are you coming with us?” Indirect:

Imperatives appear often. The key is choosing the reporting verb from the tone and using to + V1 (or not to + V1). · Imperative patterns · Order · ordered / commanded + person + to V1 · “Stand up.” → The teacher ordered the boy to stand up · Request (please) · requested + person + to V1 (drop please) · “Please help me.” → She requested me to help her · Advice · advised + person + to V1 · “Work hard.” → He advised me to work hard · Negative · told / ordered + person + not to V1 (or forbade + to V1) · “Don’t shout.” → He told me not to shout · Let’s (suggestion) · suggested / proposed that + we/they + should + V1 · “Let’s go out.” → He suggested that they should go out · Let (permission) · asked / requested + to let / allow · “Let me go.” → He requested to be allowed to go · Sir / Madam · respectfully · “Sir, please listen.” → He respectfully requested his teacher to listen · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. The teacher said to the students, “Do not make a noise.” · Command → told / ordered · Negative → not to + V1 · No tense change in a to-infinitive · The teacher told the students not to make a noise. · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. He said, “Let’s go for a picnic.” · Let’s = suggestion → suggested that · we → they; add should · He suggested that they should go for a picnic. · He suggested them to go is wrong — suggest does not take person + to. Use suggested that they should go. Also requested me please to help is wrong: drop please. · Please → requested. Don’t → not to. Let’s → suggested that … should. Three patterns cover almost all imperatives. · She said to me, “Please close the door.” Indirect:

Asked regularly in Tier 1 and Tier 2. The trick is choosing the reporting verb with an adverb and turning the exclamation into a statement. · Exclamatory & optative patterns · What / How …! · exclaimed (with joy / wonder) that it was a very … · “What a lovely view!” → She exclaimed that it was a very lovely view · Alas! · exclaimed with sorrow / sadly that · “Alas! I am ruined.” → He exclaimed sadly that he was ruined · Hurrah! · exclaimed with joy that · “Hurrah! We have won.” → They exclaimed with joy that they had won · Bravo! / Well done! · applauded / praised + person + saying that · “Well done!” → He applauded me · May you …! · wished / prayed that + person + might · “May you live long!” → She prayed that I might live long · Good morning / night · wished + person + good morning · “Good morning, sir.” → He wished his teacher good morning · Thank you · thanked + person · “Thank you.” → She thanked me · Goodbye · bade + person + goodbye · “Goodbye, friends.” → He bade his friends goodbye · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. She said, “What a beautiful garden this is!” · What a … ! → exclaimed that it was a very … · this → that; is → was · She exclaimed that that was a very beautiful garden. · Keep the joining word that after exclaimed, and turn What a / How into very. Options that keep the exclamation mark are wrong. · May you … is always a wish or prayer → wished / prayed that … might. · The old man said to me, “May God bless you!” Indirect:

Tier 2 likes longer speech: a statement plus a question, an answer with Yes/No, or two sentences. Each part gets its own reporting verb, joined by and. · Joining patterns · Statement + statement · said that … and added that … · “I am tired. I will rest.” → said that he was tired and added that he would rest · Statement + question · said that … and asked … · “I am lost. Can you help me?” → said that he was lost and asked if I could help him · Yes / No answer · replied in the affirmative / negative · “Yes,” he said → He replied in the affirmative · Yes + clause · replied that + clause · “Yes, I will come.” → He replied that he would come · Vocative (name / Sir) · becomes the object of the reporting verb · “Ravi, sit down.” → He told Ravi to sit down · Order + reason · told … to … as / because … · “Hurry up, we are late.” → told me to hurry up as we were late · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. He said to me, “I am new here. Can you show me the way?” · First part: told me that he was new there · Second part: and asked if I could show him the way · He told me that he was new there and asked if I could show him the way. · Do not use one reporting verb for two different kinds of sentence. He told me that he was new there and that could I show him the way is wrong. · Split the speech at each full stop or question mark. Convert each piece with its own pattern, then join with and added / and asked / and told. · “Yes,” she said, “I can drive.” Indirect:

About one SSC narration question in four asks for the direct form. Reverse each step: put the words back in inverted commas and move tenses one step forward. · Reverse the steps · Reporting verb · told + person → said to + person; asked → said to + person · He told me → He said to me · Remove that / if · add inverted commas and the right punctuation (. ? !) · asked if → said, “Are …?” · Pronouns · the speaker becomes I; the listener becomes you · told me that he … → said to me, “I …” · Tense forward · was → is, had → has/have (or simple past), would → will, could → can · he would come → “I will come” · Time words · then → now, the next day → tomorrow, that → this, there → here · the previous day → yesterday · Commands · ordered / requested + to V1 → imperative (add Please for requested) · requested me to sit → said to me, “Please sit.” · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech. He told me that he was busy then. · told me → said to me · he → I; was → am · then → now · He said to me, “I am busy now.” · had + V3 in indirect may come from simple past or present perfect in direct. Check the time words: the previous day → yesterday (simple past); no time word → often has / have. · Check punctuation in the options: a question must end with ? inside the commas, a command must start with a bare verb, an exclamation with What / How / Alas and end with !. · She asked me if I was hungry. Direct:

Tier 2 uses longer, formal sentences: reporting verbs in the present tense, must, conditionals, let for permission, and questions with shall I. · Tricky types · Present reporting verb · says / tells → no backshift · He says, “I am busy.” → He says that he is busy · Shall I / Shall we (offer / advice) · asked + if / whether + he/they + should · “Shall I open the window?” → He asked if he should open the window · Shall (pure future) · would · “I shall be late.” → He said that he would be late · Conditional · if-clause: type 1 backshifts; types 2 and 3 stay · “If it rains, I will stay.” → … if it rained he would stay · Question tag · drop the tag, report as a statement · “You are new, aren’t you?” → asked if I was new · Let (permission) · asked to be allowed / requested … to let · “Let me go home.” → He asked to be allowed to go home · Must (deduction) · stays must · “She must be at home.” → he said that she must be at home · Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech. He said to me, “Shall I bring you a glass of water?” · Shall I (offer) → asked if he should · you → me · He asked me if he should bring me a glass of water. · With says or will say nothing backshifts. An option with was for “He says, ‘I am …’” is wrong. · Before converting, look at the reporting verb’s tense. Present → keep tenses; past → backshift. That one glance decides two options. · She says, “I am going to the market.” Indirect:

narration.h: नवीन पैटर्न अभ्यास · अंतिम दिन के सुझाव
narration.x: This lesson’s question bank is a mixed set modelled on recent CGL, CHSL and CPO shifts (2023–2025): office, school, family and travel sentences across every type, in both directions. Do it in one sitting with a 35-second limit per question. · What changed recently. Sentences are longer, mix two kinds of speech, and more often ask for the direct form. Options now differ in a single word, so the five-step check from L1 matters more than ever. · Last-day checklist · Reporting verb · said to → told / asked / ordered / requested / suggested · Joining word · that · if / whether · wh-word · to · not to · Pronouns · SON: 1st → subject, 2nd → object, 3rd → no change · Tense · one step back after a past reporting verb; none after says · Exceptions · universal truth, past perfect, would / could / might / should · Time words · now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, ago → before · If two options look correct, compare them word by word — the difference is usually one time word or one pronoun. · Error-spotting sometimes hides a narration error: He asked me where was I going or She said me that …. The same rules earn marks there too.

formulas.x: Not a chapter in the paper, but every chapter needs these values. Knowing them by heart saves 10–15 seconds per question. · Squares 11–30 · Cubes 1–20 · Fractions ↔ percentages · Powers and roots · Pythagorean triplets · Squares ending in 5: (a5)² = a(a+1) followed by 25 → 65² = 6·7 | 25 = 4225. · Squares near 50: (50 ± x)² = (25 ± x) hundreds + x² → 47² = 22|09 = 2209. · Unit digit of a perfect square is never 2, 3, 7 or 8. · 1/7 = 14.28 % (not 14.5); 1/11 = 9.09 % (not 9.9). · √5 = 2.236, √6 = 2.449 — candidates often swap them.

Divisibility (find the missing digit), remainders, unit digit, number of factors, trailing zeros, sums of series. · Division: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder · Divisibility by 3 / 9: sum of digits divisible by 3 / 9 · Divisibility by 4 / 8: last 2 / last 3 digits divisible by 4 / 8 · Divisibility by 11: (sum of odd-place digits) − (sum of even-place digits) = 0 or a multiple of 11 · Divisibility by 7, 11, 13: abcabc is always divisible by 7, 11, 13 (= abc × 1001) · Number of factors: N = a^p × b^q × c^r → (p + 1)(q + 1)(r + 1) (72 = 2³·3² → 4·3 = 12) · Sum of factors: (a^p+1 − 1)/(a − 1) × (b^q+1 − 1)/(b − 1) · Trailing zeros of n!: ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + … (100! → 20 + 4 = 24) · Unit digit cycles: 2, 3, 7, 8 → cycle 4; 4, 9 → cycle 2; 0, 1, 5, 6 → same (divide power by 4; remainder 0 → use 4th term) · Remainder of product / sum: (a × b) mod n = (a mod n × b mod n) mod n (negative remainders allowed) · aⁿ − bⁿ: divisible by (a − b) always; by (a + b) when n is even · aⁿ + bⁿ: divisible by (a + b) when n is odd · Sum 1 to n: n(n + 1)/2 · Sum of squares: n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 · Sum of cubes: [n(n + 1)/2]² · First n odd / even numbers: sum = n² / n(n + 1) · AP: Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d; Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2 (first + last) · GP: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); S∞ = a/(1 − r), |r| < 1 · Recurring decimals: 0.ababab… = ab/99; 0.abbb… = (ab − a)/90 (0.454545… = 45/99 = 5/11) · Fermat: aᵖ⁻¹ mod p = 1 (p prime, a not a multiple of p) (2¹⁰⁰ mod 101 = 1) · Primes up to 100: 25. 1 is neither prime nor composite; 2 is the only even prime. · Co-primes have HCF 1 (they need not be prime: 8 and 9). · Every prime > 3 is of the form 6k ± 1. · Product of n consecutive integers is divisible by n!. · A number and its digit-sum leave the same remainder on division by 9. · Remainder of a big power: write the base as (divisor ± 1). 17²⁰⁰ ÷ 18 → (18 − 1)²⁰⁰ → remainder (−1)²⁰⁰ = 1. · Unit digit of a sum/product: work only with unit digits. · Missing digit for 11: set (odd − even) = 0 or 11 and test options. · Unit digit when power ÷ 4 leaves 0: use the 4th term of the cycle (e.g. 2⁴ → 6), not 1. · Trailing zeros: 25 contributes two 5s, 125 three — don’t stop at ⌊n/5⌋.

HCF × LCM, bells tolling together, largest number leaving given remainders, smallest number with given remainders. · Two numbers: HCF × LCM = product of the numbers (only for two numbers) · Numbers with HCF h: a = hx, b = hy, x and y co-prime (count co-prime pairs) · HCF / LCM of fractions: HCF = HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators); LCM = LCM(numerators)/HCF(denominators) · Largest number dividing a, b, c leaving remainders r₁, r₂, r₃: HCF(a − r₁, b − r₂, c − r₃) · Largest number leaving the same remainder: HCF(|a − b|, |b − c|, |c − a|) · Smallest number leaving remainder r with each of a, b, c: LCM(a, b, c) + r · Smallest number leaving remainders that are k less than each divisor: LCM(a, b, c) − k (5 when ÷6, 6 when ÷7 → LCM − 1) · Greatest n-digit number divisible by a, b, c: largest n-digit number − (its remainder ÷ LCM) · Bells / lights together: after LCM of the intervals · HCF always divides LCM. · HCF of co-primes = 1; LCM = product. · HCF of numbers ≤ the smallest; LCM ≥ the largest. · Options test: LCM must be divisible by HCF — strike out options that fail. · HCF × LCM = product holds for TWO numbers only, not three.

BODMAS simplification, comparing surds, rationalising, infinite roots, laws of indices. · BODMAS: Brackets (), {}, [] → Of → Division → Multiplication → Addition → Subtraction (‘of’ before ÷) · Indices: aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ · Fractional power: a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(aᵐ) · Rationalise: 1/(√a + √b) = (√a − √b)/(a − b) · Root of a + 2√b: √(a + 2√b) = √x + √y where x + y = a, xy = b (√(5 + 2√6) = √3 + √2) · Infinite root (+): √(x + √(x + …)) = (1 + √(1 + 4x))/2 (= n + 1 if x = n(n + 1)) · Infinite root (−): √(x − √(x − …)) = (−1 + √(1 + 4x))/2 (= n if x = n(n + 1)) · Infinite product root: √(x√(x√(x…))) = x · Finite product root: n roots of x → x^((2ⁿ − 1)/2ⁿ) · Comparing surds: make the root order equal: LCM of indices (∛3 vs √2 → ⁶√9 vs ⁶√8) · If aˣ = aʸ (a ≠ 0, ±1) then x = y. · Add/subtract surds only when the radical is the same: 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3. · (√a + √b)² = a + b + 2√(ab). · Approximate: √2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732 and eliminate options by size. · For long fractions, look for a ± b and a² − b² patterns before multiplying out. · ‘of’ is done before division: 24 ÷ 4 of 3 = 24 ÷ 12 = 2. · −3² = −9 but (−3)² = 9.

Successive change, population/depreciation, consumption–price, elections, exam pass marks, income–expenditure. · Percentage change: (change ÷ original) × 100 · Successive change a %, b %: a + b + ab/100 (use − for a decrease) · Up r % then down r %: net loss of r²/100 % · A is r % more than B: B is r/(100 + r) × 100 % less than A (25 % more → 20 % less) · A is r % less than B: B is r/(100 − r) × 100 % more than A (20 % less → 25 % more) · Price up r %, keep spending same: cut consumption by r/(100 + r) × 100 % · Population growth: P(1 + r/100)ⁿ · Depreciation: P(1 − r/100)ⁿ · x % of y: = y % of x · Product constant (A × B fixed): A up by 1/n → B down by 1/(n + 1) (price × quantity, speed × time) · Express percentages as fractions: 12.5 % = 1/8, 16.67 % = 1/6, 37.5 % = 3/8. · Elections: votes for winner − loser = margin; invalid votes are removed first. · Successive changes: multiply fractions. +25 % then −20 % → 5/4 × 4/5 = 1 → no change. · Exam pass mark: if a student scoring x % fails by a marks and one scoring y % passes by b marks, maximum marks = (a + b)/(y − x) × 100. · ‘Percentage of’ vs ‘percentage points’: 10 % to 12 % is a 2-point rise but a 20 % rise. · Base changes in successive steps — never just add the percentages.

Profit %, MP–discount–profit chains, successive discounts, dishonest dealer, buy-x-get-y offers. · Profit %: (SP − CP)/CP × 100 (always on CP) · SP from profit: SP = CP × (100 + P%)/100; loss: CP × (100 − L%)/100 · Discount: on MP: SP = MP × (100 − d%)/100 · MP : CP: = (100 + P%) : (100 − d%) · Successive discounts: d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100 · Mark up m %, discount d %: net profit % = m − d − md/100 · Same SP, x % gain and x % loss: always a loss of x²/100 % · False weight: gain % = (true − false)/false × 100 (900 g for 1 kg → 11.11 %) · CP of x articles = SP of y articles: profit % = (x − y)/y × 100 · Buy n get m free: discount = m/(n + m) × 100 % · Profit and loss are on CP; discount is on MP. · Overhead / transport costs are added to CP. · Use multiplying factors: 20 % profit = ×6/5, 25 % discount = ×3/4. Chain them in one line. · Dishonest dealer + profit: final factor = (1 + p) × true/false weight. · Discount % is never calculated on CP. · Two successive 10 % discounts = 19 %, not 20 %.

CI − SI for 2/3 years, half-yearly compounding, doubling time, instalments, amount after n years. · Simple interest: SI = P × R × T/100; A = P + SI · Compound amount: A = P(1 + R/100)ᵀ; CI = A − P · CI − SI (2 years): P(R/100)² · CI − SI (3 years): P(R/100)²(3 + R/100) · Half-yearly / quarterly: rate R/2, time 2T / rate R/4, time 4T · Effective rate, 2 years: 2R + R²/100 (10 % → 21 %) · Different rates: A = P(1 + R₁/100)(1 + R₂/100)(1 + R₃/100) · SI doubling: doubles in T years → R = 100/T · CI multiplying: becomes x times in n years → x² in 2n, x³ in 3n · SI from two amounts: SI per year = (A₂ − A₁)/(T₂ − T₁) · CI from two amounts: R = (A₂/A₁ − 1) × 100 for consecutive years · Equal instalments (CI): P = x/(1 + r) + x/(1 + r)² + … (r = R/100) · SI is the same every year; CI grows every year. · For 1 year with yearly compounding, CI = SI. · CI for 2 years at R % on P: use 2R + R²/100 as the total % (10 % → 21 %, 20 % → 44 %). · Fractional rates: 12.5 % = 1/8 → A/P = (9/8)ⁿ. · Half-yearly: change BOTH rate and time. · CI − SI for 3 years is not 3 × (CI − SI for 2 years).

Combining ratios, mean/third/fourth proportional, incomes and savings, coins, partnership profit share. · Proportion: a : b = c : d ⇔ ad = bc · Mean proportional: √(ab) · Third proportional: b²/a (of a and b) · Fourth proportional: bc/a (of a, b, c) · Combine ratios: A:B = 2:3, B:C = 4:5 → A:B:C = 8:12:15 (make B common) · Duplicate / sub-duplicate: a² : b² / √a : √b · Componendo–dividendo: a/b = c/d ⇒ (a + b)/(a − b) = (c + d)/(c − d) · Partnership: profit share ∝ capital × time · Income–expenditure: saving = income − expenditure · Adding x to both terms: (a + x)/(b + x) = c/d → solve for x · If incomes are a:b and expenditures c:d with savings S each, write 'a k − c m = S' for both and solve. · Working partner’s salary is paid first; the rest is split by capital × time. · Answer must make the units whole — test options with the ratio’s multiples. · Coins: value ratio = number ratio × denomination. · Partnership with capital changed midway: multiply each amount by its own months.

Ratio to mix two qualities, replacement of liquid, milk–water profit. · Alligation: cheaper qty : dearer qty = (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper) · Repeated replacement: pure left = V(1 − x/V)ⁿ (x litres taken out n times) · Mixing two mixtures: convert each to fraction of one component, then use alligation · Water to gain p % at CP: water : milk = p : 100 · Alligation works for any average: prices, speeds, percentages, marks. · Draw the cross: cheaper and dearer on top, mean in the middle, differences diagonally. · The mean must lie between the two values; check the ratio order (cheaper first).

Average after adding/removing a member, average speed, consecutive numbers, ages in ratio. · Average: sum ÷ number of items · Consecutive numbers: average = (first + last)/2 · New member joins, average rises by d: new value = old average + (n + 1)d · Member replaced, average rises by d: new person = old person + n·d · Average speed (equal distances): 2xy/(x + y) · Three equal distances: 3xyz/(xy + yz + zx) · First n naturals / odds / evens: (n + 1)/2 / n / n + 1 · Ages: n years ago each age falls by n; ratio method with ‘k’ · If every value rises by k, the average rises by k; if multiplied by k, the average is multiplied by k. · Average of an AP = average of first and last term. · Deviation method: pick an assumed average, add the deviations, divide. · Average speed is not (x + y)/2 unless the TIMES are equal.

formulas.h: समय और कार्य, नल और टंकी
formulas.x: Together/alone, efficiency, M-D-H rule, alternate days, leaks, wages. · Together (two): ab/(a + b) days · Together (three): abc/(ab + bc + ca) · LCM method: total work = LCM of days; efficiency = work ÷ days · Man-days: M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂ · Efficiency: A is k times as efficient → A’s time = B’s time ÷ k · Fill a, empty b: net time = ab/(b − a) · A alone after working together: remaining work ÷ A’s rate · Wages: share ∝ work done (efficiency × days) · Efficiency and time are inversely proportional. · Pipes: filling = +, emptying = −, then same as work. · Always use the LCM method — it avoids fractions. · Alternate days: find work done in one 2-day cycle, then count full cycles. · In alternate-day questions, the last day may be partial — check who finishes it.

Trains, boats and streams, relative speed, late/early problems, races and circular tracks. · Basic: Distance = Speed × Time · Units: km/h × 5/18 = m/s; m/s × 18/5 = km/h · Relative speed: same direction: S₁ − S₂; opposite: S₁ + S₂ · Train crosses a pole / man: time = train length ÷ speed · Train crosses a platform / train: time = (L₁ + L₂) ÷ relative speed · Boats: downstream = u + v; upstream = u − v; u = (D + U)/2; v = (D − U)/2 · Late at s₁ by t₁, early at s₂ by t₂: D = s₁s₂(t₁ + t₂)/(s₂ − s₁) · After meeting, times t₁, t₂: S₁ : S₂ = √t₂ : √t₁ · Speed ratio a : b: time ratio b : a (same distance) · Circular track: first meeting = L ÷ relative speed; meet at start = LCM of lap times · Race: A beats B by x m in L m: B runs L − x while A runs L · Stoppage time per hour = (speed without stops − speed with stops)/speed without stops × 60 min. · Average speed for a round trip = 2xy/(x + y). · Convert km/h to m/s by ×5/18 — speeds like 36, 54, 72, 90 km/h become 10, 15, 20, 25 m/s. · In ‘late and early’ questions, the time difference is t₁ + t₂ (one late, one early) or |t₁ − t₂| (both late). · Train crossing a platform: add the platform length. · Boats: ‘against the stream’ = upstream.

x + 1/x type values, identities, a + b + c = 0, simplifying expressions, linear equations, quadratic roots. · Square identities: (a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b²; a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) · Cube identities: (a ± b)³ = a³ ± b³ ± 3ab(a ± b) · Sum / difference of cubes: a³ ± b³ = (a ± b)(a² ∓ ab + b²) · Three terms: (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2(ab + bc + ca) · a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc: = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca) · If a + b + c = 0: a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc · x + 1/x = k: x² + 1/x² = k² − 2; x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k · x − 1/x = k: x² + 1/x² = k² + 2; x³ − 1/x³ = k³ + 3k · x⁴ + 1/x⁴: = (x² + 1/x²)² − 2 · Special values: x + 1/x = 2 → x = 1; = −2 → x = −1; = 1 → x³ = −1; = √3 → x⁶ = −1 · Sum of squares = 0: a² + b² + c² = 0 (real) → a = b = c = 0 · a² + b² + c² = ab + bc + ca: → a = b = c · Quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0: sum of roots = −b/a; product = c/a; D = b² − 4ac · Linear pair: unique: a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂; none: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂; infinite: all equal · Remainder theorem: p(x) ÷ (x − a) leaves p(a) · Min / max of ax² + bx + c: at x = −b/2a; value = c − b²/4a · Degree check: in an expression that must be constant, terms of different degree cannot cancel. · Symmetric expressions: put easy values (a = b = c = 1, or x = 1) when the answer is a number. · Value putting: if a + b + c = 0, try a = 1, b = 1, c = −2 in the options. · x + 1/x = 3 → x² + 1/x² = 7 → x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = 47: build the ladder k, k² − 2, (k² − 2)² − 2. · x − 1/x squared gives x² + 1/x² − 2, so x² + 1/x² = k² + 2 (plus, not minus). · D < 0 means no real roots — not ‘roots equal’.

Triangle centres and their angles, similarity, Pythagoras, angle bisector, medians, special triangles. · Angle sum: A + B + C = 180°; exterior angle = sum of opposite interior angles · Side rule: sum of any two sides > third; difference < third · Pythagoras: c² = a² + b² (right); c² > a² + b² (obtuse); c² < a² + b² (acute) · Centroid (G): meets the medians; divides each in 2 : 1 from the vertex · Incentre (I): ∠BIC = 90° + A/2 (angle bisectors) · Excentre: ∠BEC = 90° − A/2 · Circumcentre (O): ∠BOC = 2A (perpendicular bisectors) · Orthocentre (H): ∠BHC = 180° − A (altitudes) · Median length: AD = ½√(2b² + 2c² − a²) · Apollonius: AB² + AC² = 2(AD² + BD²) · Angle bisector theorem: BD/DC = AB/AC · Areas: ½ × base × height; ½ab sin C; Heron √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) · Inradius / circumradius: r = Area/s; R = abc/(4 × Area) · Equilateral (side a): h = √3a/2; area = √3a²/4; R = a/√3; r = a/(2√3); R = 2r · Right triangle: R = hypotenuse/2; r = (a + b − c)/2; altitude to hypotenuse = ab/c · Similar triangles: area ratio = (side ratio)² · Special triangles: 30-60-90 → 1 : √3 : 2; 45-45-90 → 1 : 1 : √2 · Midpoint theorem: segment joining midpoints ∥ third side and half of it · Parallel lines with a transversal: alternate angles equal, corresponding equal, co-interior add to 180°. · In an equilateral triangle all four centres coincide. · Congruence: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS (not SSA, not AAA). · Centroid divides the triangle into 6 equal-area parts; a median halves the area. · If a figure is ‘any triangle’, draw an equilateral one and measure. · Area ratios of triangles with the same height = ratio of bases. · ∠BIC uses +A/2, the excentre −A/2 — don’t swap them. · Similarity gives side ratio; area needs its square.

Angles of regular polygons, number of diagonals, properties of rhombus/parallelogram/cyclic quadrilateral. · Interior angle sum: (n − 2) × 180° · Each exterior angle (regular): 360°/n; interior = 180° − 360°/n · Diagonals: n(n − 3)/2 · Parallelogram: area = base × height; d₁² + d₂² = 2(a² + b²) · Rhombus: area = d₁d₂/2; 4a² = d₁² + d₂² · Trapezium: area = ½(a + b)h · Square / rectangle diagonal: a√2 / √(l² + b²) · Regular hexagon: area = (3√3/2)a² (6 equilateral triangles) · Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum 180°; area = √((s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d)) · Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other; of a rhombus also at 90°; of a rectangle are equal. · Joining midpoints of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram with half the area. · Exterior angle = 360/n gives n quickly: exterior 24° → 15 sides. · Interior angle sum uses (n − 2), not n.

Tangent lengths, common tangents, chord distance, angles in segments, intersecting chords. · Angle at centre: = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc) · Semicircle: angle in a semicircle = 90° · Same segment: angles in the same segment are equal · Tangent: ⟂ radius at the point of contact; two tangents from a point are equal · Tangent length: √(d² − r²) · Direct common tangent: √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²) · Transverse common tangent: √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²) · Chord: perpendicular from centre bisects it; length = 2√(r² − p²) · Intersecting chords: AP × PB = CP × PD · Secant–tangent: PT² = PA × PB · Alternate segment: angle between tangent and chord = angle in the alternate segment · Touching circles: external: d = r₁ + r₂; internal: d = r₁ − r₂ · Common tangents: apart 4; touch outside 3; intersect 2; touch inside 1; one inside other 0 · Equal chords are equidistant from the centre. · The angle between two tangents from P and the angle at the centre add to 180°. · Common tangent questions: direct uses the DIFFERENCE of radii, transverse the SUM. · Angle at the centre doubles only for the SAME arc.

Slope, intercepts, area of triangle by a line with the axes, section formula, reflection. · Distance: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²) · Section (m : n internal): ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)) · Midpoint / centroid: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, …) / ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, …) · Area of triangle: ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|; = 0 → collinear · Slope: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); ax + by + c = 0 → m = −a/b · Parallel / perpendicular: m₁ = m₂ / m₁m₂ = −1 · Intercept form: x/a + y/b = 1 · Line ax + by = c with the axes: area = c²/(2|ab|) · Point to line: |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²) · Reflection: in x-axis (x, −y); y-axis (−x, y); origin (−x, −y); y = x → (y, x) · x-intercept: put y = 0; y-intercept: put x = 0. · Quadrants: I (+,+), II (−,+), III (−,−), IV (+,−). · For a line with the axes, find the two intercepts and use ½ × base × height. · Slope of ax + by + c = 0 is −a/b, not a/b.

Areas and perimeters, paths, sectors, % change in area, wheels, inscribed figures. · Rectangle / square: area lb, a²; perimeter 2(l + b), 4a; diagonal √(l² + b²), a√2 · Circle: area πr²; circumference 2πr · Semicircle: area πr²/2; perimeter πr + 2r · Sector: area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360)2πr · Ring: π(R² − r²) · Segment: sector − triangle · Isosceles triangle: area = (b/4)√(4a² − b²) (a = equal side) · Path outside a rectangle (width w): 2w(l + b + 2w) · Path inside a rectangle: 2w(l + b − 2w) · Two crossroads: w(l + b − w) · % change in area: sides change x % → 2x + x²/100 % · Wheel: revolutions = distance ÷ 2πr · Inscribed / circumscribed: circle in square r = a/2; square in circle a = r√2 (area 2r²) · Equilateral triangle and circle: incircle r = a/(2√3); circumcircle R = a/√3 · Area ratio of similar figures = (ratio of sides)². · Minute hand sweeps 6° per minute; hour hand 0.5° per minute. · π = 22/7 → choose radii that are multiples of 7. · Shaded-region questions: total − unshaded is usually faster. · Semicircle perimeter includes the diameter (πr + 2r). · Percentage change in area is not 2x — add x²/100.

Volumes and surface areas, melting and recasting, water flow, painted cubes, frustum. · Cube: V a³; TSA 6a²; LSA 4a²; diagonal a√3 · Cuboid: V lbh; TSA 2(lb + bh + hl); diagonal √(l² + b² + h²) · Cylinder: V πr²h; CSA 2πrh; TSA 2πr(r + h) · Cone: V ⅓πr²h; l = √(r² + h²); CSA πrl; TSA πr(l + r) · Sphere: V (4/3)πr³; SA 4πr² · Hemisphere: V (2/3)πr³; CSA 2πr²; TSA 3πr² · Frustum: V (πh/3)(R² + r² + Rr); CSA π(R + r)l; l = √(h² + (R − r)²) · Prism: V = base area × h; LSA = base perimeter × h · Pyramid: V = ⅓ × base area × h; LSA = ½ × perimeter × slant height · Regular tetrahedron: V = a³/(6√2) · Hollow cylinder: V = π(R² − r²)h · Melting & recasting: volume stays the same; number = big volume ÷ small volume · Painted cube cut into n³: 3 faces: 8; 2 faces: 12(n − 2); 1 face: 6(n − 2)²; none: (n − 2)³ · Water flow: volume per unit time = cross-section area × speed · Cone from a sector: sector radius = slant height; arc length = 2πr of base · Cylinder, cone, hemisphere of same radius and height = r: volumes 3 : 1 : 2. · Sphere in a cube: diameter = side. · Scale factor k on all lengths → area ×k², volume ×k³. · Keep π symbolic until the end — it often cancels. · CSA vs TSA: read whether the top/bottom is included (open tank, hollow pipe). · Frustum slant uses (R − r), not (R + r).

Values of standard angles, identities, complementary angles, max–min, value putting. · Ratios: sin = P/H, cos = B/H, tan = P/B; cosec, sec, cot are reciprocals · Values: sin 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° = 0, ½, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 (cos in reverse) · tan values: tan 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° = 0, 1/√3, 1, √3; tan 90° undefined · Identities: sin² + cos² = 1; sec² − tan² = 1; cosec² − cot² = 1 · sec + tan = x: sec − tan = 1/x (same for cosec + cot) · sin + cos = x: sin θ cos θ = (x² − 1)/2 · Higher powers: sin⁴ + cos⁴ = 1 − 2s²c²; sin⁶ + cos⁶ = 1 − 3s²c² · Complementary: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ; tan(90° − θ) = cot θ; sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ · A + B = 90°: tan A tan B = 1; sin²A + sin²B = 1 · Max / min: a sin θ + b cos θ: ±√(a² + b²); a sin²θ + b cos²θ: between a and b; a tan²θ + b cot²θ: min 2√(ab) · Compound: sin(A ± B) = sAcB ± cAsB; cos(A ± B) = cAcB ∓ sAsB; tan(A ± B) = (tA ± tB)/(1 ∓ tAtB) · Double angle: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ; cos 2θ = 1 − 2sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1 · A + B = 45°: (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 2 · Allied (ASTC): All, Sin, Tan, Cos positive in quadrants I–IV · Special: tan 15° = 2 − √3; tan 75° = 2 + √3; sin 18° = (√5 − 1)/4 · Radians: π rad = 180°; 1 rad ≈ 57.3° · Every ratio depends only on the angle, not the triangle size. · sin and cos lie between −1 and 1; sec and cosec are never between −1 and 1. · Value putting: numbers in the options → put θ = 0° or 45°; ratios in the options → put 30° or 60°. · Given one ratio, draw the right triangle using a triplet (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 7-24-25, 8-15-17). · sin²30° + cos²60° = ½ (different angles) — the identity needs the SAME angle. · Never put 45° when options contain both tan and cot — they tie.

Tower with one or two angles, moving observer, shadows, angles of depression. · Basic: tan θ = height ÷ distance · Ratios h : d: 30° → 1 : √3; 45° → 1 : 1; 60° → √3 : 1 · Two angles, same side: h = x/(cot α − cot β) · 30° → 60° by walking x: h = (√3/2)x; remaining distance = x/2 · Complementary angles from a and b: h = √(ab) · Shadow: shadow = h cot θ; shadow = height at 45° · Depression: angle of depression = angle of elevation (alternate angles) · Angles are measured from the horizontal line through the observer’s eye. · Draw the triangle and write the side ratio straight from the 30-60-90 / 45-45-90 pattern. · Two ships on opposite sides: ADD the distances; same side: subtract.

Mean, median, mode of raw and grouped data, range, variance and standard deviation (Tier 2). · Mean: Σx/n; grouped: Σfx/Σf · Median (raw): odd n: ((n + 1)/2)th term; even n: average of (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th (sort first) · Mode: most frequent value · Empirical relation: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean · Range: maximum − minimum · Variance: σ² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n = Σx²/n − x̄² · Standard deviation: σ = √variance · Grouped median: L + ((N/2 − cf)/f) × h · Grouped mode: L + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × h · Coefficient of variation: σ/x̄ × 100 · First n natural numbers: mean (n + 1)/2; variance (n² − 1)/12 · Adding k to every value: mean + k, median + k, SD unchanged. · Multiplying every value by k: mean × k, SD × |k|, variance × k². · Median questions: always arrange in order first — options are often built from the unsorted middle. · Variance changes by k², SD by |k| when values are multiplied by k.

Coins, dice, cards, balls from a bag (Tier 2). · Probability: P = favourable ÷ total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1 · Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) · Addition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) · Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) · Combinations: ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!) · Coins / dice: n coins: 2ⁿ outcomes; n dice: 6ⁿ outcomes · Two dice: sum 7 has 6 ways (most likely); sums 2 and 12 have 1 way each. · Cards: 52 = 4 suits × 13; 26 red, 26 black; 12 face cards; 4 aces. · ‘At least one’ → 1 − P(none). · Face cards are J, Q, K only (12) — aces are not face cards.

Tables, bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts: percentages, ratios, averages, growth. · Percentage share: part ÷ total × 100 · Pie chart: angle = value ÷ total × 360°; 1 % = 3.6° · Growth %: (new − old) ÷ old × 100 · Average: total ÷ number of years/items · Ratio: compare two values; simplify by common factors · Difference of percentages: use the same base before comparing · Read the units and the scale before calculating (thousands, lakhs, %). · ‘By what percent more’ uses the second value as the base. · Approximate and pick the nearest option — DI options are usually far apart. · Convert pie-chart degrees to percent with ÷3.6 only when needed; ratios work directly on degrees. · Percentage growth from year 1 to year 3 is not the sum of yearly growth rates.
